Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The Critical levers address the central tensions of the plan: detection credibility versus exposure and cost (Identity Trust Anchor, Inspector Presence, Zone Geometry and Filtering), empirical defensibility versus realism (Challenge Exercises), and continuity versus obstruction without a casting vote (Deadlock and Suspension). High levers cover ledger integrity, parity measurement, vendor binding, entry gating, counterintelligence and verdict thresholds. No major dimension is missing, though an explicit staffing and surge-capacity lever is absent.

Decision 1: Equipment Identity Trust Anchor

Lever ID: a3421ed3-ab90-4c56-9cd2-07f23e2a35da

The Core Decision: Sets the evidentiary hierarchy the Intake Protocol uses to conclude that a unit in controlled staging is the declared unit. It drives inspector shift counts, staging-area layout, accredited examiner demand and the false-negative profile for substituted equipment. Success is measured by equipment-identity confidence in blind challenges, intake time per unit and the share of units resolved without escalation to unverifiable status.

Why It Matters: This sets which evidence layer carries the most weight when the Intake Protocol decides that a unit in staging is the unit declared. Leaning on cryptographic attestation scales across many units but depends on vendor cooperation and key custody. Leaning on physical marks and witnessed movement is slower and more labor-intensive but less exposed to a single compromised vendor or firmware chain, and it directly shapes inspector headcount and staging-area design.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Anchor identity primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation validated independently by accredited examiners from both countries, using physical inspection and customs records as corroborating layers at intake.
  2. Anchor identity primarily on physical inspection and witnessed movement in controlled staging areas, treating attestation, customs records and maintenance logs as layers that can raise or lower confidence but never settle it alone.
  3. Apply bilateral tamper-evident tags jointly in the staging area by both mirrored teams, so identity continuity rests on markers neither country's manufacturers or logistics firms controlled before arrival.

Trade-Off / Risk: Attestation scales but concentrates trust in vendor keys and firmware; physical anchoring resists that failure yet multiplies inspector shifts and staging time, so the choice quietly determines both staffing cost and the single-source-failure profile.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Opening Inventory Baseline and Starting-State Seal, since a trusted anchor lets baseline units be re-identified consistently, and Departure Disposition Evidence Ladder, since the same identity method supports witnessed destruction and transfer records.

Conflict: Trades off against Inspector Presence and Rotation Model: physical anchoring demands resident shift coverage and staging time, while attestation reliance shifts cost to Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism and vendor key cooperation.

Justification: Critical, Central hub: it sets the evidentiary hierarchy for intake, which drives inspector shifts, staging design, vendor dependence and the false-negative profile for substitution. It feeds baseline and exit evidence and trades directly against Inspector Presence and Vendor Binding.

Decision 2: Inspector Presence and Rotation Model

Lever ID: 1cc2d357-5ce9-4e5f-a937-f7cb5e021cf6

The Core Decision: Determines when and how mirrored inspectors are physically present: continuous residence, event-triggered response or randomized rotation. It sets workforce size, shift and leave coverage, exposure to unreported events and the cumulative risk to individual inspectors. Success is measured by detection rate for unreported arrivals, response-window compliance, delayed-access incidents and staffing cost against the personnel envelope.

Why It Matters: This determines whether inspectors sit continuously at sites, arrive on event notification, or move on randomized schedules. Continuous presence maximizes detection of unreported arrivals but enlarges the counterintelligence surface and the shift-coverage workforce. Event-triggered presence is cheaper and less intrusive but depends on the operator reporting the event, which is exactly what the unreported-arrival exercise tests.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Station resident mirrored teams at every participating site on continuous shift coverage, confined to bounded inspection zones with escorted movement and filtered evidence handling.
  2. Deploy inspectors on operator notification within fixed response windows, supplementing with filtered remote evidence and unannounced spot visits to test whether declarations are complete.
  3. Rotate inspectors across sites on randomized schedules with no repeat assignment to the same zone in succession, limiting relationship capture, site familiarity and cumulative exposure of any one inspector.

Trade-Off / Risk: Resident teams give the strongest detection but concentrate espionage risk and cost; notification-based models are cheaper yet rest on the operator honesty being tested, and random rotation erodes the site knowledge inspectors need to spot anomalies.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring, since presence mode decides which unreported-arrival events can be detected, and strengthens Equipment Identity Trust Anchor when physical inspection and witnessed movement carry identity decisions.

Conflict: Conflicts with Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture, because continuous presence enlarges the espionage surface, and with the inspector and security budget envelopes, where resident teams compete with other funding needs.

Justification: Critical, Controls the detection-versus-espionage-exposure-versus-cost trade-off and sets workforce size, shift coverage and unreported-arrival detectability. It connects to identity anchoring, exercises, counterintelligence, exit witnessing and the budget envelopes.

Decision 3: Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics

Lever ID: 213da8e6-7982-4d9e-bd77-042854f828cb

The Core Decision: Defines how a contested site finding is resolved without a casting vote, and which enumerated events suspend a site or the whole test. Scope covers deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension states, escalation timers, and resumption conditions. Success metrics: unresolved discrepancy age, time from trigger to suspension, share of triggers later judged spurious, and absence of any unilateral override path.

Why It Matters: This defines what happens when co-chairs cannot agree on a site finding, and which events suspend the test without any chair action. Automatic triggers protect against one side stalling to shield an operator but can be gamed by manufactured incidents. Defaulting to the status quo keeps the pilot running but lets a blocked finding age, which is itself a tracked KPI and a Stop-criterion risk.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Define enumerated objective triggers that suspend a site automatically, with resumption requiring double-key authorization and a documented corrective action from the responsible government.
  2. Hold the status quo on deadlock but start escalating timers that move the dispute from co-chair level to designated principals, with unresolved findings reported as aging discrepancies.
  3. Convene paired technical referees from both countries to issue dual-signed advisory fact statements, with deadlock defaulting to heightened inspection and impaired-confidence status instead of suspension.

Trade-Off / Risk: Automatic suspension prevents one side from stalling but invites manufactured triggers; status-quo defaults protect continuity yet reward delay, so neither design removes the underlying incentive to obstruct a finding.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration by turning evidence thresholds into objective trigger definitions, and gives Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism enforcement force, since a shielded or refusing operator has a defined suspension consequence.

Conflict: Automatic triggers can be set off by seeded scenarios, so they collide with Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring unless exercise events are excluded; heavy escalation timers also slow resolution of Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting Method disputes.

Justification: Critical, Controls the core governance tension between continuity and obstruction without a casting vote. It converts evidence thresholds and parity trip points into consequences, enforces vendor and operator duties, and determines whether blocked findings age into a Stop condition.

Decision 4: Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring

Lever ID: 71663499-b57e-4749-ab29-21230bb34c8e

The Core Decision: Governs who authors, injects and scores live challenges for unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal and reluctant operators. The aim is a Go/Modify/Stop basis that neither government can later contest. Success metrics: blind-detection rate by event type, false positives and negatives, scoring-criteria agreement before injection, and zero disruption to active computation.

Why It Matters: This controls who designs and injects the live challenges, and how detection results are scored so neither government can later dispute the outcome. Independent seeding yields credible blind-detection data but needs careful containment so staging, spare-inventory and maintenance areas are not disrupted. Pre-committed scenarios make scoring defensible but constrain adaptive tests that might expose unanticipated weaknesses.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Have independent testers design and inject blind scenarios in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas, unknown to operating inspectors and scored against jointly agreed detection criteria.
  2. Have each country's red team challenge the counterpart's inspectorate at the other's site, using reciprocal adversarial exercises so both detection capability and access parity are tested in a single event.
  3. Publish cryptographic commitments to a sealed catalog of challenge scenarios before Phase One, then reveal and score them afterward so neither government can redefine success post hoc.

Trade-Off / Risk: Independent seeding gives credible blind results but cannot fully replicate a determined state adversary; sealed catalogs make scoring defensible while constraining adaptive tests, so the Go decision may rest on scenarios anticipated in advance.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies the empirical test for Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design and Equipment Identity Trust Anchor, showing whether filtered evidence still catches substitution, and feeds Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration with defensible detection data.

Conflict: Sealed or pre-committed scenarios limit adaptive testing, trading realism against defensibility; injecting blind challenges also risks tripping Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics triggers and straining Inspector Presence and Rotation Model coverage during staging and maintenance windows.

Justification: Critical, Produces the only empirical evidence for the Go/Modify/Stop verdict and validates filtering, identity and presence choices. It sits between realism and defensibility and interacts with suspension triggers, coverage and thresholds.

Decision 5: Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design

Lever ID: 2d8049b3-25c0-44b9-be65-c968e82934b5

The Core Decision: Specifies physical boundaries for inspector access and the reduction of raw records, sensor outputs and telemetry before data leaves the host site. It protects workloads, model weights, topology, security architecture and source code while retaining enough evidence to establish identity. Success metrics: IP or cybersecurity incidents, identity-confidence scores under filtering, operator acceptance, and filter-adequacy results from challenge exercises.

Why It Matters: Sets where inspectors may stand, what they may see, and how raw sensor or record data is reduced before leaving the host site. Tight zones and heavy filtering protect workloads, topology and source code, but every filtered field removes corroborating detail and raises the odds that identity confidence falls short. Looser zones improve evidence quality at the expense of the operator's willingness to participate.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Fix physical inspection zones to staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas with painted and access-controlled boundaries, and admit only inspector-carried instruments that have been pre-validated.
  2. Run an operator-operated redaction gateway that converts raw records and telemetry into schema-limited evidence packets, with the counterpart's engineers auditing the gateway rules but not its inputs.
  3. Have each side's cleared engineers design the filters that will be applied at the counterpart's sites, so the party most worried about leakage writes the rules and the host executes them.

Trade-Off / Risk: Filters designed by the exposed party minimize leakage but can quietly strip the very fields needed to detect substitution, so filter adequacy must be tested by challenge exercises rather than asserted.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism by giving operators and vendors credible containment guarantees, and supports Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture by defining what information can cross national boundaries at all.

Conflict: Tighter zones and heavier filtering reduce evidence available to Equipment Identity Trust Anchor and Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration, raising false-negative and unverifiable-equipment risk; looser zones instead erode operator willingness and Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture.

Justification: Critical, Controls the fundamental tension between protecting sensitive assets and retaining enough evidence to detect substitution. It determines operator willingness, identity confidence, false negatives and unverifiable equipment, and is a hub across binding, counterintelligence and verdict levers.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Matched Site Equivalence Basis

Lever ID: f2b187bc-f45f-463a-a734-daa54f767583

The Core Decision: Defines the yardstick for 'matched' declared datacenters and thereby the baseline against which reciprocal-access parity is scored. The choice determines whether the pilot tests verification activity, legal and commercial friction, or an idealized interface. Success is measured by the parity disputes avoided, how defensible the pairing is to both national authorities, and how well Phase One findings transfer to operating sites.

Why It Matters: This defines what 'matched' means when selecting the small set of declared datacenters, and therefore what reciprocal-access parity is measured against. Matching by function keeps the test about verification activity rather than capacity, but invites disputes over whether a staging area in one country is comparable to one in the other. Purpose-built interfaces lower exposure of production halls but narrow what the pilot can say about real operating sites.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Match sites by verification function, pairing staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas across countries so that parity is judged on equivalent inspection activity rather than equivalent compute.
  2. Match sites by operator type and ownership model, pairing commercial with commercial and state-run with state-run facilities, and accept uneven scale as the price of comparable legal and commercial friction.
  3. Build dedicated bonded staging annexes beside participating datacenters in both countries, so every declared equipment flow passes through an identical-by-design verification interface before reaching production halls.

Trade-Off / Risk: Functional matching makes parity measurable but hides scale asymmetries, while purpose-built annexes give clean symmetry at the cost of testing a controlled artifact rather than the messy operating facilities Phase One is meant to represent.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting Method, which needs a stable definition of equivalence to count access, and supports Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design by fixing which zones are comparable.

Conflict: Constrains Entry Gate Certification and Appropriation Release Order, because purpose-built annexes or contested pairings delay site selection and site preparation spending, and strains Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring where realism is reduced.

Justification: Medium, Defines the yardstick for parity and comparable zones, enabling Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting. Important for defensibility, but it is largely a selection-time choice and mostly feeds other levers rather than controlling core trade-offs.

Decision 7: Ledger Synchronization and Divergence Doctrine

Lever ID: bd7671a4-4f75-4033-876d-b6da5078c203

The Core Decision: Specifies how the two national ledger copies remain independently verifiable yet reconcilable within a bounded delay, including checkpoint format, cadence, transport and the mismatch response. It governs how quickly tampering or error is detected and how large the reconciliation workload becomes. Success is measured by synchronization latency, divergence detection time, reconciliation time and the count of unresolved divergences.

Why It Matters: This fixes how the two national ledger copies stay independently verifiable while remaining reconcilable within a bounded delay. Tighter synchronization shrinks the window in which one side can alter records but increases network exposure between national secure systems. Looser or offline synchronization reduces cyber risk but lengthens divergence-detection time and raises the reconciliation workload that feeds the Stop criterion on unresolved divergence.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Record events locally at once on each national copy and exchange signed hash-chain checkpoints over a dedicated authenticated link at fixed intervals, triggering formal reconciliation on any mismatch.
  2. Exchange checkpoint digests only, with no event content, through an escrow held by a mutually accepted neutral custodian, so either side can prove after the fact that its copy was not rewritten.
  3. Synchronize by air-gapped physical media carried by paired mirrored couriers on a fixed schedule, accepting longer divergence-detection windows in exchange for no live connection between national systems.

Trade-Off / Risk: A neutral digest custodian strengthens non-repudiation but introduces a third party into a strictly bilateral design, and offline courier sync removes network risk while making the bounded-latency KPI harder to meet.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics with a defined divergence trigger for impaired-confidence and automatic suspension, and supports Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration by giving a trustworthy evidence record.

Conflict: Trades off against Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture, since tighter synchronization widens network exposure between national secure systems, and against the bounded-latency KPI when offline couriers or neutral escrow lengthen detection windows.

Justification: High, Governs tamper-evidence, divergence detection and reconciliation workload, supplying the trigger for impaired-confidence suspension and the Stop criterion on unresolved divergence. It trades cyber exposure against latency, but is narrower in reach than the hub levers.

Decision 8: Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism

Lever ID: 53d3ae18-4058-41e6-9a09-d2e16db7abcd

The Core Decision: Governs how reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation duties reach manufacturers, maintenance providers and logistics firms through contracts, eligibility registries or shared examination centers. It determines vendor-refusal outcomes, supply continuity and the evidence available when a critical vendor withholds cooperation. Success is measured by binding coverage of declared equipment flows, refusal resolution time, compensation cost and unverifiable-equipment counts.

Why It Matters: This decides how reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation duties are pushed from operators down to manufacturers, maintenance providers and logistics firms. Binding through supplier eligibility is durable but may remove critical vendors from the pilot entirely. Shared accredited examination facilities preserve vendor secrets and widen the evidence pool but add capital cost and a new facility to protect.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require operators to flow verification duties into every vendor contract, with each government compelling its own operators and charging resulting compensation against its own contribution.
  2. Establish a pre-qualified vendor registry so only suppliers who have accepted verification terms may service declared sites, making refusal a supply-eligibility event rather than a bilateral dispute.
  3. Operate shared accredited clean-room examination centers where refusing vendors submit units for supervised testing, producing filtered evidence without exposing source code, firmware or design details.

Trade-Off / Risk: A registry makes refusal costly but may exclude the vendors whose equipment matters most; clean-room centers keep those vendors in play yet add a high-value target whose security burden falls on the very envelopes funding inspection.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Covered-Equipment Schedule Abstraction Ladder and Equipment Identity Trust Anchor, because bound vendors supply the identifiers, attestations and maintenance records needed to apply schedule categories and corroborate identity.

Conflict: Constrains Entry Gate Certification and Appropriation Release Order, as vendor binding must finish before Phase One starts, and competes with Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture when clean-room centers add a high-value target.

Justification: High, Determines vendor-refusal outcomes and unverifiable-equipment counts, which can fail a site outright. It enables schedule and identity evidence, and binds entry-gate timing, but its effect is concentrated on a single failure pathway.

Decision 9: Covered-Equipment Schedule Abstraction Ladder

Lever ID: 26c8332c-6546-4970-84be-0bdaebf704f9

The Core Decision: Sets how abstractly the confidential, versioned technical schedule defines frontier-relevant equipment so that it outlives any manufacturer, product or architecture. It determines boundary-case handling, update cadence and who may change definitions. Success metrics: share of boundary cases resolved within an agreed time (TBD), schedule-version change latency, count of unlisted devices discovered, and absence of vendor-specific anchors.

Why It Matters: Determines whether the confidential technical schedule describes covered equipment by functional role, by performance tier, or by operator declaration. A role-based schedule resists obsolescence and avoids tying the regime to any manufacturer or architecture, but needs specialist judgment at every boundary case. A looser schedule is easier to agree on but widens the gap through which unlisted equipment can arrive unseen.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Define covered equipment by functional role, such as any device performing accelerated parallel computation, and let accountable specialists on both sides revise the role definitions through versioned, double-key schedule updates.
  2. Adopt a tiered schedule with core, watch and exempt categories, where items migrate between tiers at fixed review points and each migration is recorded in the ledger with a justification.
  3. Hold the exact classification thresholds in split escrow between the two national specialist groups, so inspectors verify equipment against a classification result without ever seeing the underlying thresholds.

Trade-Off / Risk: A schedule abstract enough to survive hardware generations may be too vague to adjudicate at the margin, and a sealed threshold regime invites each side to suspect the other of tuning it.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Gives Equipment Identity Trust Anchor a stable classification target and makes Opening Inventory Baseline and Starting-State Seal comparable across hardware generations, so intake and exit records share one definition of covered equipment.

Conflict: A more abstract schedule needs specialist judgment that strains Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture, since classification thresholds are sensitive, and it can complicate Matched Site Equivalence Basis when each side's declared equipment maps differently onto roles.

Justification: Medium, Provides the stable classification target that keeps the regime vendor-neutral and durable. Useful and connected to identity and baseline, but a mandated design requirement with fewer open trade-offs and limited effect within a 90-day test.

Decision 10: Entry Gate Certification and Appropriation Release Order

Lever ID: 2e34687c-0915-4e1c-8571-953b896a8dba

The Core Decision: Determines how the mandatory entry conditions (signed instrument, appropriations, domestic access authority, site selection, inspector approval, operator and vendor participation, provisional schedule) are certified, and how each USD 2.5 billion contribution is released before the 90-day clock starts. Success metrics: funding timeliness, certification completeness at clock start, matched cumulative disbursement, and time lost to single-condition stalls.

Why It Matters: Controls how the mandatory entry conditions are certified and how the two USD 2.5 billion contributions flow before the 90-day clock starts. Strict single-gate certification prevents a half-ready start but can stall the whole program on the slowest condition. Staged certification with tranche release speeds visible progress, yet creates partial commitments that a government could abandon after the other has already spent.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require one simultaneous gate in which every entry condition is certified by both co-chairs before any operational funds beyond preparation are released and before the Phase One clock starts.
  2. Certify entry conditions individually with joint countersignature, and release each national contribution in matched tranches so neither side's cumulative disbursement leads the other's.
  3. Place both appropriations in a reciprocal escrow whose release is triggered by a single ledger event signed by both national copies, making funding timeliness itself a verifiable gate output.

Trade-Off / Risk: Matched tranches protect against one-sided exposure, but they also give each government a visible, low-cost way to stall by delaying a single certification while appearing compliant.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Provides a verified clean start for Opening Inventory Baseline and Starting-State Seal and Matched Site Equivalence Basis, because sites, schedule and funds are fixed before baselining, which also gives Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting Method a fair opening position.

Conflict: A strict single gate delays deployment of Inspector Presence and Rotation Model, which needs funded, cleared staff early; staged tranche release conflicts with Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics by letting a government stall while appearing compliant.

Justification: High, Governs how mandatory entry conditions and the USD 2.5 billion contributions are certified before the clock starts, tied to funding timeliness and a Stop trigger. It is a precondition lever with significant timing conflicts, but is largely one-time.

Decision 11: Departure Disposition Evidence Ladder

Lever ID: 2089051f-2718-4437-854f-e03ef413d4ce

The Core Decision: Defines the proof tier each of the five Exit Protocol dispositions must reach before the ledger records closure, and the exact wording that marks where Consortium knowledge ends. Key metrics: share of departures with a closed disposition, count and age of unresolved dispositions, witness-hours consumed per departure, and zero entries implying tracking beyond the agreed boundary. Penalties for vague or deviating declarations should be set.

Why It Matters: Defines how much proof each Exit Protocol disposition requires and how the boundary of knowledge is stated once equipment leaves. Strong evidence for destruction and disablement raises inspector workload and facility needs. Weak evidence for release beyond the boundary risks overstating what the Consortium knows, which undermines the explicit limit of the program's claims.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Set an evidence ladder in which witnessed destruction and verified permanent disablement each require two mirrored witnesses plus residual-material or state sampling before the ledger may record closure.
  2. Require operators to pre-declare the intended disposition path before any removal, so any deviation between declared and observed path triggers an automatic unresolved-disposition entry.
  3. Treat every release beyond the monitored system as a hard boundary event, recording a sealed handover and then marking the item permanently out of scope without any later tracking claims.

Trade-Off / Risk: Rigorous destruction witnessing consumes scarce mirrored-team capacity during surge periods, and a pre-declared path rewards operators who declare vaguely, so the ladder needs a defined penalty for unresolved cases.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Builds on Equipment Identity Trust Anchor, since exit witnesses can only close a disposition if the departing item matches its intake identity, and relies on Ledger Synchronization and Divergence Doctrine so closure entries stay consistent across both national copies.

Conflict: Competes with Inspector Presence and Rotation Model for scarce mirrored witness capacity during surges, and residual-material sampling presses against Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design by requiring closer access to removed equipment.

Justification: Low, Tactical refinement of the Exit Protocol that depends on the identity anchor and ledger doctrine. It affects witness capacity during surges but does not control a foundational trade-off for the Phase One verdict.

Decision 12: Counterintelligence and Compartmentation Posture

Lever ID: 3b7b12d2-cad3-43bb-b4f5-034c46d06631

The Core Decision: Sets the shielding rules that keep inspectors, evidence handlers and secure facilities from becoming a collection channel for the counterpart government, and thereby protects host consent. Scope covers personnel segregation, device controls, evidence-handling spaces and insider-threat testing. Success metrics: IP or cybersecurity incidents, time to reconcile compartmented findings, inspector-context loss in substitution cases, and host-government confidence in the regime.

Why It Matters: Establishes how inspectors, evidence systems and secure facilities are shielded from espionage while inspectors hold sensitive visibility at the counterpart's sites. Heavy compartmentation limits exposure but isolates teams, slows reconciliation and raises staffing needs. Light compartmentation speeds work and trust-building yet increases the risk that the inspectorate becomes a collection channel, which could cause the host government to withdraw consent.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Compartment inspectors by site and by event type, with no individual holding cross-site knowledge, supported by rotation schedules and device-free secure facilities for all evidence handling.
  2. Embed a standing host-side counterintelligence liaison at each site who reviews inspector notes and outputs before release, with the counterpart's reciprocal liaison reviewing the same class of material.
  3. Fund a jointly authorized insider-threat red cell that attempts to compromise inspectors and evidence handlers on both sides, with findings feeding directly into the audit record and suspension criteria.

Trade-Off / Risk: Compartmentation that is strict enough to reassure the host may fragment the very context inspectors need to recognize a substitution, and a joint red cell requires trust that the regime has yet to earn.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Reinforces Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design, because compartment boundaries and physical zone limits protect the same sensitive assets, and supports Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism by making escort and confidentiality obligations credible to hosts.

Conflict: Strict siloing conflicts with Inspector Presence and Rotation Model, since rotation and site-bound knowledge fragment continuity, and it slows Ledger Synchronization and Divergence Doctrine reconciliation when compartmented findings must be cleared before comparison.

Justification: High, Protects host consent and constrains inspector presence, ledger synchronization and schedule specialists. It governs the exposure-versus-context trade-off with many conflicts, but is largely a constraint on the more central detection levers.

Decision 13: Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration

Lever ID: b420a001-5aa3-44a2-8507-76b5a0d5a1bc

The Core Decision: Fixes how Go, Modify and Stop are defined and defended so that verdicts rest on evidence sufficiency rather than political preference. Covers threshold-setting method, provisional-figure labeling, validation of detection-rate assumptions, and the rule mapping outcomes to verdicts. Success metrics: share of thresholds with a documented validation method, number of post-start threshold changes, and scoring divergence between national teams at verdict time.

Why It Matters: Establishes how the Go, Modify and Stop thresholds are set and defended, and how evidence of sufficiency is separated from either government's political preference. Thresholds fixed in advance reduce post-hoc bargaining but may rest on unvalidated assumptions about detection rates. Thresholds calibrated during the test are better grounded, though they open the door to goalposts moving after results appear.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Pre-register every Go, Modify and Stop threshold before the clock starts, marking each unsupported figure provisional, with a documented validation method and a fixed rule for how outcomes map to verdicts.
  2. Calibrate thresholds against a baseline of early blind exercises and then freeze them before the scored exercises, with the calibration and freezing steps both recorded in the ledger.
  3. Have each national team score the evidence independently and sealed, then compare, so the size and direction of scoring divergence becomes a reported measure alongside the verdict itself.

Trade-Off / Risk: Pre-registration guards against moving the goalposts, but locking thresholds before any real detection data exists risks encoding guesses that either force an unwarranted Modify or hide a genuine weakness.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Draws its empirical grounding from Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring, whose blind-challenge results validate thresholds, and converts Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting Method trip points into defined verdict conditions rather than ad hoc judgments.

Conflict: Pre-registered thresholds must be locked under Entry Gate Certification and Appropriation Release Order before real detection data exists, while calibrating inside Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring risks moving goalposts; the two cannot both be satisfied fully.

Justification: High, Determines whether the Go/Modify/Stop outcome rests on evidence rather than politics, balancing pre-registration against calibration. It consumes exercise data and parity trip points, but is downstream of the levers that produce evidence.

Decision 14: Opening Inventory Baseline and Starting-State Seal

Lever ID: 5ec44ee7-e60c-4d2e-9b0d-6a4d3ca0a070

The Core Decision: Establishes the zero point against which every later arrival, removal and maintenance change is read, without becoming a capacity estimate. Choice governs how much of each operator's installed base is exposed, and how confidently early discrepancies can be interpreted. Metrics: share of declared zones with a sealed count, baseline-related discrepancies per site, time to seal, and explicit disclosure of any unverified starting population in reports.

Why It Matters: Because Phase One verifies changes rather than total capacity, this lever decides how the starting state of each site is established so that later changes have a reference point. A full opening census gives clearer change detection but exposes more of each operator's installed base. A thin or progressive baseline limits exposure but leaves early discrepancies harder to interpret and may let pre-existing undeclared items persist unseen.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Seal a declared opening inventory at each site through a joint count of covered-equipment categories within the declared zones, and treat it as the zero point for all later changes.
  2. Accept each operator's self-declared inventory without a count and verify only changes after entry, stating explicitly in every report that the starting population is unverified.
  3. Build the baseline progressively, verifying each item only when a maintenance or movement event first touches it, so coverage grows without a full opening census.

Trade-Off / Risk: A progressive baseline protects operator secrecy and avoids an intrusive census, but it leaves long periods where the covered population is unknown, which weakens the credibility of a Go conclusion within a 90-day window.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Covered-Equipment Schedule Abstraction Ladder, which defines the categories to be counted, and Matched Site Equivalence Basis, which keeps the starting-state seals comparable across the two countries' sites.

Conflict: A full census strains Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design by exposing more installed base, and heightens operator reluctance under Vendor and Operator Binding Mechanism; a thin baseline instead weakens change-detection credibility.

Justification: Medium, Sets the reference point for change detection and trades operator exposure against early discrepancy interpretability. Dependent on the schedule and site matching, with moderate connectivity, and secondary to the intake and presence choices.

Decision 15: Reciprocal Access Parity Accounting Method

Lever ID: 2f26510b-2612-4944-a42d-4d71d11be910

The Core Decision: Defines operationally what reciprocal access means and how it is measured, since parity underpins both the Go and Stop conditions and triggers impaired-confidence review. Scope covers the unit of comparison, tolerance bands, reason-coded denials and delays, and how non-identical sites are normalized. Metrics: parity variance between matched sites, count and age of unexplained denials, and time from trip point to review.

Why It Matters: This lever defines what 'reciprocal access' means in operation and how it is measured, since parity drives the Go and Stop conditions. Counting access events is simple and auditable but can be satisfied with low-value access, while measuring outcomes captures real verification capability but requires comparable test conditions. The chosen method also determines when impaired-confidence procedures are triggered.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Count parity by matched events, requiring that each entry, inspector-hour and evidence request granted at one country's site be mirrored at its counterpart within a jointly set tolerance.
  2. Measure parity by outcome, comparing the detection performance and evidence sufficiency each side achieves at its matched site in blind challenges rather than the amount of access granted.
  3. Keep a standing parity ledger that logs every denial, delay and filter with a reason code, and tie jointly set trip points in it to automatic impaired-confidence review.

Trade-Off / Risk: Outcome-based parity is the more meaningful measure, but it depends on exercise comparability across non-identical sites, so a disputed comparison can stall the very Go decision the metric is meant to support.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics with objective trip points for impaired-confidence and automatic suspension, and depends on Matched Site Equivalence Basis to make site comparisons defensible.

Conflict: Outcome-based parity requires comparable trials from Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring across non-identical sites, and disputed comparisons can stall Verdict Evidence Sufficiency and Threshold Calibration, delaying the very decision parity is meant to support.

Justification: High, Defines how reciprocal access, a Go and Stop condition, is measured and supplies objective trip points for impaired-confidence review. It links site matching, exercises, suspension and verdict, with disputes able to stall the decision.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Very high. A first-of-kind bilateral US–China verification inspectorate with USD 5 billion (user constraint, 50/50), full-time mirrored national teams, a replicated tamper-evident ledger and double-key governance. Scale is bounded by design: a small matched set of declared sites, change verification only, and a 90-day Phase One operational test that starts only after mandatory entry conditions are met.

Risk and Novelty: Highly novel and adversarial. There is no trust, legal symmetry or willingness to expose sensitive technology. Main risks: espionage and counterintelligence exposure, IP leakage, vendor refusal, operator shielding, manufactured incidents, ledger divergence and asymmetric access. The Go/Modify/Stop decision must be hard for either government to contest later, so evidence credibility is the dominant concern.

Complexity and Constraints: High operational complexity. Staffing is modelled from site count, shift coverage, mirrored teams, separation of duties, leave and surge, with no single-person critical functions. Required: layered evidence with no single decisive source, deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures, blind live exercises without disrupting active compute, and a KPI dashboard covering detection, parity, latency, divergence and fiscal timeliness. Fixed budget envelopes and a short 90-day clock constrain design choices.

Domain and Tone: Sovereign public-sector national-security verification program. Formal, adversarial-realist and governance-heavy; explicitly not a business, nonprofit or governance regime. Physical, in-person work at declared datacenters, supported by secure digital ledger and attestation systems.

Holistic Profile: A high-ambition, high-risk, trust-free bilateral verification test whose value depends on credible, hard-to-contest evidence of detection capability and reciprocal access within a short 90-day window. It favours strong physical presence, blind and adversarial testing, objective suspension triggers and layered evidence over cost minimisation or political comfort.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Pioneer's Gambit

Strategic Logic: Maximizes detection power and reciprocal-access testing from Month 0 (2026-10-12) by pairing continuous resident mirrored presence with attestation-anchored identity, automatic suspension triggers and adversarial reciprocal red-teaming. Accepts higher cost, vendor-key concentration, espionage exposure and the risk of manufactured triggers in exchange for the most demanding evidence base for a Go, Modify or Stop decision. Filter adequacy and attestation integrity must be proven by the exercises themselves rather than assumed.

Fit Score: 8/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Resident mirrored shift teams, objective automatic-suspension triggers and reciprocal adversarial red-teaming match the plan's full-time mirrored staffing, required automatic-suspension procedures and reciprocity-as-Go-criterion. Weaknesses are vendor-key concentration and manufactured-trigger risk, which the plan's layered-evidence rule and exercise exclusions must contain.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Equipment Identity Trust Anchor: Anchor identity primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation validated independently by accredited examiners from both countries, using physical inspection and customs records as corroborating layers at intake.
  • Inspector Presence and Rotation Model: Station resident mirrored teams at every participating site on continuous shift coverage, confined to bounded inspection zones with escorted movement and filtered evidence handling.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Define enumerated objective triggers that suspend a site automatically, with resumption requiring double-key authorization and a documented corrective action from the responsible government.
  • Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring: Have each country's red team challenge the counterpart's inspectorate at the other's site, using reciprocal adversarial exercises so both detection capability and access parity are tested in a single event.
  • Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design: Run an operator-operated redaction gateway that converts raw records and telemetry into schema-limited evidence packets, with the counterpart's engineers auditing the gateway rules but not its inputs.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Fit with ambition and risk: a trust-free US–China test with a short 90-day clock needs the strongest, hardest-to-contest evidence base. Continuous resident mirrored shift teams match the plan's full-time staffing model and detect unreported arrivals directly.
  • Governance: enumerated automatic-suspension triggers with double-key resumption implement the required suspension procedure and the Stop condition for a government shielding an operator.
  • Reciprocity: reciprocal red-teaming tests detection and access parity in one event, the two Go criteria.
  • Why not Pragmatic Foundation: randomized rotation and suspension-free deadlock defaults dilute detection and let obstruction persist.
  • Why not Consolidator's Ledger: notification-based presence, aging-discrepancy deadlocks and a sealed catalog depend on the operator honesty under test.
  • Residual risk: attestation concentration and manufactured triggers must be managed through layered corroboration and exercise-event exclusions.

Alternative Paths

The Pragmatic Foundation

Strategic Logic: Balances detection credibility against exposure and cost by anchoring identity on bilateral tamper-evident tags that neither side's supply chain controlled, rotating inspectors to limit capture, and using paired technical referees to keep deadlocks factual rather than political. Independent blind exercises supply a defensible Go/Modify/Stop basis, while fixed, access-controlled zones keep the leakage boundary simple and testable.

Fit Score: 6/10

Assessment of this Path: Independent blind exercises and bilateral tags are credible and cost-aware, but randomized rotation erodes site familiarity and continuous shift coverage. Deadlock defaulting to heightened inspection instead of suspension weakens the plan's Stop logic against a government shielding an operator.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Equipment Identity Trust Anchor: Apply bilateral tamper-evident tags jointly in the staging area by both mirrored teams, so identity continuity rests on markers neither country's manufacturers or logistics firms controlled before arrival.
  • Inspector Presence and Rotation Model: Rotate inspectors across sites on randomized schedules with no repeat assignment to the same zone in succession, limiting relationship capture, site familiarity and cumulative exposure of any one inspector.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Convene paired technical referees from both countries to issue dual-signed advisory fact statements, with deadlock defaulting to heightened inspection and impaired-confidence status instead of suspension.
  • Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring: Have independent testers design and inject blind scenarios in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas, unknown to operating inspectors and scored against jointly agreed detection criteria.
  • Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design: Fix physical inspection zones to staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas with painted and access-controlled boundaries, and admit only inspector-carried instruments that have been pre-validated.

The Consolidator's Ledger

Strategic Logic: Prioritizes continuity, cost control and political survivability by relying on proven physical inspection and witnessed movement, notification-based deployment with unannounced spot checks, and status-quo deadlock handling with escalating timers and aging-discrepancy reporting. A sealed, pre-committed challenge catalog makes scoring defensible and prevents post hoc redefinition of success, at the cost of weaker adaptive testing and greater reliance on operator honesty.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: Notification-based deployment leans on operator honesty, which the unreported-arrival and reluctant-operator exercises are meant to test. Status-quo deadlock lets findings age, and a sealed catalog limits adaptive blind detection, which undercuts the credible-detection requirement for a Go.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Equipment Identity Trust Anchor: Anchor identity primarily on physical inspection and witnessed movement in controlled staging areas, treating attestation, customs records and maintenance logs as layers that can raise or lower confidence but never settle it alone.
  • Inspector Presence and Rotation Model: Deploy inspectors on operator notification within fixed response windows, supplementing with filtered remote evidence and unannounced spot visits to test whether declarations are complete.
  • Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics: Hold the status quo on deadlock but start escalating timers that move the dispute from co-chair level to designated principals, with unresolved findings reported as aging discrepancies.
  • Challenge Exercise Commitment and Scoring: Publish cryptographic commitments to a sealed catalog of challenge scenarios before Phase One, then reveal and score them afterward so neither government can redefine success post hoc.
  • Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design: Fix physical inspection zones to staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas with painted and access-controlled boundaries, and admit only inspector-carried instruments that have been pre-validated.

Purpose

Purpose: other. This plan doesn't clearly fit into personal or business categories.

Purpose Detailed: Sovereign public-sector national-security and verification program: a bilateral, double-key governed inspectorate and tamper-evident ledger system, funded 50/50 (USD 5 billion total), to test reciprocal, bounded change verification of declared AI compute equipment through a 90-day Phase One operational test, culminating in a Go/Modify/Stop decision. Covers intake and exit protocols, layered evidence, live challenge exercises, discrepancy adjudication and suspension, and KPI-based fiscal and operational accountability. It is explicitly not a business, not revenue-generating, and not a comprehensive AI-governance regime.

Topic: US–China jointly governed "Consortium" verifying changes (arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance, decommissioning) of declared frontier-relevant computing equipment at a small matched set of declared datacenters

Domain

Primary domain: Arms Control Verification

Secondary domains: Cybersecurity, International Law, Hardware Supply Chain Security

Rationale: Arms Control Verification best names a jointly governed bilateral inspectorate verifying declared equipment changes at matched sites with reciprocity and a Go/Modify/Stop decision. Hardware Supply Chain Security ties on score but covers only the identity-verification mechanism; other candidates are methods or constraints.

Disciplines this project involves:

Domain Importance Specificity Role Reason
Arms Control Verification 5 5 outcome Bilateral inspectorate verifying declared equipment changes at matched sites is a treaty-verification regime.
Hardware Supply Chain Security 5 5 outcome Equipment identity, intake, chain of custody and tamper evidence are the core verification mechanism.
Cybersecurity 4 4 method Tamper-evident ledger, attestation, evidence filtering and counterintelligence protect IP and evidence integrity.
Counterintelligence 4 4 constraint Mirrored inspectorates must be shielded from espionage and sensitive technology exposure.
Applied Cryptography 4 4 method Tamper-evident replicated ledger and validated attestation depend on cryptographic design.
Digital Forensics 4 4 method Layered evidence, chain of custody and tamper-evident records underpin equipment identity verification.
Data Center Operations 4 4 stakeholder Installation, maintenance and decommissioning at declared sites must proceed without disrupting active compute.

Bilateral Diplomacy 4 3 constraint Reciprocity, double-key governance and deadlock procedures require negotiated US–China diplomatic mechanisms.

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is physical. The Consortium's whole mission is verifying changes to physical computing equipment (arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes and decommissioning) at declared datacenters. This cannot be done only online and requires a physical presence at several points. Inspectors must be deployed in person to matched sites in the United States and China. Equipment identity must be verified in controlled physical staging areas before installation, using physical inspection, equipment identifiers and witnessed movement. Exit verification requires witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement and transfers between sites. Live challenge exercises involve unreported arrivals, substituted equipment and delayed access in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas. The plan also requires secure facilities, clean rooms, shipment and customs records, and site preparation funded from the USD 1 billion envelope. Staff include full-time mirrored inspection, logistics, counterintelligence and adjudication units, who need physical workspaces and travel. The ledger and attestation systems are digital, but they only record and corroborate events at physical sites, and they depend on secure hardware and facilities. The plan also needs in-person bilateral governance, such as co-chair double-key decisions, and domestic access authority over physical sites. Its digital components are supporting elements within a clearly physical, real-world verification program.

Physical Locations

This plan implies one or more physical locations.

Requirements for physical locations

  • Matched set of declared datacenters in the United States and China with comparable staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas
  • Controlled staging areas for pre-installation identity verification, with bounded inspection zones
  • Secure facilities for evidence handling, clean rooms, ledger nodes and counterintelligence-protected workspaces
  • Proximity to logistics hubs (airports, ports, customs) for shipment records and witnessed movement
  • Operator and vendor willingness plus domestic legal authority to compel access
  • Neutral-feeling or jointly acceptable venue for co-chair double-key governance sessions
  • Capacity to house full-time mirrored resident inspection, technical, legal, translation and adjudication units
  • No disruption to active computational work; separation from production halls

Location 1

United States

Northern Virginia datacenter corridor (Loudoun and Prince William Counties)

Declared commercial or operator datacenter campus with a dedicated staging and spare-inventory zone near Washington Dulles International Airport

Rationale: Dense datacenter cluster with airport and customs access, many operators and vendors, and proximity to federal authority for domestic access enactment. Supports a US-side matched site with staging, maintenance and expansion areas.

Location 2

China

Beijing–Hebei (Zhangjiakou/Langfang) or Shanghai region datacenter cluster

Declared datacenter campus with bonded staging and spare-inventory area near a major airport or port with customs facilities

Rationale: Large datacenter clusters with strong logistics and customs access and state authority to compel operator participation. Offers a functional match to the US site on staging, maintenance and expansion areas.

Location 3

Third-country or jointly agreed venue

Geneva, Switzerland or Singapore

Secure meeting and adjudication facility for co-chair double-key sessions, technical referees and ledger reconciliation reviews

Rationale: A jointly acceptable venue for governance, deadlock handling and Go/Modify/Stop deliberation, without placing either government on home ground. Site inspection work stays at the matched US and Chinese datacenters.

Location Summary

The plan inherently requires physical presence at a small matched set of declared datacenters in the United States and China, where equipment arrivals, changes and departures are verified. Suggested locations are a US Northern Virginia campus, a matched Chinese datacenter cluster (Beijing–Hebei or Shanghai region), and a jointly acceptable venue for co-chair governance and adjudication. Final site selection remains an entry condition decided by both governments before the 90-day clock starts.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • USD: Primary budget allocation currency. Both governments contribute USD 2.5 billion each (total USD 5 billion) across seven fixed envelopes: secure ledger (USD 1.25B), site preparation (USD 1B), personnel (USD 750M), facilities (USD 750M), testing (USD 500M), legal/audit (USD 250M), contingency (USD 500M). All international reporting, bilateral tracking and budget reconciliation use USD.
  • CNY: Required for Chinese domestic administration of operator and vendor compensation charged against China's USD 2.5 billion contribution. The Chinese government must convert or allocate its share into RMB for payments to Chinese operators, vendors, staff and facilities. Exchange-rate tracking and conversion rules should be set at the entry gate to ensure transparent 50/50 parity accounting.

Primary currency: USD

Currency strategy: USD serves as the consolidated primary currency for all bilateral budgeting, appropriations, reporting and accountability. The Chinese government administers its domestic contribution (operator compensation, vendor payments, staff salaries, facility costs) in CNY against its USD 2.5 billion share, requiring a transparent conversion methodology or fixed exchange rate established before the appropriation-release entry gate. Parity accounting between the two governments' cumulative disbursements is tracked in USD to detect one-sided spending drift. The 90-day Phase One window (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-12 to 2027-01-12) presents minimal exchange-rate exposure, but the plan should document the conversion rule and any revaluation provisions in the bilateral instrument and budget governance. No external hedging or derivative instruments are anticipated for a sovereign government-to-government transaction.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Permitting

Mandatory entry conditions—signed bilateral instrument, both governments' appropriations, domestic access authority, site selection, inspector approval, vendor/operator participation, and provisional schedule—may not be simultaneously satisfied before the 90-day clock starts. A single condition lagging (e.g., China's domestic access authority delayed by legislative procedures, US vendor binding incomplete) halts the entire program, burning preparation costs without operational start.

Impact: Delay of 2–6 months from current Month 0 (2026-10-12) target start; loss of stakeholder momentum; accumulated operational costs (facility rental, staff deployment) without revenue/benefit; political embarrassment that either government weaponizes to withdraw entirely. Estimated sunk cost: USD 100–200 million in preparation and preliminary staffing without Phase One operational data.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Establish a certified entry-gate workstream with a single project-manager cadre tracking each condition weekly; assign a bilateral contingency account (USD 50 million from contingency envelope) to accelerate rate-critical path items such as site-preparation infrastructure and inspector clearances; pre-position escrow funding mechanisms so matched tranches can be released immediately upon joint certification; define a 'near-ready' grace period and partial operational start with subset of sites if only one condition has a defined near-term resolution.

Risk 2 - Technical

Vendor-issued cryptographic attestation keys, if concentrated in a small number of manufacturers and those keys are compromised, forged or withheld, render identity verification unachievable despite layered corroboration. A critical vendor (e.g., NVIDIA, AMD, or their Chinese equivalent) may refuse verification terms or withdraw cooperation under government pressure, leaving unknown quantities of equipment unverifiable and triggering site failure.

Impact: One or more declared sites fail Phase One outright due to unverifiable equipment count; Go decision blocked; reputational damage to both governments as evidence of a failed inspectorate; estimated 10–40% of declared equipment becomes unverifiable depending on vendor mix; estimated 2–4 week delay per site to escalate vendor disputes or explore alternative evidence layers.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Finalize vendor binding by Month -1 (before entry gate) with non-negotiable confidentiality and reporting requirements; establish pre-qualified vendor registry with supply-chain consequences for refusal; for each critical vendor, pre-stage accredited clean-room examination centers (funded from USD 500M testing envelope) where refusing vendors can submit units for supervised testing without exposing source code; document fallback evidence ladder (customs, maintenance logs, physical marks) for each vendor tier before Phase One; require operators to declare supplier list by Month -0.5 so missing vendors can trigger entry-gate delays rather than operational surprises.

Risk 3 - Governance & Procedural

Deadlock on a contested site finding or equipment identity creates an unresolved discrepancy with no casting vote and no defined escalation path. Automatic-suspension triggers, if inadequately defined or gaming-prone, allow one government to stall through manufactured incidents (seeding a false positive challenge result) while appearing to comply. Status-quo defaults let findings age without resolution, which itself becomes a Stop criterion if unresolved discrepancy age exceeds agreed thresholds.

Impact: Phase One extends beyond 90 days without conclusion, exhausting time-sensitive political goodwill; unresolved discrepancies age and feed Stop criteria even if the underlying technical facts are minor; estimated 2–8 week delay per escalated dispute; a manufactured false-positive challenge can trigger automatic suspension at a performing site, stranding that country's inspectors on home ground without reciprocal access; political crisis if one government claims the other seeded a fake incident.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Define deadlock and suspension procedures with exacting precision before entry gate: enumerate objective triggers (e.g., divergence > 5% on ledger checkpoints, unresolved discrepancy age > 10 days, equipment unverifiable > 3% of installed base per site) that suspend automatically without co-chair discretion; establish a three-tier escalation (site co-chairs → bilateral technical referees → principal-level review) with fixed timers at each step; exclude all deliberate challenge-exercise events from triggering suspension so manufactured incidents are administratively partitioned; require joint pre-approval of challenge-exercise design so neither side can later claim seeding; define resumption conditions requiring documented corrective action, not merely time passage.

Risk 4 - Security & Counterintelligence

Resident mirrored inspector teams stationed continuously at counterpart sites become targets for espionage, blackmail, or relationship-capture operations. A compromised inspector or translator can exfiltrate equipment identifiers, facility layouts, vendor information or classified inspection procedures. Compartmentation rules meant to limit exposure can fragment site context so severely that inspectors miss substitution patterns or accept redacted evidence they should question.

Impact: A counterintelligence breach surfaces mid-Phase One, requiring all affected inspectors to be rotated or stood down, losing 2–3 weeks of coverage; security incident report triggers impaired-confidence review or site suspension; estimated loss of detection confidence at affected site; diplomatic friction from espionage accusations; estimated cost of investigation and replacement: USD 20–40 million. Conversely, tight compartmentation may cause false negatives—inspectors miss a substitution because they lack prior context.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish a standing counterintelligence unit (funded from USD 750M facilities/security envelope) to vet, clear and continuously monitor all inspectors, technical staff and translators; implement regular polygraph testing and compartmentation audits; limit inspector tenure at a single site to 6 months with mandatory breaks between assignments; compartment inspectors by event type and site, prohibiting cross-site knowledge holdings; embed host-country counterintelligence liaison officers at each site who review inspector outputs and evidence before release, with reciprocal liaison review at counterpart sites; fund a bilateral insider-threat red team that attempts to compromise staff and reports findings directly to the audit record and suspension criteria.

Risk 5 - Technical & Operational

Ledger divergence between the two national cryptographic copies occurs due to network latency, synchronization delays, or deliberate tampering. No bounded reconciliation procedure, unclear divergence-detection latency, or asymmetric divergence resolution allows one side to drift its copy ahead while claiming the other is lagging, feeding deadlock and impaired-confidence triggers without objective truth.

Impact: Divergence detection latency exceeds agreed KPI thresholds (proposed: synchronization within 1 hour, detection within 4 hours), causing escalations on equipment identity or exit disposition before truth is established; estimated 1–3 day delay per divergence incident; if unresolved divergence exceeds agreed tolerance (proposed: > 5% of events disputed), the program triggers impaired-confidence or automatic suspension; unresolved divergence is a Stop criterion, potentially ending Phase One prematurely even if operational work is sound.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish a dedicated Ledger Synchronization and Divergence Doctrine before entry gate: define checkpoint format, cadence and signed-hash-chain validation; choose authenticated transport (e.g., dedicated IPsec tunnel with mutual TLS) over shared internet; set divergence-detection latency KPI (proposed: 4-hour maximum) and reconciliation time budget (proposed: 24 hours to closure); employ neutral-party digest escrow or coupled-ledger attestation so either side can prove its copy was not rewritten post hoc; automate reconciliation logging with reason codes and dispute classification; agree on materiality threshold (proposed: > 5 discrepancies per site per week) that triggers formal reconciliation review rather than immediate escalation.

Risk 6 - Operational

Inspector rotation, shift coverage and leave management across mirrored teams at multiple sites is modeled as a high-complexity staffing problem but no detailed surge-capacity or multi-site cross-coverage plan is defined. A health emergency, geopolitical crisis or cascading operational incident (e.g., two challenge exercises in rapid succession) strains availability below detection requirements. Single-person critical functions in any unit (e.g., the only bilingual legal specialist or the sole audit lead) create bottlenecks that compound surge risk.

Impact: Detection capability drops below thresholds during surge periods (e.g., Month 1–2 = 2026-11-12 to 2026-12-12 when multiple challenge exercises overlap with routine maintenance windows); estimated 20–40% reduction in inspector availability during peak operational load; an uncovered event window leads to missed arrival or substitution that feeds false-negative statistics; estimated cost overrun on personnel budget if backfill or surge staffing is required: USD 50–100 million against USD 750M personnel envelope.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Model full-time mirrored staffing from site count with explicit surge and leave buffers before entry gate: assume 3-person teams per site per shift (intake, monitoring, exit); calculate 7-day rotation with 2-person minimum staffing per function; model 15% leave allowance and 10% surge reserve; establish no single-person critical functions—every role must have a trained backup; pre-deploy cross-site floaters from both countries (estimated 20–30% surge capacity) before clock start; conduct staffing dry-run exercises in Month -1 to validate shift coverage under challenge-exercise load; define staffing KPIs (proposed: minimum 80% of target staff deployed, no single function below 2 FTE) with automatic operational curtailment if targets slip.

Risk 7 - Technical & Operational

Evidence filtering at the operator-controlled gateway—where raw records and telemetry are reduced to schema-limited packets before crossing to inspectors—may strip critical fields needed to detect substitution or equipment movement. The operator has incentive to filter aggressively; the counterpart's engineers audit gateway rules but not inputs, creating asymmetric visibility. Filter adequacy is not tested until live exercises, at which point failures trigger suspension or discredit the entire inspection system.

Impact: A substituted piece of equipment passes intake because the redacted records lack the serial-number or firmware-version fields that would have triggered identity questions; false-negative detection costs credibility of the entire pilot; estimated 5–15% of substitution scenarios undetectable under aggressive filtering; if discovered post Phase One, triggers Go decision reversal; estimated reputational damage: program discredited and bilateral cooperation undermined.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Design filter rules jointly before entry gate, with each country's sensitive-asset experts writing the filters applied at the counterpart's sites so exposure concerns are credibly mitigated; require operator-operated redaction gateways to log every filter decision (which fields redacted, why, by which rule) in the tamper-evident ledger so auditing can verify filtering consistency; run filter-adequacy blind exercises in Month 0.5 (2026-10-27) (before scored exercises) using staging areas to test whether critical fields are preserved; define a minimum evidence schema (proposed: equipment serial number, firmware version, cryptographic attestation digest, maintenance-event timestamp, physical identifiers) that is non-negotiable; if filtering strips any schema field, automatic escalation to unverifiable-equipment status; calibrate challenge exercises to include scenarios that test filter edge cases.

Risk 8 - Operational & Governance

Matched site equivalence is vague: US Northern Virginia datacenters and Chinese Beijing–Hebei or Shanghai facilities may have vastly different staging-area sizes, customs-access latency, operator types and logistics infrastructure. Reciprocal-access parity accounting struggles to define what 'equivalent' inspection activity means when one country's matched site is a commercial facility and the other's is state-owned, or when staging areas are 10x different in size.

Impact: Parity disputes on whether access denial at one site is justified by asymmetric site characteristics; estimated 2–4 week stalls per parity dispute; one country claims the other's site is easier to inspect, therefore unequal access is unfair; impaired-confidence review triggered without clear resolution; estimated 10–20% of access denials become parity disputes rather than resolved technical issues.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Define 'matched' explicitly before site selection: either match by verification function (e.g., both sites have staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas of defined footprint), by operator type (commercial with commercial, state-owned with state-owned), or by capacity tier (e.g., both handle 5–10 MW declared equipment); establish a Matched Site Equivalence working group by Month -2 to conduct physical surveys and document site characteristics that justify parity comparisons; publish site-pairing rationale before entry gate so both governments can contest equivalence claims; define normalization factors for parity accounting (e.g., 'access per unit of declared equipment' rather than 'total access hours') so asymmetric site size does not create spurious parity disputes; require a joint site-equivalence certification step at the entry gate so site mismatch does not emerge during Phase One.

Risk 9 - Political & Governance

One government shields an operator or vendor from verification duties by invoking national security, refusing domestic access authority or withdrawing political backing. This violates reciprocity but lacks a clear enforcement path: automatic suspension is defined as a trigger, but resumption conditions require that government to reverse course, which may never happen.

Impact: Equipment at that government's site remains partially unverified; material equipment count unverifiable, triggering site failure and Phase One Stop decision; the shielding government claims the other's inspectors are unreliable, justifying its own access restrictions as tit-for-tat retaliation; diplomatic crisis and program termination; estimated cost: entire USD 5 billion pilot rendered inconclusive and politically contested.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Define operator and vendor binding requirements explicitly before entry gate as non-negotiable conditions: each government must certify that it has legal authority to compel operator and vendor participation and that all critical vendors have agreed to verification terms or will use accredited clean-room examination. Make binding certification an entry condition so lack of authority emerges before clock start, not mid-Phase One; embed escalation procedure: any access refusal by an operator or vendor triggers an automatic two-tier response: first, escalation to principal-level bilateral review within 48 hours; second, if unresolved within 5 days, automatic site suspension until resumption conditions are met; document resumption conditions in bilateral instrument as non-negotiable (e.g., 'operator must grant full access or equipment is classified unverifiable and site fails'); publish suspension events in the KPI dashboard immediately so political cost of shielding is visible.

Risk 10 - Technical

Cryptographic attestation from vendors may be forged, time-delayed or tied to firmware that does not match physical hardware. A vendor supplies attested identity credentials that validate against its root keys, yet the physical device in the staging area is counterfeit or substituted. Layered corroboration (customs records, maintenance logs, physical marks) may be insufficient if the counterpart disputes the corroboration layers' reliability or origin.

Impact: Equipment identity confidence falls short of agreed thresholds (proposed: > 95% confidence required); equipment escalated to unverifiable status; estimated 2–5% of declared equipment at a site becomes unverifiable due to attestation-corroboration mismatches; if unverifiable count exceeds site threshold (proposed: > 3% of installed base), site fails Phase One; estimated 1–2 week delay per escalation while bilateral technical referees adjudicate equipment identity.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish an Equipment Identity Trust Anchor before entry gate that specifies the evidentiary hierarchy: cryptographic attestation is primary but requires independent validation by accredited examiners from both countries; customs records and shipment tracking are secondary layers; physical inspection and equipment identifiers (serial numbers, tamper seals, burn-in marks) are tertiary layers; no single layer is decisive; a mismatch across any two layers triggers escalation to technical referees for dual-signed adjudication; require attestation timestamps to bind to customs-entry and staging-arrival events within a fixed tolerance (proposed: ±2 hours); pre-stage bilateral attestation-validation laboratories (funded from testing envelope) to independently verify vendor signatures before intake; develop a physical-mark and tamper-seal specification that is agnostic to vendor but recognizable by both sides; if attestation cannot be validated by Month 1 (2026-11-12), automatically elevate all equipment from that vendor to unverifiable status and escalate to bilateral principals.

Risk 11 - Technical & Operational

Blind challenge exercises designed to test unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access and vendor refusal may serendipitously trigger automatic-suspension conditions, stranding inspectors or equipment and creating a cascading operational crisis. A false-positive challenge (e.g., a seeded unreported arrival that is misinterpreted as a real breach) collides with automatic-suspension triggers, halting Phase One work until the false positive is adjudicated.

Impact: A challenge exercise injects a test substitution; the intake team flags it as unverifiable; automatic-suspension trigger fires (unverifiable equipment exceeds threshold); site suspends; all inspectors at that site stood down; estimated 3–7 day operational halt to adjudicate the challenge event; estimated 10–20% schedule slip if multiple challenges trigger false-suspension cascades; bilateral recrimination if one government claims the other weaponized a challenge to manufacture a pretext for suspension.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High
