The instrument locks all suspension triggers with precise thresholds and measurement rules, so every suspension is objectively justified. The CHALLENGE-tag partition rule explicitly marks every injected scenario in the ledger before injection and prohibits tagged events from triggering suspension, impaired-confidence or KPI violations. The double-key requirement lists every decision type requiring both chairs' signatures, eliminating unilateral action claims. The covered-equipment schedule is role-based with a defined quarterly update procedure requiring both governments' technical specialists to approve all versions. Ledger synchronization doctrine specifies the exact hash algorithm, clock-sync mechanism and divergence-detection math, so both governments' copies are objectively reconcilable within 4 hours. Domestic access-authority assertions are obtained in writing by Month 7 (2027-05-12), and exemptions are explicitly prohibited, preventing retroactive claims of lack of authority. All disputes and incidents are logged in the ledger within 1 hour with defined escalation paths. When a contested finding emerges at Month 10 (2027-08-12), both governments know exactly how to escalate and by when, and both sides are confident the procedure will produce an objective resolution. Phase One completes with a defensible Go, Modify, or Stop verdict by Month 12.25 (2027-10-20), and bilateral trust in change verification as a credible mechanism is established.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full bilateral-instrument negotiation and signature cannot be achieved before Month 7 (2027-05-12), execute a skeletal executive agreement by Month -1 (2026-09-12) that locks only the core governance structure (co-chairs, double-key authorization, escalation tiers and timers, automatic-suspension triggers, CHALLENGE-tag partition rule) and defer detailed operating procedures (schedule framework, ledger synchronization doctrine, compartmentation protocols) to subsidiary annexes finalized during Phase One via joint technical working groups.
  • If legal barriers to compelling vendor or operator participation emerge during negotiation (e.g., US constitutional due-process challenges or Chinese state-enterprise ambiguity), establish a phased domestic-authority approach: secure foundational legislative or executive authorization for generic verification participation by Month 7 (2027-05-12), then resolve vendor-specific compulsion via individual bilateral vendor-binding addenda by Month 8 (2027-06-12), so Phase One can start with a subset of vendors under clear authority, with remaining vendors added post-verdict if their participation authority is later resolved.
  • If the two governments cannot agree on a single comprehensive covered-equipment schedule framework before entry, adopt a 'tiered classification' interim procedure: divide covered equipment into core (unambiguously covered), watch (disputed), and exempt categories; lock the core and exempt tiers in the instrument; place watch-tier items in a sealed joint escrow with a bilateral specialist panel that rules on individual items within 48 hours at intake, and all watch-tier rulings feed into a post-Phase-One schedule revision (do not let watch-tier disputes stall Phase One).
  • If ledger synchronization doctrine cannot be fully negotiated before signature, establish a minimum viable ledger: both governments' copies record entries locally with timestamps and hash-chain continuity; exchange daily signed digests (not full event logs) via a neutral-party escrow; divergence-detection latency is relaxed to 24 hours instead of 4 hours; reconciliation closure is 7 days instead of 24 hours; this extends the bounded window but preserves non-repudiation and truth-finding capability; lock this minimum-viable doctrine in the instrument and commit to upgrading synchronization after Phase One pending technical validation.
  • If a government's principal-level leadership cannot commit to the exact 5/8/13-day escalation timers or the status-quo default rule before signature, propose a 'contingency escalation' clause: if principals do not convene within 48 hours of a deadlock notice, a jointly agreed neutral-party Standing Arbitrator (funded from the USD 250M legal/audit envelope) issues a binding advisory ruling within 72 hours; this preserves time-bounded resolution without requiring principals to move faster than they can.

Create Document 3: Vendor-Participation Census and Binding Status Report

ID: 174daab2-40a3-42eb-8d4b-d613b6f97169

Description: Inventory of all equipment suppliers at each of the 4 participating sites, classified by vendor-binding status (A: binding signed and attestation keys validated; B: binding signed but keys pending; C: no binding or refused). Includes vendor-criticality assessment (% of declared equipment per vendor), legal-compulsion feasibility per jurisdiction, key-custody verification procedures, and escalation path for refusing vendors. Primary audience: bilateral co-chairs, legal team, clean-room operations lead, principals. Used to compute unverifiable-equipment forecast and validate the 3% material threshold.

Responsible Role Type: Vendor Binding and Equipment Identity Verification Lead

Primary Template: Supply-Chain Risk Assessment Template

Secondary Template: Vendor Qualification and Audit Matrix

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 1 (2026-11-12), request that each site operator declare at least 95% of its supplier list by equipment count, with contact information for each vendor's verification and legal representative.
  • Classify each vendor by binding status: A (binding signed + attestation keys validated by bilateral cryptography team), B (binding signed + key validation pending), C (no binding or refusal).
  • Compute unverifiable-equipment count by vendor and per site (sum of all Tier C equipment); flag any vendor representing >5% of declared equipment at a site for principal-level escalation.
  • Assess legal-compulsion feasibility per jurisdiction: identify any vendor in the US that is a private entity (compellable) vs. state enterprise in China (verify legal authority); document any anticipated litigation.
  • By Month 2 (2026-12-12), escalate all Tier C equipment (>5% of site total or representing a critical vendor) to principals for decision: accept unverifiable count, activate clean-room examination fallback, or reduce declared equipment list.
  • Document disposition of each vendor: binding execution date, attestation-key fingerprint, clean-room examination results (if applicable), or refusal reason and date.
  • By Month 8 (2027-06-12), publish final vendor-status summary with unverifiable-equipment count per site and validation that all Tier A and B vendors are on-track for Phase One start.

Approval Authorities: Bilateral Co-Chairs, Vendor Binding Task Lead, and Principals (for Tier C escalation decisions)

Essential Information:

  • Inventory of all equipment suppliers across the 4 declared sites, classified into three binding-status tiers: A (binding signed + attestation keys validated), B (binding signed + key validation pending), C (no binding or refusal), with supplier name, legal jurisdiction, contact representatives and binding execution date.
  • Vendor-criticality assessment expressed as percentage of declared equipment per vendor and per site, identifying any vendor representing >5% of a site's covered-equipment population (proposed threshold for principal escalation).
  • Key-custody verification procedures: for each Tier-A vendor, document the attestation-key fingerprint, validation method (bilateral cryptography team independent verification), timestamp of validation, and any cryptographic certificate or chain-of-custody record.
  • Legal-compulsion feasibility assessment per jurisdiction: for US vendors, classify as private entity (compellable under domestic law) vs. unclear authority; for Chinese vendors, classify by state-enterprise status and verify enacted domestic access authority covers the vendor; document any anticipated constitutional or commercial litigation and estimated delay impact (2-4 months estimated per risk assessment).
  • Escalation path for Tier-C (refusing or unbound) vendors: document refusal reason and date; compute unverifiable-equipment count (sum of all Tier-C equipment by unit count); identify vendors critical to any site (>5% of site population); specify escalation to principals with decision options (accept unverifiable count, activate clean-room examination fallback, or reduce declared equipment list).
  • Clean-room examination results for any Tier-C vendor: record whether vendor has agreed to supervised testing in accredited independent centers; document outcome (equipment accepted after testing and filtered evidence, or equipment classified unverifiable); include cost attribution and facility location.
  • Disposition summary per vendor: binding execution date, attestation-key fingerprint (Tier A), clean-room examination completion date and pass/fail status (Tier C), or refusal reason and principal escalation decision; total equipment count and percentage per site.
  • Unverifiable-equipment forecast per site: sum of all Tier-C equipment units; compare against the 3% material threshold (proposed); document whether the site is forecast to pass or fail Phase One based on unverifiable-equipment count alone, pending principal decisions on outstanding Tier-C escalations.
  • Validation of Phase One readiness: confirm all Tier-A and Tier-B vendors are on track for attestation-key validation by Month 9 (2027-07-12) (clock start); flag any vendor with key validation pending beyond Month 8 (2027-06-12) as a risk to Phase One start; confirm vendor-participation rate at each site (proposed: >=95% of equipment accounted for in supplier list by Month 1 = 2026-11-12).
  • Principal escalation summary: list all Tier-C vendors representing >5% of any site's population and the decision (accept unverifiable, clean-room option, or reduce declared equipment) rendered by bilateral co-chairs at each escalation gate (Month 2 = 2026-12-12 proposed); document any open escalations awaiting principal decision and the deadline for resolution.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete supplier list (<95% equipment accounted for by Month 1 / 2026-11-12) leaves unknown quantities of equipment without vendor binding status, preventing computation of actual unverifiable-equipment risk and forcing Phase One delay or site removal.
  • Inaccurate or missing vendor-criticality percentages misrepresent the impact of vendor refusal; if a critical vendor representing 20% of a site's equipment is misclassified as non-critical, the site's unverifiable-equipment forecast is understated, leading to a false-positive Go decision.
  • Unreliable attestation-key validation records (fingerprints unverified, validation method unclear, or timestamp errors) undermine the identity-anchor evidence layer; if Tier-A classification cannot be audited, bilateral co-chairs cannot certify that attestation validation is complete at entry gate.
  • Vague or missing legal-compulsion assessment delays vendor binding through unresolved litigation pathways; if anticipated US constitutional challenges or Chinese state-enterprise authority gaps are not documented before Month 7 (2027-05-12), escalation and workaround planning is delayed, consuming months of Phase One calendar.
  • Tardy or absent Tier-C escalation decisions leave vendors in an unresolved binding state through Phase One start; if a principal decision on a large refusing vendor (>5% of site equipment) is not rendered by Month 2 / 2026-12-12, the unverifiable-equipment count remains uncertain, blocking entry-gate certification.
  • Missing or incomplete clean-room examination results for Tier-C vendors prevent fallback evidence gathering; if a clean-room center is not operational or does not complete supervised testing before the vendor's equipment is scheduled for intake, the equipment cannot be classified and blocks site arrivals.
  • Unverifiable-equipment forecast exceeding the 3% material threshold (proposed) with no principal decision to reduce declared equipment list or accept site failure triggers Phase One cancellation without warning; if the report does not flag threshold exceedances explicitly, co-chairs may discover the failure only after entry gate is certified and sunk costs are irrecoverable.
  • Inconsistent vendor disposition records across the two national ledger copies (e.g., one country records a vendor as Tier A, the other as Tier B) trigger ledger divergence and dispute resolution delays; if the report does not align vendor records with the official ledger before publication, conflicting versions persist.
  • Post-hoc changes to vendor status (e.g., a Tier-B vendor's key validation fails after the report is finalized) are not reflected in any updated report, leaving downstream planning (challenge-exercise design, equipment-intake scheduling) based on outdated binding status; if the report lacks a version-control or refresh schedule, stale data propagates.
  • No clear identification of Phase-One-critical-path vendors (those whose binding status gates entry certification) leaves no escalation discipline; if the report does not flag vendors whose unresolved status could delay Month 9 (2027-07-12) clock start, critical escalations are missed and Phase One is delayed past the 90-day operational window.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical vendor at one of the 4 sites (e.g., representing 15% of declared equipment) is not bound by Month 6 (2027-04-12) and litigation over compulsion authority extends to Month 9 (2027-07-12) or beyond. The Vendor-Participation Census report, finalized Month 2 (2026-12-12), did not flag this vendor as critical or document the anticipated legal delay, so the co-chairs are unprepared for escalation. At entry gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-12), the vendor's binding status remains Tier C (unresolved), and the site's unverifiable-equipment count reaches 18%, far exceeding the 3% material threshold. The co-chairs cannot certify the entry condition (secured operator and vendor participation); Phase One clock does not start. Sunk costs from months of preparation (estimated USD 100–200 million) are already spent; the program faces a choice to abandon, delay 3+ months to resolve the vendor dispute, or remove the site from the test set. Reputational damage: the verification program is perceived as dysfunctional, bilateral trust erodes, and the political window for Phase One closes. The Go/Modify/Stop verdict is indefinitely delayed or rendered moot.

Best Case Scenario: The Vendor-Participation Census is finalized by Month 2 (2026-12-12) with 100% of declared equipment traced to named vendors, with each vendor explicitly classified as Tier A, B, or C. All Tier-A vendors (representing 85% of equipment) have signed binding agreements and attestation keys validated by bilateral cryptography specialists with fingerprints and custody records in the ledger. All Tier-B vendors (5% of equipment) have binding agreements but are on track for key validation by Month 8 (2027-06-12). Tier-C vendors (10% of equipment) are escalated to principals by Month 2 (2026-12-12) with a decision to use accredited clean-room examination centers; the centers are operational by Month 8 (2027-06-12), and supervised testing is complete for 90% of Tier-C equipment before Phase One clock starts. At entry gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-12), all Tier-A and Tier-B vendors are certified ready, unverifiable-equipment is <3% per site, and the Vendor-Participation Census is published as a validated entry-condition deliverable. Inspectors and co-chairs can proceed to Phase One with confidence that identity verification is anchored to bound vendors whose attestation keys and fallback evidence are secured. The equipment-identity verification mechanism avoids the single-source-failure risk that would otherwise dominate the Go verdict.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If complete vendor binding for all suppliers cannot be achieved by Month 8 (2027-06-12), adopt a phased approach: certify Phase One entry gate with vendors achieving Tier A or B status only (proposed: >=85% of equipment), then conduct escalation and clean-room testing for Tier-C vendors in parallel during Phase One Months 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12), deferring final verdict until all vendors are resolved. Document this in the bilateral instrument before Month 7 (2027-05-12) as a contingency option.
  • If legal challenges to compulsion authority delay binding beyond Month 7 (2027-05-12), substitute a bilateral legal work-around: have each government issue a binding directive (internal order) to its operators that participation is mandatory, without requiring formal vendor contracts; document the directive in the Vendor-Participation Census as a substitute binding mechanism, with co-chair attestation that the directive is equivalent to signed binding.
  • If a critical vendor (>5% of equipment) refuses participation and clean-room examination is not available, reduce the declared equipment list by removing all equipment from that vendor before Phase One starts; document the reduction in the provisional covered-equipment schedule by Month 8 (2027-06-12), treating removed equipment as out of scope for Phase One verification, and disclose in the verdict report that unverifiable-equipment exclusion resulted.
  • If the Vendor-Participation Census cannot be finalized comprehensively by Month 2 (2026-12-12), produce an interim census covering Tier-A vendors (highest confidence) by Month 2 (2026-12-12), then publish a monthly supplement documenting progress on Tier-B and Tier-C escalations through Month 8 (2027-06-12); establish a refresh cadence (e.g., monthly) so the report is kept current as binding and key-validation status changes.
  • If vendor-binding responsibility is unclear between operators and national governments, establish a Vendor-Binding Task Lead (role explicitly named in the plan) who becomes the single point of coordination for all three phases of vendor classification, attestation validation, and escalation; embed this lead in the bilateral steering committee with weekly reporting and authority to escalate vendor disputes directly to principals.
  • If attestation-key validation by the bilateral cryptography team becomes a bottleneck, pre-position certified key-validation auditors (e.g., from national cryptography institutes) at each site so key validation can occur in parallel during vendor outreach (Months 1–7 = 2026-11-12 to 2027-05-12) rather than sequentially; establish a validation-completion dashboard tracking each vendor's key-fingerprint verification status in real time.

Create Document 4: Equipment Identity Verification and Attestation-Validation Protocol

ID: 38f18bb8-a7db-4417-a9d2-a30cdd929baf

Description: Detailed procedure for intake-protocol identity verification, including the three-tier evidence ladder (attestation + customs/maintenance + physical inspection; no single layer decisive), conflict-resolution rule (>=2 independent layers must agree within ±2 hours for 95% confidence), accredited-examiner validation process for vendor attestation keys, and fallback pathways (clean-room examination, supervised testing, unverifiable escalation). Primary audience: intake inspectors, accredited examiners, bilateral attestation-validation specialists. Tied to the Equipment Identity Trust Anchor strategic decision.

Responsible Role Type: Vendor Binding and Equipment Identity Verification Lead, Cryptographic Hardware Attestation Engineer

Primary Template: Equipment Identity Verification and Chain-of-Custody Procedure Template

Secondary Template: Cryptographic Attestation Validation and Key-Escrow Protocol

Steps to Create:

  • Specify the three-tier evidence hierarchy: (Tier 1) vendor-issued cryptographic attestation independently validated by accredited examiners from both countries; (Tier 2) customs records, shipment tracking, maintenance logs and witnessed movement; (Tier 3) physical inspection (serial numbers, equipment identifiers, tamper seals), facility records and inventory counts.
  • Define the 'no single layer decisive' rule: attestation alone, customs records alone, or physical inspection alone cannot establish identity confidence >90%; at least two tiers must independently and affirmatively agree within ±2 hours.
  • Document accredited-examiner process: each country designates >=2 examiners per site (by Month 8, 2027-06-12) with cryptographic-key validation training; examiners independently verify vendor signatures on attestation chains using pre-distributed bilateral public keys; mismatch flags require bilateral referee adjudication within 2 days.
  • Specify attestation-key custody verification: each critical vendor (>5% of declared equipment) must participate in a bilateral key-derivation ceremony or deposit a key fingerprint with both governments' cryptographic specialists by Month 7 (2027-05-12); keys are stored in Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) under shared custody (one half-key per country) where feasible.
  • Define conflict-resolution rule: if attestation and physical inspection disagree on identity (e.g., firmware version mismatched between attested claim and actual device), the unit escalates to the Bilateral Technical Referee Panel for dual-signed adjudication within 2 business days; unresolved conflicts default to unverifiable status.
  • Document fallback evidence layers for vendor refusal or attestation-key unavailability: Tier 2 (customs + maintenance + physical) is sufficient for identity confirmation if both tiers are independently available and agree within ±2 hours; Tier 3 (physical + facility records) can establish identity if Tier 1 and Tier 2 are unavailable.
  • Specify clean-room examination fallback: if vendor refuses attestation validation, the unit enters supervised independent examination at an accredited clean-room center; examiners conduct non-destructive forensic analysis (firmware extraction, hash computation, physical-mark verification) and issue a sealed report confirming or denying identity match.
  • Define unverifiable escalation: any unit failing identity confirmation across >=2 tiers is classified unverifiable; unverifiable status is logged in the tamper-evident ledger with reason code (attestation unavailable, customs records absent, physical marks tampered, etc.); cumulative unverifiable count per site is reported weekly in the KPI dashboard.
  • Establish identity-confidence scoring: assign a confidence percentage to each intake decision (100% = >=2 tiers agree; 80-90% = tiers mostly agree with minor timestamp/label discrepancies; <80% = conflicting tiers, escalate to referees); target: >=95% of intake decisions reach >=95% confidence; <95% is a leading indicator for filter-adequacy or corroboration-layer issues.
  • Lock this protocol in the bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12); validate accuracy and bi-country agreement in the filter-adequacy pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27).

Approval Authorities: Bilateral Co-Chairs and Accredited Examiner Task Lead (for each examiner certification and key-validation ceremony)

Essential Information:

  • Define the complete three-tier evidence hierarchy for equipment identity verification: (Tier 1) vendor cryptographic attestation independently validated by bilateral accredited examiners; (Tier 2) customs records, shipment tracking, maintenance logs and witnessed movement; (Tier 3) physical inspection (serial numbers, identifiers, tamper seals) and facility inventory records.
  • Specify the 'no single layer decisive' rule with mathematical precision: attestation alone, customs alone, or physical inspection alone cannot establish >90% identity confidence; require >=2 independent tiers affirmatively agreeing within ±2 hours for 95% confidence threshold.
  • Document accredited-examiner certification process: designate >=2 examiners per country per site by Month 8 (2027-06-12); require cryptographic-key validation training; specify bilateral public-key distribution and independent signature verification; define two-day bilateral referee escalation for attestation-customs-physical mismatches.
  • Establish attestation-key custody mechanism: each critical vendor (>5% of declared equipment) must participate in bilateral key-derivation ceremony or deposit key fingerprints with both governments' cryptographic specialists by Month 7 (2027-05-12); specify Hardware Security Module (HSM) shared-custody storage (one half-key per country where feasible).
  • Define conflict-resolution rule with decision path: when attestation and physical inspection disagree (firmware version mismatch, serial-number discrepancy, timestamp divergence), escalate unit to Bilateral Technical Referee Panel; referees issue dual-signed adjudication within 2 business days; unresolved conflicts default to unverifiable status and log reason code.
  • Specify fallback evidence layers for vendor refusal or attestation unavailability: Tier 2 (customs + maintenance + physical) sufficient if both independently available and agree within ±2 hours; Tier 3 (physical + facility records) sufficient if Tiers 1-2 unavailable; document which vendor refusals trigger which fallback (supervised testing vs. clean-room examination vs. attestation validation delay).
  • Document clean-room examination procedure for refusing vendors: non-destructive forensic analysis (firmware extraction, hash computation, physical-mark verification); sealed examiner report confirming or denying identity match; timing constraint (complete within 5 days of referral).
  • Define unverifiable escalation: any unit failing >=2-tier identity confirmation classified unverifiable; log reason code (attestation unavailable, customs absent, physical marks tampered, mismatch unresolved); track cumulative unverifiable count per site in KPI dashboard weekly; >3% unverifiable per site triggers material failure and site closure.
  • Establish identity-confidence scoring methodology: assign confidence percentage (100% = >=2 tiers agree perfectly; 80–90% = tiers mostly agree with minor timestamp/label discrepancies; <80% = conflicting tiers, escalate to referees); target >=95% of intake decisions at >=95% confidence; <95% is leading indicator for corroboration-layer or filtering issues.
  • Specify attestation timestamp binding rule: attestation timestamps must correlate to customs-entry event timestamp and staging-arrival timestamp within ±2 hours; divergence >±2 hours flags a discrepancy requiring referee adjudication or manual customs-records review.
  • Lock protocol in bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12); validate in filter-adequacy pre-test Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with >=10 injected substitutions, confirming >=9 of 10 detected under proposed filtering and corroboration.
  • State explicitly: this protocol applies only to intake identity verification for declared equipment at participating sites; does not estimate total capacity, verify workloads, or prove absence of hidden facilities.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • An ambiguous or single-layer identity rule (e.g., 'attestation is decisive') concentrates all intake confidence on one source; if that source fails (vendor-key compromise, customs-record tampering, or physical-inspection human error), all intake identity confidence collapses, rendering 10–40% of equipment unverifiable and failing one or more sites outright.
  • Undefined conflict-resolution rule for attestation-customs-physical mismatches creates intake bottlenecks: inspectors cannot decide whether a firmware-version discrepancy is a major red flag or a documentation error; escalations age without closure, delaying the entire intake baseline by weeks.
  • Missing examiner-certification standards or key-validation procedures allow unqualified examiners to validate attestation, creating plausible false positives (accepting forged or compromised keys) or false negatives (rejecting valid keys due to procedural confusion); either way, intake credibility is damaged.
  • Unspecified fallback procedure for vendor refusal leaves inspectors and operators uncertain whether refusing a vendor means that vendor's equipment is automatically unverifiable (risking operator withdrawal if they depend on that vendor) or whether some other evidence path exists (creating ambiguity and delay).
  • Vague or absent identity-confidence scoring rule allows intake decisions to rest on subjective judgment; without documented confidence percentages, the bilateral counterpart cannot verify whether intake met the 95% threshold or whether unverifiable escalations were justified, triggering parity disputes on every contested intake.
  • Failure to bind attestation timestamps to customs-entry and staging-arrival events allows equipment with stale or forged attestation (issued days before actual arrival) to pass identity verification; similarly, equipment that sat in a warehouse for months could have attestation and customs records pointing to different arrival dates, undetected.
  • Omitting the clean-room examination procedure leaves no credible fallback when a critical vendor refuses attestation validation; forcing that vendor's equipment to unverifiable status may cause operator withdrawal and site failure; absence of a clean-room pathway is itself a site-failure risk.
  • Failure to explicitly state the scope exclusion (this protocol applies to intake identity only, not total-capacity estimates) allows inspectors or counterpart auditors to later claim the identity protocol was meant to verify total equipment deployed, opening disputes about whether unverifiable equipment represents hidden capacity or merely missing documentation.
  • Lack of clarity on who designates accredited examiners (national government, bilateral committee, or existing certification body) and by what date creates Month 8 (2027-06-12) slip risk; if examiners are not designated and trained by end of Month 7 (2027-05-12), the staffing dry-run and filter-adequacy pre-test cannot proceed, delaying Phase One.
  • Undefined timelines for bilateral referee adjudication (e.g., 'within 2 business days' vs. 'immediately') create disputes about whether a referee panel failed to meet its deadline, feeding deadlock and aging-discrepancy escalations.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical vendor's cryptographic attestation keys are compromised mid-Phase One (or are withheld, or prove unvalidatable), and the protocol lacks a clear fallback pathway. Inspectors cannot confidently establish identity for 15–25% of equipment from that vendor; cumulative unverifiable count across sites climbs to 4–6% (above the 3% material-failure threshold). One or more sites fail outright due to unverifiable equipment. Intake baseline cannot be sealed. The Phase One Go decision is blocked. The bilateral counterpart disputes whether the vendor-refusal pathway was followed correctly, claiming the host government withheld access to examiners or clean-room facilities. A 2–3 week adjudication loop ensues; unresolved divergence ages to 15+ days, triggering automatic suspension. The program stalls mid-Phase One without a verdict, consuming USD 200–400 million (estimate) of the USD 5 billion budget on preparatory work without operational data. Political fallout: one government accuses the other of sabotaging the program via vendor shielding; the pilot is abandoned; bilateral relations are damaged.

Best Case Scenario: The protocol establishes identity confidence >95% for >=97% of intake units through a well-sequenced three-tier hierarchy. Accredited examiners are pre-designated, trained and in place by Month 8 (2027-06-12). Attestation-key custody is established in a bilateral HSM configuration. Filter-adequacy pre-testing at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) validates that the minimum evidence schema (serial number, firmware version, attestation digest, timestamp, physical identifiers) is preserved under proposed filtering. A small number of vendor-refusal cases (estimated 1–3 per site) are resolved via clean-room examination within 5 days, with sealed forensic reports confirming identity. The opening inventory baseline is sealed by Month 9 (2027-07-12), Day 5, establishing a clean zero-point reference for all change detection. By Month 12.25 (2027-10-20), intake identity confidence data support a defensible Go verdict; neither government can later dispute the identity anchor or claim the protocol was ambiguous. The bilateral counterpart's auditors certify the protocol as credible and reproducible.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If bilateral HSM shared-key custody is not feasible by Month 7 (2027-05-12), substitute a neutral-party key-escrow arrangement: deposit all vendor public keys with a mutually acceptable neutral custodian (e.g., Switzerland-based cryptographic notary); both governments hold the key to retrieve keys on demand; this trades operational latency (key-escrow lookup time) for reduced bilateral infrastructure complexity.
  • If accredited examiners cannot be designated by Month 8 (2027-06-12), delay Phase One by 4 weeks and conduct examiner recruitment and training in parallel to other entry-gate work; use pre-cleared personnel from each country's national cryptographic institutes; fast-track training (proposed: 2-week intensive course) for an estimated 4–8 examiners per country.
  • If clean-room examination facilities cannot be built and operational by Month 9 (2027-07-12), substitute a phased approach: use Tier-2 (customs + maintenance) evidence for vendor-refusal cases in Phase One; escalate unresolved Tier-1 cases to a bilateral forensic panel; conduct clean-room construction in Month 9–10 (2027-07-12 to 2027-08-12) in parallel to Phase One, then validate clean-room adequacy for Phase Two.
  • If attestation-timestamp binding to customs and staging events proves impossible (e.g., customs records lack timestamps to ±2-hour precision), relax the timestamp tolerance to ±24 hours and require a customs-records witness statement explaining any divergence >2 hours; this trades precision for operational feasibility at cost of slightly lower identity confidence.
  • If a Bilateral Technical Referee Panel cannot be established by Month 8 (2027-06-12), substitute a standing adjudication committee of senior technical specialists from each country's national laboratory; define their authority and escalation timers in the bilateral instrument; pre-fund and pre-staff them at Month 7 (2027-05-12).
  • If identity-confidence scoring requires too much documentation overhead, adopt a binary classification: either identity is confirmed (>=2 tiers agree within defined tolerance) or it is not (escalate to referees and mark unverifiable if unresolved within 2 days); eliminate numerical confidence percentages; rely on binary accept/reject and audit trails to document every escalation.
  • If the scope exclusion cannot be adequately stated in this protocol alone, embed a scope-limiting affidavit into the bilateral instrument: 'This Equipment Identity Verification Protocol applies to intake and exit identity verification only and does not establish, estimate or verify total equipment deployed, workload capacity, model weights, or the absence of facilities outside the declared sites.'

Create Document 5: Inspection Zone Geometry and Evidence Filtering Design Specification

ID: f24ea99b-4483-4a40-9ceb-8a513a2437bd

Description: Physical and logical design of bounded inspection zones at each of the 4 participating sites (staging, spare-inventory, maintenance, expansion areas only; production halls and model-weight data areas strictly off-limits), including zone boundaries, access-control specifications, pre-validated instruments allowed, and the operator-controlled redaction-gateway filtering rules. Specifies minimum evidence schema (serial number, firmware hash, attestation digest, maintenance timestamp, physical identifiers, tamper-seal state; cluster membership and power state redactable only by bilateral agreement) and audit trail for filter decisions. Primary audience: facility operators, inspectors, zone-security personnel. Operationally validated in filter-adequacy pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27).

Responsible Role Type: Filtered Evidence and Redaction-Gateway Architect

Primary Template: Physical Security and Facility Access-Control Specification

Secondary Template: Data Redaction and Filtering Rule Specification Template

Steps to Create:

  • Define zone boundaries: staging (500–1000 sq m estimated), spare-inventory (300–500 sq m estimated), maintenance (200–300 sq m estimated), equipment-expansion (200–300 sq m estimated); mark all boundaries with paint lines and electronic-access control points.
  • Install physical access controls: biometric card readers (+ iris recognition at entry) for zone access; no manual keys; event logging (name, date, time, purpose) of every entry/exit in the tamper-evident ledger within 30 minutes.
  • Specify allowed instruments: pre-validated and host-country-approved only; examples: serial-number readers (air-gapped), firmware-extraction devices (isolated, no internet), cryptographic-attestation validation tokens (pre-loaded with bilateral public keys), photographic equipment (film-based preferred, or secured-digital with restricted export).
  • Prohibit: recording devices not pre-approved, connected IT systems (laptops, tablets, smartphones) except air-gapped assessment terminals, external storage media, or copying of sensitive materials beyond the approved redaction gateway.
  • Define the redaction gateway: operator-staffed, host-country-personnel-operated (counterpart does not operate the host's gateway); gateway converts raw records and telemetry into schema-limited evidence packets before export; all filter decisions logged in the tamper-evident ledger with timestamp, field name, reason code and authorizing engineer.
  • Specify minimum evidence schema (non-redactable): equipment serial/unique identifier, firmware version or cryptographic hash, attestation digest, maintenance-event timestamp and type, physical identifiers with tamper-seal state, cluster membership only if necessary for identity verification.
  • Define redactable fields (bilateral agreement required for each): power-consumption telemetry, cluster topology details, workload-specific parameters, source-code paths, model-weight or quantization data.
  • Lock all redaction rules in a bilateral-signed filter-rule document by Month 7 (2027-05-12); require both countries' sensitive-asset experts to co-sign; document that any field stripping without explicit bilateral written agreement automatically escalates equipment to unverifiable status.
  • Establish auditing procedure: counterpart's engineers review and validate all redaction rules (but not the raw input data or the gateway's internal operations) by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27); any rule that appears to strip non-redactable fields triggers bilateral legal review within 48 hours.
  • Embed full-time host-country operator liaisons at each site by Month 1 (2026-11-12); liaisons audit inspector zone compliance daily, monitor all redaction-gateway operations, and alert co-chairs to any boundary violations within 2 hours.
  • Include zone-violation penalties in the bilateral instrument: minor violation (inspector >1 step beyond marked line, resolved within 1 hour) = formal warning; major violation (deliberate entry to production hall or model-weight area) = immediate removal from site and investigation; repeat violations = personnel rotation or site closure.
  • Validate zone geometry and redaction-gateway adequacy in the filter-adequacy blind pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27): inject test substitutions with edge-case fields near redaction boundaries and measure detection rate with proposed filters applied; require >=85% detection before scored exercises begin.

Approval Authorities: Bilateral Co-Chairs (zone geometry approval), both Countries' Sensitive-Asset Experts (filter-rule co-signature), and Operators (facility safety certification)

Essential Information:

  • Define the exact painted and electronically access-controlled boundaries of four zone types (staging, spare-inventory, maintenance, equipment-expansion areas) with target square-meterage ranges: staging 500–1000 sq m, spare-inventory 300–500 sq m, maintenance 200–300 sq m, expansion 200–300 sq m; include biometric (+ iris recognition) entry-control specifications, event-logging requirements (name, date, time, purpose logged in tamper-evident ledger within 30 minutes), and electrical/physical interlock details preventing inadvertent production-hall entry.
  • Specify the complete pre-validated-instruments allowlist, with rationale for each category: serial-number readers (air-gapped), firmware-extraction devices (isolated, no internet), cryptographic-attestation validation tokens (pre-loaded with bilateral public keys), photographic equipment (film-based preferred, or secured-digital with restricted export); explicitly prohibit recording devices, connected IT systems, external storage media, and sensitive-data copying outside the redaction gateway.
  • Document the minimum evidence schema (non-redactable fields) that must survive any redaction-gateway filtering: equipment serial/unique identifier, firmware version or cryptographic hash, attestation digest, maintenance-event timestamp and type, physical identifiers with tamper-seal state, cluster membership only if necessary for identity verification; specify redactable fields (power telemetry, topology details, workload parameters, source-code paths, model weights) requiring explicit bilateral written agreement to filter.
  • Design the operator-controlled redaction-gateway architecture: host-country personnel operation (counterpart does not operate), raw-records-to-schema-limited-evidence-packet conversion, decision logging (timestamp, field name, reason code, authorizing engineer, all entered in tamper-evident ledger within agreed latency), audit trail supporting evidence-integrity validation and filter-rule compliance.
  • Establish the bilateral filter-rule document and co-signature process: both countries' sensitive-asset experts jointly author redaction rules by Month 7 (2027-05-12); any field stripped without explicit bilateral written agreement automatically escalates affected equipment to unverifiable status; counterpart engineers validate rules (not raw data or gateway internals) by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27); bilateral legal review within 48 hours if rules appear to strip non-redactable fields.
  • Define zone-violation penalty tiers and escalation procedures: minor violation (inspector >1 step beyond marked line, resolved <1 hour) = formal warning; major violation (deliberate entry to production or model-weight area) = immediate removal and investigation; repeat violations = personnel rotation or site closure; embed operator liaisons as daily compliance auditors and 2-hour violation-alert mechanisms.
  • Specify the filter-adequacy blind pre-test protocol for Month 8.5 (2027-06-27): inject >=10 substitution scenarios with edge-case fields near redaction boundaries; measure detection rate with proposed filters applied; require >=85% detection (9 of 10 minimum) before scored exercises begin; if <85%, halt scored exercise schedule and renegotiate filters before proceeding.
  • Document the full chain-of-custody and tamper-evidence handling for all redacted and unredacted records: how raw data is captured, how redaction decisions are logged in the ledger, how evidence packets are transferred between inspector teams, how counterpart engineers audit redaction-rule compliance, timestamps and authorization checksums for each step, and escalation if any chain-of-custody event diverges from the protocol.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If zone boundaries are vaguely defined or access controls are not enforced in real-time (e.g., electronic logging lags >30 minutes), inspectors may inadvertently access production halls, model-weight areas or proprietary infrastructure; operator consent is withdrawn or legal action is triggered, failing the entire site and triggering Stop.
  • If the pre-validated-instruments list is incomplete or enforcement is loose, inspectors may use connected devices, recording equipment or external storage, exfiltrating sensitive topology, workload or design data; counterintelligence breach surfaces mid-Phase One, requiring staff rotation and investigation, costing USD 20–40M (estimate) and causing 2–3 week coverage loss.
  • If the minimum evidence schema is not locked in writing before Phase One, operators may apply redaction rules that strip serial numbers, firmware hashes or attestation digests; identity confidence falls below the 95% (proposed) threshold, material equipment is escalated to unverifiable status, and sites fail identity verification, triggering Stop.
  • If the bilateral filter-rule document is not jointly signed and if each country's sensitive-asset experts do not co-author the rules, one side may later dispute whether redaction was appropriate; escalation deadlock arises without an agreed-upon baseline, delaying equipment identity confirmation by 1–2 weeks per dispute (estimate).
  • If redaction-gateway decision logging is incomplete or tamper-evident ledger integration is missing, auditors cannot verify whether filters were applied correctly; evidence integrity is questioned; Go verdict is undermined or reversed, damaging bilateral credibility.
  • If zone-violation penalties are not defined or enforced (e.g., informal warnings instead of documented escalation), repeated boundary incursions occur without consequences; operator detects pattern and withdraws consent, failing the site; regulatory compliance audit surfaces violations, creating political liability.
  • If the filter-adequacy blind pre-test is not run or if detection targets are not validated before scored exercises, substitution-detection failures may emerge mid-Phase One; if discovered post-verdict, Go decision is reversed or discredited, forcing a Modify or Stop reassessment and damaging program credibility internationally.

Worst Case Scenario: A US operator discovers that inspectors conducted informal tours of production halls or that redaction-gateway filters secretly stripped the firmware-version field needed to detect equipment substitution. The operator withdraws consent for all future inspections; the US government cannot compel re-engagement without litigation. That country's 2 matched sites fail Phase One outright. The Chinese government claims asymmetric access bias; the bilateral program collapses into mutual recrimination. Alternatively, a blind challenge-exercise substitution is missed because redaction rules eliminated the serial-number field; the undetected scenario is discovered months after Phase One; the Go verdict is reversed, forcing a Stop reassessment that publicly discredits the entire USD 5 billion pilot. Either scenario terminates bilateral cooperation on verification and creates a trust deficit lasting years. Estimated reputational cost: severe damage to US-China diplomatic engagement on arms control and technology governance.

Best Case Scenario: Zone boundaries are precisely painted and electronically enforced; inspectors never inadvertently breach them. Pre-validated instruments are trusted and routinely confirmed compliant in audit spot-checks. The bilateral filter-rule document locks sensitive-asset protection at Month 7 (2027-05-12) with both countries' experts co-signing; redaction-gateway logging is auditable in near real-time via the ledger. The filter-adequacy blind pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) achieves 92% detection (all substitutions caught despite redaction), validating that the schema is sufficient. Operators express confidence in compartmentation; both governments' counterintelligence units sign off on containment. The document becomes the defensible, jointly authored specification underpinning operator consent and evidence credibility for the entire Phase One test. This enables a credible Go verdict supported by verifiable evidence of detection capability and reciprocal access.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If joint filter-rule co-authorship deadlocks before Month 7 (2027-05-12), adopt a neutral-party arbitrator (e.g., mutually agreed independent security expert) to propose a compromise filtering scheme by Month 7.25 (2027-05-20); both countries pre-commit to accepting the arbitrator's recommendation, unblocking the entry gate and phase-one start.
  • If the pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) reveals that proposed filters strip critical fields and detection falls below 85%, immediately escalate to bilateral principals with three options: (1) loosen filters to restore schema completeness and repeat pre-test within 10 days; (2) accept a lower detection threshold (80% instead of 90% proposed) and proceed with modified scoring rules; (3) halt and revise the entire filtering architecture, delaying Phase One start to Month 10 (2027-08-12).
  • If an operator refuses to implement the redaction gateway or demands exemption from redaction-rule enforcement, escalate to the operator's government within 48 hours; leverage vendor binding and participation pre-conditions to compel compliance; if unresolved within 5 days, treat as operator shielding, trigger automatic site suspension, and escalate to principal-level bilateral dispute resolution.
  • If zone-access-control logging repeatedly lags beyond 30 minutes due to technical failures, establish a supplementary manual sign-in and exit log maintained by operator liaisons in parallel until the electronic system is fixed; if failures persist beyond 10 days, escalate to the Facility Security Review Panel (bilateral oversight) and consider alternative zone-security designs.
  • If the filter-adequacy pre-test reveals that the redaction gateway cannot be trusted to apply rules consistently (e.g., same field is redacted inconsistently across equipment), adopt a human-in-the-loop verification approach: every redacted record is visually reviewed by a clearance-holding auditor from the counterpart country within 4 hours before it leaves the gateway; this slows evidence flow but ensures filtering compliance at the cost of estimated 2–3 additional auditor FTE per site.

Create Document 6: Challenge-Exercise Design and Independent Testing Plan

ID: 1417806b-8bbd-448a-b79e-0f0620b66dd5

Description: Comprehensive plan for blind challenge exercises testing detection of unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, and reluctant operators across 7 event types. Specifies independent-tester authorship and injection procedure, sealed hash-committed scenario catalog (published in advance, scenarios encrypted until injection), blind scoring by each country's independent team, sealed-score comparison, and false-positive containment. Includes filter-adequacy pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27, >=10 injections, target 9 of 10 detected, halt if <85%), preliminary calibration exercises (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27, unscored), and scored exercises (Months 10.5–11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27). Validates detection rates, evidence-filtering adequacy, reciprocal access and inspector presence effectiveness. Primary audience: challenge-exercise design panel, independent testers, bilateral co-chairs, adjudication referees.

Responsible Role Type: Challenge Exercise Design and Independent Testing Lead

Primary Template: Blind Exercise Design and Scoring Protocol Template

Secondary Template: Independent Testing and Validation Procedures

Steps to Create:

  • Establish independent Challenge Exercise Design Panel by Month 1 (2026-11-12): 2 technical experts + 1 CI officer per country, pre-cleared by both governments' security services, funded from USD 500M testing envelope.
  • Specify independent tester role: each country's red-team personnel design and inject blind scenarios at the counterpart's sites without advance notice to operating inspectors; injection occurs in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas only; zero disruption to active compute or customer-data areas.
  • Design 7 event types with 10+ injections each (70+ total): (1) unreported arrival: add 5-10 undeclared units to spare-inventory overnight; (2) substituted equipment: replace a declared unit with a similar unit under different serial/firmware; (3) inaccurate records: falsify maintenance logs or customs records for a known unit; (4) delayed access: simulate an access-denial scenario during scheduled inspection; (5) disputed identity: submit a unit with conflicting attestation and physical marks; (6) vendor refusal: withhold cryptographic attestation keys for a unit; (7) reluctant operator: require extensive justification before granting access to a zone.
  • Define sealed scenario commitment: each country's exercise panel designs scenarios, computes cryptographic hash digest, and publishes the digest in the ledger by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27) without revealing scenario details; scenarios are encrypted and stored offline until injection time.
  • Specify injection procedure: at injection time (unannounced), the injecting team logs the scenario UUID, timestamp, and bilateral digital signature into the ledger; the CHALLENGE tag is applied simultaneously; operating inspectors and systems are blind to the injection.
  • Document blind-scoring process: each country's independent observers (separate from operating inspectors) score the detection outcome for each injected scenario against jointly agreed criteria (e.g., 'substituted equipment is detected if the intake inspector flags identity-confidence <90% and escalates to unverifiable status'); scoring is done independently and sealed (no communication between national teams until after scores are compared).
  • Define sealed-score comparison: by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05), both countries' sealed scores are opened simultaneously in the presence of bilateral observers; scores are compared for divergence; if national-team scoring diverges >10% on any event type, technical referees issue a dual-signed fact statement reconciling the scores.
  • Specify false-positive containment: any challenge event that is misclassified as operational (e.g., a CHALLENGE substitution is not detected and is classified as unverifiable, triggering a site suspension) is escalated to co-chairs within 2 hours; automatic site reinstatement pending principal adjudication; documented as MISCLASSIFICATION_RESOLUTION in the ledger.
  • Include filter-adequacy pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27): inject at least 10 substitution scenarios in staging and spare-inventory areas with full redaction-gateway filtering applied; measure detection rate (target >=90%, minimum 85%); if <85%, halt all scored exercises and renegotiate filters with operators.
  • Specify preliminary (unscored) calibration exercises Months 9.5–10.5 (2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27): run a subset of scenarios (10–15 injections) to validate exercise procedures, measure staff familiarity and baseline detection performance, and fine-tune scoring criteria; results are not used for Go/Modify/Stop verdict, but inform threshold-calibration decisions.
  • Lock all exercise procedures in the bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12); publish exercise schedule (dates, general descriptions, but not scenario details) by Month 2 (2026-12-12) to allow operators to prepare secure facilities and evidence-handling procedures.
  • Include post-exercise audit: by Month 12 (2027-10-12), publish a redacted exercise summary report listing: number of injections per event type, detection rates, false positives and negatives, and major findings; document any systemic weaknesses in detection capability.

Approval Authorities: Challenge Exercise Design Panel (exercise design), Bilateral Co-Chairs (injection authorization), and Technical Referees (sealed-score divergence reconciliation)

Essential Information:

  • Define the complete taxonomy of 7 event types for blind challenge injection (unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator) with specific technical parameters for each: injection size, detection criteria, false-positive avoidance triggers, and escalation thresholds.
  • Specify the sealed hash-committed scenario-catalog mechanism: cryptographic digest publication timeline (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-27), encryption and offline storage protocol, injection-time ledger tagging with bilateral digital signature, and audit trail for scenario lifecycle.
  • Document the independent-tester role and injection procedure: each country's red-team personnel structure, authorization and clearance requirements, unannounced injection logistics across staging/spare/maintenance/expansion areas without disrupting active compute, site-access coordination, and incident containment.
  • Define the blind-scoring process and criteria: independent observer teams per country, sealed scoring methodology, jointly pre-agreed detection criteria per event type (e.g., 'substituted equipment detected if identity confidence <90% and escalated to unverifiable'), no inter-country communication until score sealing, and timestamp requirements.
  • Establish the sealed-score comparison and reconciliation procedure: simultaneous opening of national scores by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05), divergence threshold (>10% on any event type), technical-referee dual-signed fact statement for divergence reconciliation, and incorporation into verdict calibration.
  • Specify false-positive containment protocol: CHALLENGE-tag partition in ledger, exemption of tagged events from triggering suspension/impaired-confidence/KPI violation, misclassification escalation to co-chairs within 2 hours, automatic site reinstatement pending principal adjudication, and documented MISCLASSIFICATION_RESOLUTION record.
  • Design the filter-adequacy pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27): minimum 10 injected substitution scenarios with full redaction-gateway filtering, detection-rate target >=90% (minimum acceptable 85%), halt rule for scored exercises if <85% detected, and renegotiation protocol with operators if thresholds unmet.
  • Document the unscored preliminary-calibration exercise phase (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27): subset of 10-15 scenarios to validate procedures, measure staff familiarity and baseline performance, fine-tune scoring criteria, exclude results from Go/Modify/Stop verdict, and document lessons-learned for threshold calibration.
  • Define the scored-exercise phase (Months 10.5–11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27): full 70+ injection runs across all 7 event types with >=10 per type, sealed scoring and national-team independence, threshold-freeze decision point at Month 10.5 (2027-08-27) before scored injections, and detection-rate aggregation by event type.
  • Specify the bilateral-instrument lock and procedural governance: include exercise procedures, injection schedule, and dual-country authorization gates in the bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12); publish operator-facing schedule (dates and general scope, no scenario details) by Month 2 (2026-12-12) to allow facility preparation.
  • Include post-exercise audit and documentation: redacted summary report by Month 12 (2027-10-12) listing injection counts per event type, detection rates, false positive/negative counts, systemic findings, and any unresolved detection gaps; state explicitly what detection capability was shown for which event types under which conditions.
  • Establish the Challenge Exercise Design Panel composition and funding: 2 technical experts + 1 counterintelligence officer per country, pre-cleared by both governments, funded from USD 500M testing envelope, established by Month 1 (2026-11-12), with documented biographies and security clearance status.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague or non-binding event-type definitions allow interpreters to apply inconsistent detection criteria at injection time; a substitution that one country scores as 'detected' the other scores as 'not detected,' inflating scoring divergence and blocking Go verdict.
  • Sealed-scenario commitment not documented in blockchain or ledger allows one side to claim post-hoc that a scenario was designed after injection, weaponizing the exercise integrity as a political dispute rather than an empirical test.
  • Independent tester authorization unclear; operating inspectors and injecting testers from the same country could collude to suppress or exaggerate detection, undermining blind-exercise credibility before results are known.
  • False-positive containment not partitioned in the ledger permits a seeded challenge (e.g., injected substitution) to trigger automatic suspension if misclassified, halting Phase One operationally for 3-7 days without clear adjudication path.
  • Filter-adequacy pre-test not run before Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) leaves redaction-gateway adequacy unknown; scored exercises may reveal that >15% of substitutions are undetectable due to filtered-out identity fields, forcing Go reversal mid-Phase One.
  • Scoring-divergence threshold not pre-defined allows bilateral dispute over what divergence magnitude invalidates a verdict; one country claims 92% detection (Go), the other 87% (Modify), with no agreed arbiter or second-opinion protocol.
  • Misclassification escalation path absent means a false-positive CHALLENGE event triggers suspension, site halts, and no documented procedure returns operations; principals are surprised by the escalation and lack a standard adjudication template.
  • Post-exercise audit delayed to after the verdict or omitted entirely prevents transparent reporting of detection gaps; program claims 'Go' without disclosing that vendor-refusal scenarios had <50% detection rate, undermining credibility with oversight authorities.
  • Scenario injection logistics not documented (who physically injects, at what time, with what security controls) allow claims that injections were discovered pre-deployment or leaked to operating inspectors, destroying the blind-exercise validity.
  • No chain-of-custody for challenge scenarios from design through injection to score sealing invites dispute over whether scenario parameters were altered, injected quantity matched published quantity, or scoring data was tampered with between submission and comparison.

Worst Case Scenario: The sealed-scenario catalog is published by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27) as required, but during the scored-exercise phase (Months 10.5–11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27), one injected substitution triggers automatic suspension because the intake inspector does not detect it (true positive test failure) but the system misclassifies it as an operational breach, escalating to site suspension. The CHALLENGE tag is present in the ledger but the automatic-suspension trigger fires because threshold-violation rules do not properly filter on the tag. Operations halt for 3-7 days. By the time principals adjudicate and reinstate the site, 40 days remain before the verdict deadline (Month 12.25 = 2027-10-20). The remaining scored exercises cannot run at full pace; detection data for Months 11-12 (2027-09-12 to 2027-10-12) is sparse. At Month 12.25 (2027-10-20), both governments' technical teams report divergent detection rates (US team claims 91% Go-qualifying detection, China team reports 84% unverifiable-equipment driven failure). The scoring divergence exceeds 10% on vendor-refusal scenarios. With no sealed-score reconciliation protocol executed before the verdict deadline, the co-chairs cannot agree. The Go/Modify/Stop decision is blocked. The 90-day Phase One test ends without a conclusive verdict, political blame ensues, and the bilateral program is suspended or terminated as dysfunctional, with reputational damage globally and a USD 5 billion investment yielding no actionable evidence. The root cause: the Challenge-Exercise Design and Independent Testing Plan did not fully partition CHALLENGE-tagged events from automatic triggers, did not lock scoring-divergence reconciliation into the timeline, and did not document the misclassification escalation procedure with timers and automatic resolution.

Best Case Scenario: The Challenge-Exercise Design and Independent Testing Plan specifies 7 event types with precise detection criteria, sealed scenarios committed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27), and a filter-adequacy pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) that validates redaction-gateway adequacy at ≥90% detection before any scored runs. Preliminary calibration exercises (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27) refine procedures and thresholds freeze at Month 10.5 (2027-08-27). Scored exercises (Months 10.5–11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27) inject 70+ scenarios across all event types with CHALLENGE tags and automatic-suspension exemptions locked in the ledger protocol. National teams score independently and sealed scores are opened and compared by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05). Scoring divergence is <10% across event types, with technical referees issuing a dual-signed reconciliation report by Month 12 (2027-10-12). Detection data shows ≥90% blind detection for all 7 event types with <10% false-negative rate. By Month 12.25 (2027-10-20), both co-chairs can point to objective, independently verified, sealed-and-reconciled detection evidence; the Go verdict is defensible against political challenge; Phase One closes successfully on schedule within the 90-day window; and both governments have a credible, hard-to-contest empirical basis for assessing whether bilateral equipment-change verification is viable for Phase Two.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If sealed hash-committed scenario-catalog infrastructure is unavailable by Month 1 (2026-11-12), substitute a witnessed-scenario-design procedure: both countries' panels convene jointly to design scenarios in a secure facility (no separate red teams), sign a joint design document by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27), and inject scenarios according to the jointly signed specification with bilateral observers present at every injection point. Trade-off: loss of true 'blind' status because both teams see scenario parameters before injection, but maintains objectivity through joint design and witnessed execution.
  • If independent-tester clearance and staffing cannot be staffed for both countries by Month 8 (2027-06-12), substitute reciprocal red-team exercises: each country's inspectorate team assumes the role of attacking the counterpart's detection capability at the counterpart's site using pre-approved scenarios, with the host-country security liaison validating that attacks stay within bounds and the counterpart's inspectors document detection or miss. Trade-off: reduces true independence (testers are part of the regular inspectorate hierarchy) but maintains adversarial realism and avoids the need for a separate red-team hiring effort.
  • If sealed-score comparison infrastructure is unavailable by Month 11 (2027-09-12), substitute real-time scoring with bilateral observers: scoring occurs simultaneously at each country's site, with observers from the other country present to witness scoring decisions and initial tabulation, then both teams publish sealed scores for digital signature and comparison within 24 hours. Trade-off: introduces some opportunity for score tampering between local scoring and sealing, but mitigates by having foreign observers witness the initial count and spot-check sensitive results.
  • If the filter-adequacy pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27) reveals that redaction-gateway filtering exceeds acceptable limits (<85% substitution detection), substitute progressive filter loosening rather than halt: identify which evidence fields are critical to substitution detection, map them to the evidence schema, and incrementally reduce aggressive filtering on those fields while keeping topology and workload filtering tight. Run a second pre-test at Month 9 (2027-07-12) with adjusted filters, aiming for >=85% detection before scored exercises start. Trade-off: timeline compression and potential for incomplete field recovery if operators resist, but preserves exercise schedule and avoids a full renegotiation stall.
  • If reconciliation of scoring divergence >10% cannot be resolved by technical referees by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05), substitute blind third-party auditor: an independent technical auditor (not from either country, funded from legal/audit envelope) re-scores a random sample of 10–20% of the injected scenarios using the sealed videos and ledger records, then publishes a report on whether divergence reflects real detection differences or scoring-methodology disagreement. Trade-off: adds cost (USD 5-10M estimate) and 2-3 day delay, but provides a credible third-opinion if bilateral referees deadlock.
  • If CHALLENGE-tag exemption from automatic suspension is not embedded in the protocol by Month 7 (2027-05-12), substitute manual challenge-event exclusion at review time: allow automatic suspension to fire for CHALLENGE-tagged events, but establish a mandatory principal-level review within 2 hours to determine whether the suspension was triggered by a true detection (go ahead with suspension for exercise evaluation) or a misclassification (reinstate immediately). Trade-off: introduces delay and requires emergency principal availability, but preserves exercise conduct if the protocol infrastructure is incomplete.
  • If post-exercise audit report cannot be drafted by Month 12 (2027-10-12) due to scoring disputes, substitute interim findings release: publish the detection-rate data by event type and site (positive findings), flag unresolved scoring divergences as 'technical referees in progress,' and schedule a final audit report by Month 12.5 (2027-10-27) after referees complete their work. Trade-off: verdict announcement may precede complete audit transparency, weakening post-verdict scrutiny, but maintains reporting momentum.

Create Document 7: Filter-Adequacy Blind Pre-Test Specification and Execution Plan

ID: 11366718-9c0a-4768-a7d4-64c3c752a810

Description: Comprehensive specification for conducting the filter-adequacy blind pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with ≥10 injected equipment-substitution scenarios in staging and spare-inventory areas under operator-controlled redaction-gateway filtering. Includes: scenario design (wrong serial, firmware rollback, physical-mark tampering, attestation forgery), injection procedures (no inspector knowledge), blind-detection measurement by operating inspectors, scoring against jointly agreed criteria, and halt-if-<85%-detection rule. Documents the test's role as a prerequisite for Phase One entry certification. Primary audience: independent testers, intake inspectors, bilateral co-chairs.

Responsible Role Type: Challenge Exercise Design and Independent Testing Lead, Filtered Evidence and Redaction-Gateway Architect

Primary Template: Blind Exercise and Scenario-Injection Test Plan

Secondary Template: Detection-Rate Measurement and Halt-Criteria Procedure

Steps to Create:

  • Design 10+ equipment-substitution test scenarios spanning multiple detection-difficulty levels: (1) obvious substitution (different serial number, completely different device); (2) subtle substitution (same model, different firmware version, serial number off by 1 digit); (3) cryptographic-only discrepancy (physical marks match, attestation digest doesn't); (4) physical-only discrepancy (serial and marks match, but physical weight/dimensions don't match); (5) attestation-forgery scenario (forged cryptographic signature on a real device).
  • Schedule injection window by Month 8 (2027-06-12) involving staging and spare-inventory areas at both US and China representative sites; coordinate with operators to ensure injection areas are controlled and free from legitimate activity.
  • Specify blind-injection procedure: independent testers (not operating inspectors) inject substitutions overnight or during maintenance windows; injectors do not inform operating inspectors of injection; all injected scenarios are marked CHALLENGE in the ledger.
  • Define detection measurement: operating inspectors conduct routine intake or maintenance inspections of the staging/spare-inventory area; measure whether inspectors flag identity-confidence issues, escalate to unverifiable, or miss the substitution.
  • Specify scoring criteria: 'detection' = inspector flags ≥2 evidence layers in disagreement or escalates to unverifiable within 1 hour of inspecting the unit; 'non-detection' = inspector clears the unit without identity escalation within 1 hour.
  • Document redaction-gateway filtering applied: all raw records, sensor outputs and telemetry pass through the operator-controlled gateway before inspectors see them; measure impact of filtering on detection performance.
  • Set detection-rate target: ≥9 of 10 detected (90% baseline); ≥8.5 of 10 = acceptable (85% minimum threshold); <8.5 of 10 = HALT all scoring exercises and renegotiate filters.
  • Include halt-and-renegotiation procedure: if pre-test detection is <85%, both countries' sensitive-asset teams must jointly review which evidence fields are being filtered and whether redaction rules are stripping identity-critical information (serial, firmware hash, attestation digest); renegotiate filter rules and re-test within 2 weeks.
  • Publish pre-test results in the KPI dashboard and ledger by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27); include detailed results by scenario type, evidence-layer performance, filter impact, and any shortfalls identified.
  • Gate entry certification on pre-test results: Phase One entry certification cannot be finalized at Month 9 (2027-07-12) unless pre-test detection rate is ≥85%; if <85%, entry gate is deferred until renegotiation and re-test complete.

Approval Authorities: Challenge Exercise Design Panel and Independent Testers (pre-test design and execution), Bilateral Co-Chairs (halt decision and filter renegotiation authorization), and Principals (for entry-gate deferral if halt condition triggered)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the complete test-scenario design for ≥10 equipment-substitution injections spanning 5 difficulty tiers: (1) obvious substitution (serial mismatch, entirely different device model), (2) subtle substitution (same model, firmware rollback, serial off-by-1 digit), (3) cryptographic-only discrepancy (physical marks match, attestation digest doesn't), (4) physical-only discrepancy (serial and marks match, weight/dimensions don't), (5) attestation-forgery scenario (forged signature on real device). Include scenario randomization method so no test substitution is predictable.
  • Detail the blind-injection procedure: which sites (staged staging and spare-inventory areas at both US and China representative sites), which dates in Month 8 (2027-06-12) window (specify 2-3 maintenance windows), how injectors will enter areas unobserved, insertion method for each scenario type, ledger-tagging (CHALLENGE tag) before injection, and explicit instruction that operating inspectors receive zero foreknowledge.
  • Document the detection-measurement method: define 'detection' operationally as 'inspector flags ≥2 evidence layers in disagreement or escalates to unverifiable within 1 hour of inspecting unit'; define 'non-detection' as 'inspector clears unit without identity escalation within 1 hour'; specify who scores (independent observers, not inspectors), when scoring occurs (within 2 hours of inspection), and how false positives are distinguished from true positives.
  • Analyze the impact of operator-controlled redaction-gateway filtering on detection performance: map which raw fields (serial, firmware hash, attestation digest, physical marks, maintenance timestamp) are being filtered or redacted by the gateway; predict which detection scenarios are most vulnerable to field loss (e.g., if serial number is redacted, obvious substitution becomes undetectable); specify the filtering rules that will be applied during this pre-test.
  • Set detection-rate targets and scoring rules: primary target 9 of 10 detected (90%); acceptable threshold 8.5 of 10 (85%); HALT condition <8.5 of 10 (<85%), with mandatory filter renegotiation before any scored exercises; define how score is calculated (count of detected scenarios divided by total injections).
  • Define the halt-and-renegotiation procedure in detail: if pre-test detects <85%, both countries' sensitive-asset teams (specify team composition: ≥2 per country) convene within 48 hours; document which filter rules stripped identity-critical information; propose revised redaction schema; define 2-week re-test window and re-test success criteria (must reach ≥85% or entry gate is deferred); specify escalation to bilateral co-chairs if renegotiation stalls.
  • Specify the ledger-recording requirements: every injected scenario must be logged with CHALLENGE tag, injection timestamp, scenario type, injector identity (without inspector knowledge), inspector identity, inspection completion time, detection result (flag: yes/no), escalation decision (if any), and final disposition; reconcile logs between US and China within 4 hours.
  • Document results publication and entry-gate gating: pre-test results must be published in KPI dashboard and ledger by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27); include breakdown by scenario type (5 tiers), evidence-layer performance (which layers—physical, cryptographic, customs, maintenance—were sufficient to detect, which were insufficient), filter-impact analysis (identify specific redacted fields that reduced detection confidence), and narrative explaining any shortfalls; define explicit gate rule: 'Phase One entry certification cannot be finalized at Month 9 (2027-07-12) unless pre-test detection rate ≥85%; if <85%, entry gate is deferred until renegotiation and re-test complete.'
  • Specify the measurement of how the pre-test validates filter adequacy before scored exercises: document which specific scenarios would have been undetectable under the original filters (scenario-by-filter-failure mapping); confirm that the evidence schema (serial, firmware hash, attestation digest, timestamp, physical marks) is preserved by the gateway (non-negotiable); confirm minimum detection rate meets the 85% threshold; state that if pre-test fails, no scored exercises can begin until filter rules and re-test succeed.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Vague scenario design (e.g., 'test some substitutions' without specifying difficulty tier, serial numbers, firmware versions) leads to exercises that do not actually stress the detection system; inspectors may detect obvious substitutions while missing subtle ones, creating false confidence about filter adequacy that is later exposed during Phase One scored exercises.
  • Lack of strict blind-injection protocol allows inspectors to anticipate injections, consciously or unconsciously heightening vigilance and artifically inflating detection rates; pre-test results then do not predict Phase One performance, and confidence in filter adequacy is unsupported.
  • Undefined or subjective detection-measurement criteria ('detected' if inspector 'seems concerned' or 'asks questions') creates scoring disagreements between co-chairs; if US and China score the same scenario differently, the pre-test result is contested, entry gate stalls, and renegotiation timelines slip.
