  • Incomplete or outdated IAEA unique-identifier standards risk locking the Consortium's schedule to manufacturer-specific or generation-specific equipment classes that become obsolete within 5 years, violating the requirement for vendor-neutrality and schedule durability across hardware generations.
  • Missing IAEA inspector-training curricula on compartmentation and chain-of-custody will force the Consortium to develop counterintelligence and evidence-handling procedures from first principles, increasing the risk of procedural failures during Phase One and reducing the credibility of the evidence record.
  • Absence of documented IAEA precedents on vendor refusal and escalation procedures leaves the Consortium without tested procedures for handling a critical vendor's non-cooperation; the vendor-refusal ladder (refusal → supervised testing → clean rooms → fallback unverifiable) lacks operational grounding.
  • If IAEA's historical filtering edge cases and failures are not analyzed, the Consortium will design a filter-adequacy blind pre-test that misses the exact scenarios where filters have historically stripped critical fields; blind-exercise detection rates will be misleadingly high, leading to false confidence in the filtering architecture.
  • Incomplete equipment-specification standards and tamper-seal benchmarks will leave the provisional covered-equipment schedule vague on what constitutes a valid attestation digest, a valid seal, or a valid physical identifier, delaying identity verification and escalating boundary-case disputes.

Worst Case Scenario: ["The Consortium adopts a redaction-gateway filtering architecture and evidence schema without grounding in IAEA managed-access experience; during Phase One filter-adequacy blind pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27), discovered that the gateway is stripping serial numbers or firmware-version hashes needed for identity verification. At least 5–10 of the 10+ injected substitutions go undetected; blind-detection rate falls to 50%, far below the provisional 90% threshold. The filter-adequacy test halts, and a 2–3 week redesign of the gateway and re-test cycle begins, compressing the subsequent 90-day Phase One operational window and reducing the number of scored exercise cycles available for validation. The Go verdict is forced by calendar pressure rather than evidence sufficiency, and the program's credibility is undermined if filtering failures surface post-Phase One."]

Best Case Scenario: ["The Consortium adopts IAEA's proven managed-access principles and layered-evidence hierarchy before designing the redaction gateway, evidence schema, and inspector procedures. The non-redactable evidence schema is grounded in IAEA experience showing which fields are historically critical to detecting substitution and equipment diversion. The filter-adequacy blind pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27) includes IAEA's known edge cases and historical failure scenarios; 9 of 10 injected substitutions are detected, meeting the proposed 85% threshold and validating the filtering architecture. Inspector training incorporates IAEA compartmentation and chain-of-custody protocols, reducing counterintelligence and evidence-handling risk. Equipment-identity procedures and unique-identifier standards are anchored to IAEA's vendor-neutral, generation-agnostic seal-design benchmarks. Phase One proceeds with high confidence in the evidence system and the blind-exercise results credibly support the Go/Modify/Stop verdict."]

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Conduct urgent expert briefing sessions with IAEA Safeguards Division staff (available via iaea.org contact or Vienna office request, Month 7–7.5 = 2027-05-12 to 2027-05-27). Request focused technical guidance on: (1) managed-access filtering design and non-redactable evidence fields, (2) unique-identifier and seal-design standards, (3) vendor-refusal escalation procedures from IAEA experience. Distill guidance into a classified reference document for the filter-architecture design team before Month 8 (2027-06-12).
  • Obtain official copies of IAEA Safeguards Techniques and Equipment handbook and INFCIRC/540 Additional Protocol model from the IAEA website or official request channel; extract equipment-specification sections and unique-identifier requirements; cross-reference with Consortium's proposed covered-equipment schedule to validate compatibility and harvest generation-agnostic classification approaches.
  • Engage ESARDA (European Safeguards Research and Development Association) as a secondary source for peer-reviewed practitioner papers on managed access, seal validation and equipment identity; request permission to cite operational lessons learned from European safeguards implementations.
  • If IAEA technical guidance is not available or delayed beyond Month 7.5 (2027-05-27), establish a parallel Working Group of Consortium identity-verification specialists to develop evidence-schema and filtering requirements from first principles, explicitly labeled as 'non-validated baseline pending IAEA expert review'; flag this as a risk in the filter-adequacy pre-test plan (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27) and allocate extended schedule for redesign if independent validation reveals gaps.
  • Commission a limited contracted study on historical equipment-diversion cases from IAEA safeguards history (publicly documented cases, declassified inspection reports where available) to reverse-engineer which evidence fields would have caught each diversion; use findings to validate the proposed non-redactable evidence schema independently of real-time IAEA coordination.
  • Schedule a formal IAEA Safeguards Division liaison role (funded from USD 250M legal/audit envelope) for the 18-month period preceding Phase One (Months -6 to Month 12 = 2027-10-12), with monthly technical exchange sessions on managed access, filtering adequacy, and equipment-identity precedents; embed IAEA expert insights into procedure design checkpoints at Months 6, 7, 8 and 8.5 (2027-04-12, 2027-05-12, 2027-06-12, 2027-06-27).

  • Search the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) website for FIPS 140-3 approved modules and their validation certificates; review security policy documents for each module.
  • Access NIST standards and guidelines via csrc.nist.gov, specifically NIST SP 800-155 (Guidelines for Hardware Security Module Firmware), SP 800-193 (if published) or equivalent.
  • Search the Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement (ccra.acm.org) for certified Protection Profiles (PPs) for cryptographic modules and secure-element devices; download published PPs and Evaluation Assurance Levels (EALs).
  • Consult academic and industry sources (IEEE, ACM, Usenix security conferences) for published research on attestation-forgery attacks, firmware-rollback vulnerabilities, and key-custody best practices.
  • Contact industry cryptographic vendors (Intel Security Engines, ARM TrustZone, Qualcomm Secure Processing Unit teams) for vendor-specific attestation documentation and key-custody protocols.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium: Standards and many security-policy documents are publicly available on government and standards-body websites; vendor-specific key-custody procedures may require direct vendor contact or are proprietary.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the latest TPM 2.0 specifications and architectural requirements (2023–2026), including attestation protocols, key-storage models and quote generation mechanisms.
  • Define FIPS 140-3 validated cryptographic modules approved post-2020 and their security-policy implications for attestation-key custody and validation in accredited-examiner workflows.
  • Document Common Criteria Protection Profiles for cryptographic devices (latest versions) and required Evaluation Assurance Levels (EAL) for equipment-identity validation at intake.
  • Specify realistic error rates and failure modes for cryptographic attestation validation: key-compromise attacks, firmware-rollback vulnerabilities, time-of-check-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gaps, and vendor-specific weaknesses.
  • Describe vendor key-custody best practices and audit mechanisms that enable independent validation by accredited examiners without exposing private keys or pre-production secrets.
  • Quantify detection rates for attestation-forgery attacks and substituted firmware under realistic filtering and evidence-reduction protocols; identify which attack vectors cannot be mitigated by layered physical corroboration.
  • Define the accredited-examiner qualification criteria, training requirements and bilateral authorization procedures so that US and Chinese examiners can independently validate the same attestation signatures.
  • Provide a multi-vendor attestation landscape: Intel Security Engines, ARM TrustZone, Qualcomm Secure Processing Units, and any frontier-relevant accelerator attestation schemes; identify coverage gaps or vendor-specific failure modes.
  • Specify the binding between hardware attestation timestamps and customs-entry or staging-arrival events (proposed ±2-hour tolerance): detection procedures if attestation timestamp diverges from movement records.
  • Document fallback evidence chains when attestation cannot be validated: chain-of-custody records, physical markings, sealed containers, maintenance logs and movement witnesses that can substitute for or corroborate cryptographic proof.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated standards documentation leads accredited examiners to validate attestation signatures against deprecated cryptographic algorithms or key-custody practices, creating false confidence in identity that later fails under scrutiny.
  • Missing error-rate data on attestation-validation failures means the proposed 95% identity-confidence threshold cannot be validated by blind exercises; Phase One detection rates remain ungrounded.
  • Failure to document vendor-specific key-custody procedures leaves examiners unable to independently verify that a vendor's attestation signatures bind to actual hardware; vendor attestation becomes unvalidatable and equipment escalates to unverifiable status.
  • Omission of firmware-rollback and TOCTOU attack vectors means the Equipment Identity Trust Anchor does not address realistic compromise modes; an attacker substitutes firmware-updated equipment while preserving old attestation signatures, passing intake undetected.
  • Lack of specification on how physical corroboration (customs records, tamper seals, movement witnesses) bridges gaps left by attestation validation failures means the two-layer agreement rule cannot be operationalized; disputed identity escalations have no clear adjudication path.
  • Incomplete multi-vendor landscape assessment leaves critical accelerator or frontier-relevant equipment types without attestation-validation protocols; Phase One encounters equipment from unscoped vendors and must escalate to unverifiable.
  • Weak accredited-examiner qualification criteria allow low-confidence or untrained examiners to sign off on attestation validation; bilateral trust in identity verification erodes.
  • Missing timestamp-binding procedures mean attestation validation is decoupled from evidence of physical arrival; an attacker substitutes equipment with attestation from a different delivery, passing intake.

Worst Case Scenario: ["The entire Equipment Identity Trust Anchor rests on attestation validation, but the standards documentation provided is incomplete, unvalidated against realistic attack vectors, and does not bind attestation to physical movement or customs records. Phase One begins with no baseline confidence in whether attestation validation is reliable; blind exercises reveal that 20–30% of substituted equipment passes intake because attestation signatures are forged or firmware is rolled back without detection. Identity confidence crashes from the proposed 95% threshold to 60–70%, triggering unverifiable-equipment escalation for 20+ sites or entire Phase One failure. The Go verdict is reversed or replaced with Stop due to fundamental evidence-system failure. Bilateral cooperation is discredited; each government blames the other's attestation protocols or examiner standards. The USD 5 billion pilot is perceived as technically failed and politically compromised, with residual distrust poisoning future verification negotiations."]

Best Case Scenario: ["The attestation standards document provides detailed, up-to-date TPM 2.0, FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria specifications with quantified error rates, vendor-specific key-custody procedures and realistic attack-vector mitigations. Accredited examiners from both countries use this to independently validate attestation signatures against the same standards, achieving 95%+ identity confidence on intake. Blind exercises confirm that 90–95% of substituted equipment is detected via attestation validation, with physical corroboration (customs + maintenance logs) catching an additional 3–5% of borderline cases. Equipment unverifiable due to attestation failure remains below the 3% threshold; all sites pass Phase One on identity grounds. The Go verdict rests on validated, hard-to-contest evidence of detection capability; bilateral confidence in the Equipment Identity Trust Anchor is justified and transferable to Phase Two or ongoing operations."]

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If comprehensive TPM 2.0, FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria documentation cannot be accessed or is insufficient: engage directly with major cryptographic vendors (Intel, ARM, Qualcomm) to provide proprietary key-custody validation procedures and attestation-signature specifications under bilateral NDA; document vendor-specific protocols in a sealed, vendor-controlled technical appendix usable only by accredited examiners.
  • If realistic error rates and attack-vector data are not published: conduct accelerated adversarial testing in Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) filter-adequacy phase using certified security researchers to attempt attestation forgery and firmware rollback against representative equipment samples; use empirical Phase One pre-test results to calibrate identity-confidence thresholds before scored exercises.
  • If accredited-examiner qualification standards are unclear: establish a bilateral technical-standards committee (2 cryptographic specialists per side, funded from testing envelope) to issue dual-signed examiner certifications based on published standards and the vendor-specific protocols obtained; require all attestation validation to pass bilateral examiner review before intake closure.
  • If timestamp binding between attestation and movement records cannot be hardened: rely on physical corroboration as a mandatory second layer—require customs entry records, shipment tracking logs and staged entry-area movement witnesses to all align with attestation timestamps within the ±2-hour tolerance; escalate any timestamp divergence to technical referees for adjudication rather than allowing attestation alone to settle identity.
  • If coverage gaps exist for frontier-relevant accelerators or emerging vendor equipment: pre-emptively add those vendors to the vendor-refusal ladder; require them to provide attestation documentation by Month 8 (2027-06-12) or their equipment is classified as unverifiable pending clean-room examination; do not delay Phase One start for missing vendor documentation.
  • If the two-layer agreement rule cannot be operationalized due to insufficient corroboration channels: add a third layer—physical tamper-seal inspection in staging areas before movement, with bilaterally witnessed seal-state comparison against baseline photographs and customs documentation; use triplet agreement (attestation + movement record + seal state) to raise identity confidence to 95%+.

Find Document 5: US Domestic Access Authority and Legal Compulsion Precedents (Private Vendors, Export Control, State Enterprises)

ID: dc63f9cc-62eb-4225-8275-c9bb0c0438c9

Description: Legal opinions, statutes and case law documenting US authority to compel private vendors and equipment manufacturers to participate in verification inspections, potential conflicts with export-control regulations (EAR, ITAR), intellectual-property protections, and any exemptions for state-owned enterprises or contractors with classified government work. Source material for the bilateral legal working group to assess whether domestic access authority exists or requires new legislation. Intended audience: legal implementation team, bilateral counsel. Context: identify legal gaps or bottlenecks that could delay or prevent vendor binding.

Recency Requirement: Current statutes and precedents (2010–2026): Export Administration Regulations (EAR), International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) as currently enforced, relevant federal case law on inspection authorities, Treasury Department rulings on Chinese state-enterprise participation.

Responsible Role Type: Legal Implementation and Bilateral Instrument Lead

Steps to Find:

  • Contact the US Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) in the Department of Justice; request a legal opinion on authority to compel private-vendor participation in bilateral equipment verification inspections.
  • Access the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) export-control guidance on EAR and ITAR exemptions for government-authorized verification activities.
  • Search the US Code (title 22, title 50) for verification-authority precedents (e.g., New START inspection authorities, Open Skies Treaty implementation).
  • Contact the Export-Import Bank and the Foreign Direct Investment Committee (CFIUS) for guidance on restrictions that might apply to equipment verification at US facilities.
  • Consult the Congressional Research Service (crs.gov) for reports on US verification authorities and legal implementation of arms-control treaties.
  • Review relevant case law via Google Scholar (scholar.google.com) for judicial opinions on inspection authorities and vendor-compulsion limits.

Access Difficulty: Medium: Unclassified statutes and public case law are freely available; legal opinions from OLC or Department of State may be available through FOIA request or official channels, potentially with redactions.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the current statutory basis in US law (22 USC, 50 USC, Export Administration Regulations, International Traffic in Arms Regulations) that permits compulsory inspection authority over private vendors and equipment manufacturers in a bilateral verification regime.
  • Determine whether EAR and ITAR exemptions exist or can be created for government-authorized bilateral equipment verification without triggering export-control violations or technology-transfer restrictions.
  • Document any judicial precedents (case law, 2010–2026) establishing or limiting federal authority to compel private-sector participation in arms-control verification inspections.
  • Assess whether US intellectual-property law (trade secrets, confidential business information, patents) creates legal barriers to compulsory inspector access to equipment specifications, firmware, maintenance records or physical examination.
  • Define the legal status of state-owned enterprises (Chinese) under US law when they participate in bilateral verification; identify any Treasury Department, CFIUS or Foreign Direct Investment restrictions that might block participation or impose conditions.
  • Specify what domestic access authority (statute, executive order, delegation of authority) currently exists or must be enacted before entry-gate certification; quantify any legislative or regulatory approval timeline (months).
  • Identify potential legal challenges (constitutional due-process claims, Fifth Amendment takings, Commerce Clause limits) that private vendors might raise against compulsory participation and assess likelihood of successful litigation.
  • Document the legal mechanisms (contract flow-down, regulatory requirement, statute, licensing condition) by which reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation duties can be imposed on vendors and operators.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If domestic access authority does not exist or is legally ambiguous, vendor binding cannot be completed before the entry gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-12); delay 2–4 months estimated, pushing Phase One start to Month 11–13 (2027-09-12 to 2027-11-12) and compressing operational evidence collection.
  • If export-control exemptions are not secured in writing from BIS/DDTC, vendors may be exposed to criminal liability for technology transfer or inspection cooperation; refusal risk increases, estimated 5–15% of declared equipment becomes unverifiable.
  • If legal challenges to compulsion succeed in court, a critical vendor can block participation and exit the supply chain; that government loses access to that vendor's equipment for verification purposes, material unverifiable-equipment count climbs above the 3% threshold.
  • If IP-law barriers are not resolved (e.g., vendors can shield maintenance logs or firmware details), physical inspection and attestation alone must anchor identity; identity confidence falls below the 95% target, reducing detection credibility.
  • If state-enterprise restrictions block Chinese participation or impose conditions (escrow, compensation limits, repatriation rules), Chinese operator and vendor participation fails; sites fail outright, Phase One cannot proceed with planned scope.
  • If flow-down mechanisms are not legally sound (contract clauses do not survive review, regulatory requirements are not enacted), vendors can refuse reporting and evidence-preservation duties without legal consequence; unverifiable equipment and operator shielding risk.

Worst Case Scenario: Domestic access authority does not exist or cannot be enacted within the entry-gate timeline (by Month 9 = 2027-07-12). Legal review reveals that current US statutes do not authorize compulsory inspection over private vendors without new legislation, and legislative authorization cannot be secured until late 2027 or 2028. Concurrently, export-control counsel advises that equipment inspection by Chinese inspectors at US facilities triggers ITAR technology-transfer restrictions unless an exemption is issued, and BIS cannot issue exemptions without interagency review consuming 3–6 months. Chinese legal counsel advises that CFIUS restrictions or US criminal exposure block Chinese state-enterprise vendors from participating on terms acceptable to Beijing. Result: entry-gate certification is impossible by Month 9 (2027-07-12); Phase One start slips 6–12 months to Months 15–21 (2028-01-12 to 2028-07-12). USD 100–200 million (estimate) in sunk preparation and personnel costs are absorbed without operational data. Political momentum dissolves; both governments declare the pilot too legally complex and withdraw. Program terminates; bilateral verification credibility is damaged globally.

Best Case Scenario: Legal review confirms that US domestic access authority exists under 22 USC § 2593a (verification inspections for arms-control agreements) and can be delegated to the program by executive order; no new legislation required. Export-control counsel secures written exemptions from BIS and DDTC affirming that bilateral equipment verification is not a controlled technology transfer and does not violate EAR or ITAR. DoJ Office of Legal Counsel issues an opinion confirming federal authority to compel private-vendor participation through contractual flow-down and licensing conditions. Chinese counsel confirms CFIUS and foreign-enterprise restrictions can be satisfied through standard confidentiality agreements and sealed examination procedures. By Month 7.5 (2027-05-27), the bilateral legal working group certifies that all legal barriers are resolved and vendor binding can proceed by Month 8 (2027-06-12). Entry-gate certification is completed by Month 9 (2027-07-12) as planned. Phase One runs on schedule Months 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12) with full vendor participation and no legal holdups. Verdict is delivered with high credibility that all evidence was collected under sound legal authority.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If statutory authority does not exist, obtain expedited legislative clearance by Month 7 (2027-05-12): introduce a short authorization bill in Congress (5–10 pages, delegating verification-inspection authority to the executive) and seek unanimous-consent passage or fast-track committee approval. Budget USD 5–10 million (estimate) for legislative advocacy and legal implementation. Timeline: 4–8 weeks if leadership pushes; feasible but politically exposed.
  • If export-control exemptions are unavailable or conditional, substitute with a sealed clean-room examination model: vendors submit equipment to an independent accredited facility (not on-site) for supervised inspection by both countries' examiners, with filtered evidence returned; no controlled technology transfer occurs at US or Chinese facilities. Adds USD 20–30 million (estimate) to testing envelope and delays vendor binding by 4–6 weeks, but removes export-control barrier.
  • If private-vendor litigation risk is high, require vendors to sign liability-waiver and indemnification agreements before entry gate, funded by escrow insurance or government indemnity. Reduces legal challenge likelihood but increases vendor compensation demands and adds USD 10–20 million (estimate) to contingency.
  • If state-enterprise restrictions block Chinese participation, substitute Chinese state enterprises with privately held Chinese vendors or allow Chinese government to establish a proxy entity with independent legal status. Requires bilateral diplomatic negotiation but removes CFIUS and foreign-investment barriers.
  • If flow-down enforcement is weak, supplement contractual language with a bilateral vendor-registry statute or executive order imposing direct regulatory requirements on all vendors servicing declared sites; non-compliance = license revocation or criminal penalty. Requires legislation or strong executive authority but provides stronger enforcement.
  • If entry-gate delay becomes unavoidable (>6 weeks slippage confirmed by Month 7.5 = 2027-05-27), activate the grace-period rule: begin Phase One operations with a subset of 2 matched sites (1 US, 1 China) where legal authority is certain, and defer the remaining 2 sites by 2–4 months pending legal resolution. Reduces Phase One scope but preserves operational momentum and data collection; verdict may be qualified as 'Phase One Pilot on 2 Sites' rather than full 4-site verdict.

Find Document 6: Chinese Domestic Access Authority, Vendor-Compulsion Mechanisms, and State-Enterprise Legal Status

ID: 5a3be795-bcc8-45b6-b1f3-30fdb27d83c9

Description: Chinese legal framework governing verification-authority delegation, vendor-compulsion mechanisms for private and state-owned enterprises, export restrictions on equipment inspection or telemetry export, and potential conflicts with internal Chinese security or industrial-policy regulations. Source material for the bilateral legal working group to assess parallel-authority constraints in China. Intended audience: legal implementation team, Chinese counterpart negotiators. Context: understand Chinese legal and institutional constraints that could limit vendor binding or complicating reciprocal access.

Recency Requirement: Current Chinese laws and regulations (2015–2026): Foreign Trade Law of the People's Republic of China, Regulations on Export Control of Goods and Technologies (relevant to dual-use equipment), National Security Law (2015 version and amendments), guidance on state-owned enterprise compliance with bilateral obligations.

Responsible Role Type: Legal Implementation and Bilateral Instrument Lead

Steps to Find:

  • Contact the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Department of Arms Control and Disarmament, for guidance on verification-authority delegation and vendor participation.
  • Access the Chinese Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) for regulations on export controls and equipment-verification procedures.
  • Consult the Chinese Academy of Sciences or relevant Chinese research institutions for translations or summaries of current Chinese legal frameworks on verification authority.
  • Request information through official bilateral diplomatic channels (e.g., US–China Joint Commission meetings) on Chinese legal authorities and any anticipated legislative changes.
  • Access Chinese-language legal databases (if available through university or government partnerships) for current statutes and regulatory guidance.
  • Consult published analyses by law firms or think tanks specializing in Chinese law (e.g., Covington & Burling, Zhong Lun) for expert summaries of applicable legal frameworks.

Access Difficulty: Hard: Most detailed Chinese legal guidance and internal directives are not publicly available in English; official diplomatic channels or specialized Chinese-law expertise are required; translations may be available through academic or government partnerships.

Essential Information:

  • Define the legal mechanisms available to the Chinese government to compel state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and private domestic vendors to participate in the bilateral verification program and to comply with verification duties (reporting, evidence preservation, confidentiality, escrow, inspection access).
  • Identify any Chinese laws or regulations (Foreign Trade Law, Export Control Regulations, National Security Law, SOE governance directives) that restrict or prohibit the export, inspection, telemetry export, or foreign scrutiny of equipment, firmware, or facility data that would conflict with reciprocal-access obligations.
  • Determine whether Chinese domestic-security regulations or industrial-policy rules create legal ambiguities or exemptions for critical vendors (telecommunications, semiconductor manufacturing, state research institutes) that could prevent their binding participation.
  • Specify the enforceability hierarchy: which Chinese government bodies (MOFCOM, State Council, Ministry of National Defense, relevant line ministry) have authority to issue binding directives for vendor participation, and what legal instruments (administrative order, regulation amendment, contract-flow requirement) carry enforcement weight.
  • Document any required legislative changes, State Council approvals, or inter-ministerial coordination that must occur before the bilateral instrument can be implemented domestically, and estimate the approval timeline.
  • Assess whether parallel US and Chinese legal authorities are substantively symmetric: can both governments equally compel their domestic operators and vendors, or do asymmetries exist (e.g., US reliance on private law vs. Chinese SOE administrative hierarchy) that would affect binding credibility or enforcement.
  • Identify anticipated legal challenges or reinterpretation risks: courts, administrative bodies, or internal directives that could contest vendor-compulsion authority, restrict equipment telemetry export, or revoke SOE participation orders post-signature.
  • Provide translations or authoritative summaries of current Chinese statutes and regulations relevant to verification authority, export control, and SOE compliance obligations.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or inaccurate assessment of Chinese legal authority leaves vendor-binding gaps at the entry gate: critical vendors claim they cannot legally participate due to SOE status, security classification, or export-control conflicts; vendor binding is incomplete and Phase One entry conditions cannot be certified.
  • Asymmetry between US and Chinese legal mechanisms becomes apparent mid-Phase One: China cannot legally compel a critical vendor that the US side assumed would be bound, leaving material equipment unverifiable and the site unable to meet the ≤3% unverifiable threshold.
  • Unanticipated legislative requirement discovered post-instrument-signature: Chinese legal review determines that a State Council or National People's Congress amendment is needed to authorize vendor participation; estimated 3–6 month delay to enact domestically, pushing Phase One start to Month 12+ and compressing the 90-day test window.
  • Vendor participation order is legally challenged in Chinese administrative court or contested by an SOE on national-security grounds: legal uncertainty persists through Phase One, vendors refuse to implement verification duties until challenge is resolved, and material equipment counts remain unverifiable.
  • Export-control conflict emerges: Chinese regulations prohibit the telemetry or equipment-data export needed to satisfy the evidence-schema minimum fields; filters must strip critical identity fields, detection confidence falls below 95% threshold, identity anchor breaks.
  • Enforcement asymmetry: US government can legally compel vendor participation through contract flow-down and regulatory authority; Chinese government lacks equivalent enforcement power over private vendors or issues ambiguous directives that vendors interpret as optional, leading to asymmetric participation rates and parity disputes.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical vendor (e.g., a leading semiconductor manufacturer or telecommunications SOE) is determined to be legally exempt from verification obligations under Chinese law, or participates under conditions that materially narrow the evidence available to inspectors. Entry conditions cannot be certified because vendor binding is incomplete; Phase One is delayed until legislation is enacted or vendor exemptions are negotiated, adding 3–6 months to the program and compressing the 90-day test window to a point where credible challenge-exercise coverage is impossible. The bilateral instrument becomes operationally unimplementable on one side, creating a fatal asymmetry in which the US can enforce vendor compliance but China cannot, triggering a Go-decision reversal or Stop verdict due to unequal enforcement of reciprocal obligations.

Best Case Scenario: Chinese legal framework is confirmed to give the government unambiguous authority to compel both SOEs and private vendors to participate in verification through existing administrative mechanisms or a narrow statutory amendment that can be enacted by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27). Export-control and national-security laws are confirmed to have a carve-out or waiver mechanism for bilateral verification activities. Vendor binding can be completed by Month 8 (2027-06-12) through a binding administrative directive or contract-flow requirement, with symmetric enforcement mechanisms that match US-side authority. Entry-gate certification is achieved on schedule, Phase One starts at Month 9 (2027-07-12), and 90-day test window runs uninterrupted with full vendor participation and unobstructed evidence collection, enabling credible detection and reciprocal-access demonstration.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Chinese legal authority over vendors is found to be limited or ambiguous, negotiate a narrower bilateral instrument that exempts certain vendor categories (e.g., state research institutes performing classified work) from direct participation, and instead route their equipment through a neutral-party clean-room examination center (referenced as USD 30–50M option in the plan) where evidence is collected without exposing sensitive details to foreign inspectors.
  • If legislative amendment is required but cannot be enacted by the entry-gate deadline (Month 9, 2027-07-12), establish a temporary executive-order or State Council directive with a 90-day renewable authority (covering Phase One), then ratify via legislation post-verdict. Document this as a provisional legal mechanism with stated duration in the bilateral instrument.
  • If export-control restrictions prevent certain telemetry or equipment-data fields from leaving China, pre-agree with the US counterpart that those fields will be redacted consistently under an operator-controlled gateway, validate that redaction does not eliminate the minimum evidence schema, and run filter-adequacy blind exercises (Month 8.5, 2027-06-27) to confirm detection capability is not materially degraded. Mark the redaction as a documented constraint in all Phase One reports.
  • If a critical vendor cannot be legally compelled to participate, activate the vendor-refusal ladder early (Month 7, 2027-05-12): offer vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, or independent examination via clean-room centers as alternatives. If vendor still refuses, escalate to principals within 48 hours and classify that vendor's equipment as unverifiable; document the exemption in entry-condition certification so both governments understand the constraint before Phase One starts.
  • If parallel US and Chinese legal mechanisms are found to be asymmetric, supplement the bilateral instrument with a Procedural Equivalence Annex that specifies how the US will accept Chinese directives and orders as legally equivalent to US regulatory enforcement, and vice versa, so asymmetry does not become a dispute vector during Phase One.
  • Consult published analyses by leading Chinese-law firms (Covington & Burling, Zhong Lun, DLA Piper) specializing in export control, SOE governance and bilateral compliance to obtain expert-vetted summaries of current Chinese legal frameworks if direct government access is limited.

Find Document 7: Cryptographic Ledger and Distributed-Consensus Specifications and Protocols

ID: 96c3c85b-8358-4405-9e88-49552adb49b1

Description: Technical specifications for replicated tamper-evident ledgers, hash-chain-based audit trails, Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols, cryptographic checkpoint formats, key-exchange ceremonies and non-repudiation mechanisms. Source material for designing the Ledger Synchronization and Divergence Doctrine. Intended audience: ledger architects, cryptographic specialists. Context: understand available distributed-ledger technologies and cryptographic primitives suitable for bilateral evidence systems.

Recency Requirement: Current technical standards and research (2015–2026): NIST recommendations on cryptographic hash functions and digital signatures, academic research on Byzantine fault tolerance (Practical BFT, PBFT variants), ledger-synchronization protocols, audit-trail standards.

Responsible Role Type: Secure Ledger and Tamper-Evidence Systems Architect

Steps to Find:

  • Access NIST cryptographic standards via csrc.nist.gov; download NIST FIPS 180-4 (Secure Hash Standard) and FIPS 186-5 (Digital Signature Standard).
  • Search academic databases (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Arxiv) for published research on Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols, replicated state machines and audit-trail architectures.
  • Consult industry blockchain and distributed-ledger technology whitepapers and technical documentation (though note that Consortium ledger is NOT a blockchain; it is a bilateral cryptographic checkpoint system).
  • Request technical guidance from NIST Computer Security Division on recommended key-exchange and signature protocols for bilateral government systems.
  • Consult with cryptographic security firms or academic cryptography research groups for recommendations on checkpoint formats and divergence-detection algorithms.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium: NIST standards and academic papers are publicly available; specialized consulting or deep technical briefings may require engagement of cryptographic specialists.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific cryptographic hash functions, digital-signature algorithms and key-exchange protocols meeting NIST standards (FIPS 180-4, FIPS 186-5) suitable for bilateral government ledger systems with non-repudiation requirements.
  • Define the distributed-consensus mechanism (Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol) required to reconcile two independent national ledger copies within the 1-hour synchronization KPI (proposed threshold) while tolerating network latency, node failures and malicious divergence up to the 5%-discrepancy threshold (proposed).
  • Specify the checkpoint format (proposed: signed hash-chain) that binds events into an immutable audit trail, including event serialization, timestamp binding, signature composition and digest algorithm selection.
  • Document the key-ceremony and key-management protocols for generating, storing, validating and rotating cryptographic keys for both countries' ledger nodes, including escrow mechanisms for the neutral digest custodian.
  • Describe the divergence-detection algorithm that identifies ledger copies exceeding the 5%-discrepancy threshold (proposed) and the bounded reconciliation procedure to resolve disputes without third-party arbitration.
  • Define the non-repudiation mechanisms (dual signatures, timestamping, audit-trail immutability) that ensure neither government can later deny a ledger entry or claim its copy was unilaterally modified.
  • Specify technical requirements for the ledger transport layer: dedicated authenticated IPsec tunnel with mutual TLS, not shared internet; security properties against exfiltration, tampering and replay attacks.
  • Articulate the relationship between the Consortium's bilateral cryptographic ledger and blockchain technologies: explain why a replicated checkpoint system (not a blockchain) is appropriate for sovereign bilateral verification without a public ledger or third-party consensus participant.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Hash functions that do not meet NIST standards or are deprecated (e.g., SHA-1) render the ledger vulnerable to collision attacks; an attacker can forge entries or alter evidence without detection, invalidating the entire tamper-evident foundation.
  • Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols specified without Byzantine quorum assumptions or fault-tolerance bounds allow one country's ledger node to diverge undetectably; divergence age exceeds the 4-hour detection KPI (proposed), delaying adjudication and feeding the Stop criterion.
  • Checkpoint formats without cryptographic binding to event content or timestamps allow later reordering, deletion or insertion of entries; audit trails become questionable, undermining identity confidence and evidence sufficiency.
  • Key-management protocols that do not segregate key custody or require dual control leave keys vulnerable to single-government compromise; a compromised signing key allows unilateral ledger forgery without detection.
  • Divergence-resolution procedures that require a third-party arbiter (e.g., neutral custodian deciding which copy is authoritative) violate the bilateral double-key governance model; disputes cannot be resolved without escalating beyond the technical system.
  • Non-repudiation mechanisms insufficient to bind signatures to ledger entries or timestamps allow a government to later claim its signatures were forged or entries altered; verdict basis becomes deniable.
  • Transport-layer security gaps (shared internet, unencrypted checkpoints, lack of mutual authentication) expose ledger copies to exfiltration, tampering or cryptographic key theft; bilateral confidentiality and integrity guarantees are lost.
  • Confusion between Consortium bilateral cryptographic ledgers and blockchain consensus systems leads to overspecification (consensus with >2 nodes, public ledger, decentralized miners), architectural misfit and unnecessary complexity that a bilateral system does not need.

Worst Case Scenario: The specified cryptographic protocols are incomplete, use deprecated or non-NIST-approved algorithms, or do not satisfy Byzantine fault tolerance for two-node consensus. As a result: (1) At Month 10 (2027-08-12), a divergence emerges between the US and Chinese ledger copies; the detection algorithm fails to flag it until Day 12, exceeding the 4-hour KPI. (2) Reconciliation procedures require neutral-custodian arbitration, which violates bilateral governance; an impasse results. (3) One country claims the other's copy was forged; neither government trusts the ledger as evidence. (4) The Go verdict cannot proceed because evidence authenticity is in doubt. (5) Phase One stalls or terminates mid-phase with a Stop decision driven not by operational failure but by ledger-system distrust. (6) Reputation damage: program discredited as technically unfit; bilateral verification as a governance model is rejected.

Best Case Scenario: Specifications define cryptographic primitives (hash, signature, key-exchange) meeting NIST standards, a Byzantine fault-tolerant two-node consensus protocol (or checkpoint-exchange scheme) that reconciles ledger copies within the 1-hour KPI with no third-party arbiter, immutable audit trails binding events to timestamps and signatures, and dual-control key management preventing unilateral forgery. Divergences are detected within 4 hours and resolved by bilateral technical teams within 24 hours. Evidence authenticity is defensible: both governments independently trust the ledger records. The Go verdict rests on evidence neither government can later contest. Technical credibility is established early; Phase One proceeds uninterrupted by ledger doubts.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a full cryptographic specification document is unavailable, consult published NIST Cryptographic Standards (FIPS 180-4, FIPS 186-5, SP 800-56A for key exchange) and academic research on Byzantine consensus (Practical BFT, PBFT variants, recent consensus literature) to synthesize the required protocol design in-house with cryptographic specialists.
  • Engage a specialized cryptographic security firm (e.g., academic cryptography research groups or national security contractors with appropriate clearances) to produce a classified technical specification that can be used for implementation without public disclosure.
  • If bilateral divergence-resolution procedures cannot be designed to avoid third-party arbitration, revise the governance model to allow a jointly appointed neutral technical custodian (held in escrow, not trusted for policy decisions) to provide only digest verification, not content arbitration.
  • If two-node Byzantine protocols are deemed impractical, document the security properties that the simpler two-node checkpoint-exchange scheme (hourly signed checkpoints with offline comparison) achieves and does not achieve, then explicitly accept the residual divergence risk and set monitoring KPIs accordingly.
  • Conduct threat modeling and cryptanalysis of the selected protocol before implementation; if any attack surface remains unmitigated (e.g., key exfiltration, timestamp forgery, signature collision), document compensating controls (e.g., air-gapped key storage, offline backup verification, quarterly re-signing ceremonies) and acceptance by both co-chairs.
  • Test the ledger protocols in a bilateral dry-run (Month 8.5, 2027-06-27, proposed) injecting artificial divergences and network delays to validate that detection latency meets the 4-hour KPI and that reconciliation closes within 24 hours; if not, redesign before Phase One starts.

Strengths

  • Layered evidence with no decisive source: Attestation, customs records, physical inspection and witnessed movement must agree across at least two layers. This resists single-point forgery and gives a verdict that is hard for either government to contest.
  • Narrow, well-bounded mission: Only declared-equipment changes at about 4 matched sites are verified, with explicit exclusions (no total-capacity estimate, no workload or weight inspection). The limited claim keeps the technical problem tractable and the conclusions defensible.
  • Governance built for distrust: Double-key authorization, no casting vote, enumerated suspension triggers and a CHALLENGE-tag partition make obstruction and manufactured incidents visible and bounded. Deadlock timers (5/8/13 days) convert disagreement into a recorded process.
  • Empirical decision basis: Hash-committed blind exercises (at least 10 injections across 7 event types) with thresholds frozen before scoring turn the Go/Modify/Stop verdict into measured evidence rather than political judgment.

Weaknesses

  • Attestation concentration: Identity is anchored on vendor-issued attestation, so key compromise, forgery or vendor refusal can make a large share of units unverifiable (10-40%, estimate). Corroborating layers may not compensate when the counterpart disputes their origin.
  • Filtering can blind detection: Operator-run redaction gateways have an incentive to strip fields, and the counterpart audits rules but not inputs. Filter adequacy is untested until the pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27), so substitution may pass undetected.
  • Many thresholds are unvalidated: Figures such as 95% identity confidence, 3% unverifiable and 90% detection are proposed thresholds with no empirical grounding. Pre-registration may encode guesses that force an unwarranted Modify or hide real weakness.
  • Compartmentation versus context: Strict compartmentation and tenure limits protect hosts but fragment the site knowledge inspectors need to recognize substitution. Staffing of roughly 350-500 cleared people (estimate) is also hard to surge or backfill.

Opportunities

  • Reusable verification methods: Equipment-identity chains, tamper-evident ledgers and hash-committed exercise catalogs could inform later technical verification research. Documenting them openly where classification permits adds to the evidence base on verifying digital-hardware change.
  • Learning from precedent: IAEA seals and managed access, OPCW mock challenge inspections and New START unique identifiers offer mature, tested practices. Expert exchange with these communities can shorten design iteration and improve credibility.
  • Empirical parity measurement: Reason-coded access logging and outcome-based parity give a rare quantitative picture of reciprocity under distrust. The data can refine matched-site equivalence and inform whether bilateral change verification is credible.
  • Vendor-neutral schedule design: A role-based, versioned covered-equipment schedule can demonstrate how verification stays valid across hardware generations. This creates a template for technology-agnostic definitions.

Threats

  • Entry-gate stall: Seven mandatory conditions must be certified together, and instruments, appropriations and access authority typically take 6-12 months (estimate). Slippage past Month 12 (2027-10-12) erodes political momentum and could end the program before testing begins.
  • Espionage and IP leakage: Resident inspectors, translators and evidence systems form a collection channel for the counterpart. A single breach can cause operator withdrawal, site failure and an impaired-confidence review.
  • Political fragility and obstruction: No enforcement path exists beyond suspension, as New START's breakdown shows. A government can stall findings, shield an operator or withhold funding, and manufactured triggers can cascade into suspension.
  • Legal and supply-chain disruption: Litigation over compelling private vendors or state-enterprise ambiguity may delay binding by 2-4 months (estimate). Geopolitical or export-control shocks could also alter vendor participation mid-test.

Recommendations

  • Start instrument negotiation, legal review and supplier declarations immediately, with weekly entry-condition tracking and the principal go/no-go at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27). Owner: co-chairs' legal working group.
  • Complete vendor binding by Month 8 (2027-06-12) and stand up at least 2 clean-room centers by Month 9 (2027-07-12), with a documented refusal ladder. Owner: bilateral technical unit.
  • Run the filter-adequacy pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with at least 10 substitutions and halt scored exercises below 85% detection. Owner: exercise design panel.
  • Hold a staffing dry-run at Month 8 (2027-06-12) and validate leave, surge and tenure assumptions before clock start. Owner: mirrored personnel units.
  • Lock deadlock timers, suspension triggers and the CHALLENGE-tag rule in the instrument before signature, and rehearse a misclassification escalation within 2 hours. Owner: adjudication unit.

Strategic Objectives

  • By Month 9 (2027-07-12), certify all 7 entry conditions at a single gate with a matched instrument, schedule and site set.
  • Achieve at least 90% blind detection for each of 7 event types with at least 10 injections each by Month 11.5 (2027-09-27) (proposed threshold).
  • Hold identity confidence above 95% and unverifiable equipment at or below 3% per site through the 90-day window (provisional).
  • Keep reciprocal-access variance within 10% and ledger synchronization within 1 hour, with zero production disruption, through Month 12 (2027-10-12).
  • Deliver a Go/Modify/Stop verdict at Month 12.25 (2027-10-20) with every threshold documented, validated or marked provisional.

Assumptions

  • Both leaders give sustained political backing and domestic compulsion authority throughout Phase One.
  • Attestation-capable equipment and accredited examiner laboratories exist in both countries.
  • Four sites (2 matched US-China pairs) provide comparable staging, spare-inventory, maintenance and expansion areas.
  • Dedicated authenticated transport and hardened ledger nodes can be built before Month 9 (2027-07-12).
  • Cleared, bilingual full-time inspectors can be recruited and vetted in time (estimate).

Missing Information

  • Actual vendor mix and attestation-key custody for declared equipment at each site.
  • Validated detection rates under realistic filtering; all thresholds remain provisional.
  • Final China site location and the governance venue (Geneva or Singapore).
  • Local event-recording latency and false-positive limit (TBD).
  • Scope, criteria and funding for any Phase Two after the verdict.
  • Status of domestic legal authority to compel private vendors in each country.

Questions

  • Which evidence layer should carry the most weight if attestation and physical inspection conflict, and what would justify that ordering?
  • How can the minimum evidence schema be made detailed enough to expose substitution without revealing topology or workload information?
  • What exercise design could test a determined state adversary rather than only anticipated scenarios in a sealed catalog?
  • How should reciprocal-access parity be normalized across non-identical sites so that disputes reflect real asymmetry rather than site differences?
  • What wording and procedures will keep closed exit records from implying knowledge beyond the monitored boundary?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Bilateral Co-Chair and Governance Lead (Joint National Leadership)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral Co-Chair role requires equal national representation and double-key authorization for all major decisions. This is a sovereign governance position with continuous accountability from Month -6 through verdict and beyond. Requires absolute continuity—absence of either co-chair halts decision-making. Cannot be part-time, contracted, or temporary without violating the bilateral instrument's governance constraint. One co-chair per country, full-time employee of respective government.

Explanation: One designated lead per country who jointly controls double-key authorization for all major decisions: budgets, protocol changes, site findings, suspension and sanctions. Co-chairs chair weekly steering committees, escalate deadlocks to principals, certify entry conditions, and sign off on all Phase One verdicts. This role ensures equal national sovereignty, prevents unilateral override and operationalizes the core governance constraint that 'no casting vote' and 'double-key authorization' are non-negotiable.

Consequences: Without co-chairs with explicit double-key authority locked in the bilateral instrument, one government can act unilaterally on budget, protocol, suspension or verdict decisions. This violates the program's core governance design and creates asymmetric decision power. Deadlocks cannot be escalated credibly, and political obstruction becomes weaponizable. The Go/Modify/Stop verdict loses bilateral legitimacy.

People Count: 2 people (one per country), full-time from Month -6 through Month 12+. No alternates; continuity is essential. If either chair leaves office, successor is designated before transition. Funded from personnel envelope.

Typical Activities: Chairs weekly bilateral steering committees with Chinese counterpart to track entry-condition progress and escalate bottlenecks within 48 hours. Co-signs all major decisions: budget tranches, protocol changes, site findings, suspension orders, and the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict. Convenes the Bilateral Technical Referee Panel within 24 hours of a deadlock and enforces the 5-day consensus window. Escalates unresolved discrepancies to principals at Day 10 (proposed) if co-chairs cannot agree. Certifies entry conditions at the single gate in Month 9 (2027-07-12). Maintains a docket of aging findings and activates automatic-suspension triggers on schedule. No casting vote; all decisions require bilateral consensus or escalation. Availability is continuous; no delegations without bilateral agreement.

Background Story: Margaret Chen, based in Washington DC, holds a 22-year career in bilateral arms control and verification. She served as US lead negotiator on the New START Bilateral Consultative Commission from 2018 to 2024, managing dispute resolution and inspection access across 15 quarterly sessions. A career US Foreign Service Officer with Secret/SCI clearance, she holds a master's in international relations from Princeton and speaks Mandarin Chinese. Her expertise in reciprocal governance, deadlock procedures, and equal-authority structures makes her the natural co-chair on the US side, tasked with implementing double-key authorization on all major Consortium decisions from Month -6 through Month 12+.

Equipment Needs: Secure communications devices: government-issued encrypted phone (FIPS-140-2 approved), air-gapped laptop with cryptographic-token access to bilateral ledger systems, hardware security module (HSM) for co-signing digital documents. Bilateral steering-committee video-teleconference system with SCIF-compatible encryption and recording in the tamper-evident ledger. Physical: signed hard-copy documents for bilateral instrument, budget authorizations, suspension orders, verdict certification. No commercial cloud services. Budget allocation from USD 750M personnel envelope for secure comms infrastructure.

Facility Needs: Secure facility (SCIF equivalent) housing bilateral co-chair office with secure meeting room (Faraday-caged conference table for classified discussion, no electronic devices except approved encrypted phones and air-gapped laptops). Access control: biometric card + iris recognition, no manual keys. Continuous intrusion detection (network and HIDS). Physical segregation from operational inspectorate. Proximity to national capitals (US: Washington DC area; China: Beijing) for rapid escalation access to principals. Neutral third-country venue (Geneva or Singapore) for joint deliberations when escaping home-country pressures is needed. No public internet access from the office; all external comms via dedicated authenticated IPsec tunnels to ledger nodes and bilateral network.

2. Mirrored National Inspectorate Units (Resident On-Site Teams)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Mirrored National Inspectorate Units (200–250 front-line staff) operate 24/7 continuous shift coverage at 4 sites, Months 0–12 (2026-10-12 to 2027-10-12)+. The plan explicitly mandates 'no single-person critical functions, no temporary-agency inspectors, no part-time inspectors.' Each inspector holds security clearances, compartmentation rules, and identity-verification authority. Full-time employment is a non-negotiable constraint. No detection capability exists without continuous resident presence. Staff are hired by their respective governments.

Explanation: Full-time mirrored teams stationed continuously at each of 4 participating sites (2 US, 2 China), organized by 24/7 shift coverage with at least 2 trained inspectors per critical function (intake, monitoring, exit). Each shift works in bounded inspection zones with pre-validated instruments and escorted movement. Intake teams verify equipment identity; monitoring teams track changes and maintenance; exit teams witness departures. These teams are the primary detection mechanism for unreported arrivals, substituted equipment and inaccurate records.

Consequences: Without continuous resident mirrored teams, unreported arrivals and substituted equipment cannot be detected directly; detection depends entirely on operator reporting (which the pilot is designed to test) and delayed remote evidence. This is the core failure mode the plan explicitly rejects: 'Do not use single-person critical functions, part-time or temporary-agency inspectors.' Without this role, Go decision credibility collapses. Operator willingness also declines if foreign inspectors are not resident and visible, eroding consent.

People Count: Min 200-250 front-line inspection staff across all 4 sites and all shifts (estimate: 3 posts per shift, 2 staff per post, 4 sites, 3 shifts = 72 base; plus 15% leave = 82.8; plus 10-30% surge reserve = 100-150 total front-line), plus cross-site floaters for surge and substitution coverage. Leave allowance 15%, surge reserve 10-30% (proposed). No part-time inspectors, no temporary-agency staff, no single-person critical functions. Total inspectorate estimated 350-500 FTE including specialists. Funded from USD 750M personnel envelope.

Typical Activities: Coordinates 24/7 mirrored shift coverage with Chinese counterparts at the same site, ensuring continuous presence in bounded inspection zones. Conducts equipment intake identity verification using attestation validation, customs records, and physical inspection per the agreed evidence hierarchy. Witnesses arrival movements, inspects tamper seals, records serial numbers and firmware versions in the tamper-evident ledger. Monitors declared equipment during maintenance and movement. Witnesses departure and assigns exit disposition (destruction, disablement, transfer, release, or unresolved). Enforces compartmentation rules, zone boundaries, and pre-validated instruments only. Reports boundary violations or operator incidents to the bilateral co-chair within 1 hour. Manages leave and surge staffing within 15% leave buffer and 10-30% surge reserve.

Background Story: James Okonkwo, 15-year datacenter security and on-site inspection veteran, leads the residential inspection teams at the Northern Virginia declared site. Former DTRA on-site inspection officer with experience on New START inspections (2011–2020), he holds a bachelor's in electrical engineering and a master's in security studies. Cleared to Top Secret/SCI, experienced in 24/7 shift coordination and evidence preservation in adversarial settings. He manages three intake, three monitoring, and three exit teams across three shifts per day, ensuring at least two trained inspectors are present in every critical function at all times.

Equipment Needs: Field inspection toolkit per inspector (USD 50K-100K estimated per kit): pre-validated instruments only (no recording devices, connected IT systems, or commercial smartphones). Items: calibrated serial-number and firmware-version readers (air-gapped, vendor-approved), physical tamper-seal verification tools, cryptographic attestation-validation devices (air-gapped USB tokens loaded with validation software and bilateral public keys), photography equipment with film-only capability (no digital storage on-site), handwritten logbook and evidence chain-of-custody forms (paper-based, no IT dependency). Protective equipment (static-free clothing, gloves, shoe covers for clean areas). Communication: hardwired phones at bounded inspection zones (no cellular or wireless in staging areas). Budget from USD 750M personnel envelope. Consumables: tamper seals, evidence bags, pre-printed inspection forms, ballpoint pens.

Facility Needs: Bounded inspection zones at 4 declared sites (2 US, 2 China) marked with painted lines and electronic access controls (biometric card readers, no manual keys). Zones include: staging area (500-1000 sq m estimated), spare-inventory area (300-500 sq m estimated), maintenance area (200-300 sq m estimated), equipment-expansion area (200-300 sq m estimated). Each zone: climate control (to prevent firmware/seal degradation), 24-hour video recording (host-country operator-controlled, redaction gateway applied before export), dedicated secure inspection-team workroom (air-gapped computers for evidence logging, no internet, no external media except approved bilateral ledger node access). Mirrored bilateral rooms at each site (one for US inspectors, one for Chinese inspectors) with compartmented access and separate evidence-handling procedures. Proximity to customs facilities and logistics hubs for shipment-record verification. Zero disruption to active-compute areas; production halls and customer-data zones strictly off-limits. Shift change facilities (lockers, break rooms, secure storage for equipment and evidence).

3. Bilateral Ledger and Cryptographic Systems Architect

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral Ledger and Cryptographic Systems Architect leads the tamper-evident ledger's design, deployment, and 24/7 operations from Month 0 (2026-10-12) through Month 12+. Ledger integrity is foundational to the Go/Modify/Stop verdict. The role requires continuous presence at hardened secure facilities, cryptographic key custody, and immediate response to synchronization or divergence events. No interim gap is tolerable. Minimum 2 architects per country plus operators = full-time positions.

Explanation: Designs, deploys and operates the replicated, tamper-evident ledger system maintaining independently verifiable copies at each country's secure facility. Responsible for checkpoint format, synchronization protocol, cryptographic key generation and custody, divergence detection and reconciliation procedures. Works with counterpart's specialist to ensure both ledger copies remain synchronized within 1-hour tolerance and divergence is detected within 4 hours (proposed). Develops minimum evidence schema and filter rules applied at evidence gateways. This role ensures the evidentiary record cannot be altered unilaterally or lost.

Consequences: Without dedicated ledger architects, synchronization latency exceeds KPI targets, divergences age undetected, and one government can secretly alter its copy before the mismatch is discovered. Evidence credibility is destroyed and the entire Go/Modify/Stop verdict becomes contestable. Ledger divergence is a Stop criterion; failure in this role directly triggers program termination.

People Count: Min 2 per country (one ledger architect/lead, one cryptographic specialist), full-time from Month 0 (2026-10-12) through Month 12+, plus 2-3 technical operators per country. Total min 8-10 FTE. Ledger nodes in hardened, geographically diverse SCIF-equivalent facilities with biometric access and continuous intrusion detection. Funded from USD 1.25B ledger/attestation/comms envelope.

Typical Activities: Designs and implements replicated, tamper-evident ledger system with independently verifiable copies at each country's hardened secure facility. Conducts bilateral cryptographic key-derivation ceremony in Month -1 (2026-09-12) to generate shared secrets for checkpoint signing. Generates hourly signed hash-chain checkpoints with bilateral timestamp, nonce, and event-count validation. Monitors synchronization latency (proposed 1-hour KPI) and triggers alert if exchange exceeds 60 minutes. Conducts automated divergence detection within 4 hours (proposed), initiates reconciliation procedures, and documents all mismatches in the ledger with root-cause analysis. Maintains cryptographic key custody protocols and leads unannounced facility-security reviews quarterly. Operates the neutral-party digest-escrow interface.

Background Story: Dr. Sofia Volkov, Moscow-born cryptographer with 18 years in government secure-communications systems, designed the ledger architecture for the Consortium. PhD in cryptography from Moscow State University, cleared to equivalent-high level by both US and Russian authorities (prior work), she holds current Top Secret/SCI US and Chinese-equivalent clearances. Expert in hash-chain ledgers, Byzantine fault tolerance, and cryptographic key custody ceremonies. She leads the bilateral ledger team from the US secure facility in Virginia, coordinating hourly signed checkpoints with her Chinese counterpart to keep both national copies synchronized within one hour (proposed KPI).

Equipment Needs: Cryptographic hardware security modules (HSMs) for bilateral key custody: two hardened HSMs per country (USD 50K-100K per HSM estimated), one in primary ledger node, one as backup in geographically diverse facility. Devices for checkpoint generation, signing and validation. Air-gapped terminal for key-derivation ceremony (one per country, used once in Month -1). Network devices: dedicated IPsec firewalls and TLS termination appliances (USD 200K-500K per country estimated) for transport between national ledger nodes, no internet routing. Servers: hardened Linux systems (Common Criteria EAL 4+ estimated) running cryptographic-ledger software, with full-disk encryption and SELinux mandatory-access controls. Intrusion-detection systems (network and host-based) monitoring all ledger access 24/7. Backup media: encrypted external drives and air-gapped optical media for offline backup and neutral-custodian escrow. Budget from USD 1.25B ledger/attestation envelope.

Facility Needs: Two hardened, geographically diverse SCIF-equivalent secure facilities (one per country, each 200-400 sq m estimated): US facility in hardened datacenter (estimated: Arlington VA or Maryland suburbs); China facility in equivalent state-secured location (estimated: Beijing-area data center or equivalent). Each facility: biometric access control (card + iris, no manual keys), continuous video surveillance (tamper-evident, not exportable without co-chair authorization), armed host-country security (no shared guards), Faraday cage or RF-shielded enclosure for HSM cryptographic-key storage, UPS and backup power (no single point of failure, 72+ hours runtime), climate control and fire suppression. Physical separation from any internet-connected systems (air-gapped, no shared power or network infrastructure). Dedicated backup facility at neutral third-country custodian (Geneva or equivalent, under joint escrow agreement) holding offline copies of ledger checksums and seed material. Quarterly unannounced bilateral facility-security inspections by counterpart's security personnel. Budget from USD 1.25B ledger/attestation envelope and USD 750M secure-facilities envelope.

4. Counterintelligence and Personnel Security Unit Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Counterintelligence and Personnel Security Unit Lead establishes CI protocols, vets all 350–500 inspectorate staff, implements compartmentation and tenure limits, and runs insider-threat red cell from Month -3 through Month 12+. Continuous vetting and compartmentation monitoring cannot be outsourced or part-time; compromise during a gap in CI coverage creates undetected penetration risk. Requires sustained institutional authority. Minimum 4 senior CI specialists per country.

Explanation: Leads a bilateral CI unit tasked with vetting all inspectors and technical staff, implementing compartmentation rules and tenure limits, and running an insider-threat red cell that attempts to compromise inspectors and evidence handlers. Establishes CI protocols, conducts polygraph and background reviews, manages clearances, monitors for relationship capture or financial compromise, and investigates any suspected breach. Embedded CI liaison officers report to this lead at each site. Protects the inspectorate from becoming a collection channel for the counterpart government and preserves operator consent by demonstrating counterintelligence discipline.

Consequences: Without CI vetting and compartmentation, inspectors become high-value espionage targets. A compromised inspector can exfiltrate equipment identifiers, facility layouts, vendor information or classified procedures. Operator confidence drops if foreign inspectors appear to be intelligence collectors; operators withdraw consent and participating sites fail outright. One major breach could collapse Phase One mid-operation. CI failure is a direct path to the Stop criterion 'government shields an operator' or 'impaired-confidence suspension.'

People Count: Min 4 senior CI specialists per country (plus embedded site liaisons), full-time from Month -3 through Month 12+. Insider-threat red cell: 2 per country. Total CI unit min 12-16 FTE. Funded from USD 750M facilities/security envelope. Vetting and polygraph testing of all 350-500 inspectorate staff (estimate) by Month 8 (2027-06-12).

Typical Activities: Establishes bilateral CI vetting protocol by Month -3 (2026-07-12), requiring background investigation, financial review, counterintelligence polygraph and cleared vetting for all inspectors and technical staff. Assigns personnel to compartments (site and event type) ensuring no individual holds cross-site identity or facility knowledge. Implements 6-month tenure limits and mandatory 2-month breaks between reassignments. Oversees 2-person insider-threat red cell per country attempting to compromise inspectors through social engineering, financial offers, and technical approaches from Month 0 (2026-10-12) forward. Investigates any suspicious contact or relationship and documents all red-team findings in the ledger as audit items. Escalates credible compromise attempts to principals within 4 hours. Audits compartmentation quarterly and terminates any access violations immediately.

Background Story: Colonel David Blackwood (retired), 27-year Defense Intelligence Agency career spanning counterintelligence operations and personnel-security programs, leads the bilateral Counterintelligence Unit from Arlington, Virginia. Fluent in Mandarin, he designed the CI protocols for a prior US-allied technical-intelligence partnership (unclassified) and holds a master's in strategic intelligence. He is responsible for vetting all 350–500 inspectorate personnel, implementing compartmentation rules, running the insider-threat red cell, and ensuring no inspector becomes a collection target. His team monitors for relationship capture, financial compromise, and unauthorized information access.

Equipment Needs: Vetting and polygraph equipment: standard counterintelligence polygraph devices (USD 30K per device estimated), 2-3 units per country for concurrent testing; polygraph training and accreditation per bilateral standard (estimated 60-80 hours per operator). Secure background-investigation databases (FBI/OPM systems for US, equivalent Chinese systems): 2-3 analyst workstations per country with restricted access, no export capability, logs maintained in tamper-evident fashion. Red-team operational equipment: laptop for social-engineering scenario planning, communication-interception tools (legal, law-enforcement authorized only), financial-monitoring subscriptions for compromise-detection. Secure communication devices for CI-unit cross-border coordination (air-gapped encrypted phones, hardware security tokens). Physical security equipment: access-control card readers, intrusion-detection sensors for compartmented spaces. Budget from USD 750M security/CI envelope.

Facility Needs: Secure CI office (SCIF equivalent, 100-150 sq m estimated) with physical segregation from operational inspectorate and secure facilities (no shared access paths). Biometric access control, continuous surveillance, no recording of CI discussions (by protocol). Secure storage vault for vetting files and polygraph records (classified SECRET minimum). Interview rooms (soundproofed, no electronic devices except approved polygraph equipment and air-gapped laptops for record-keeping). Site liaison quarters at each of 4 declared sites: 50 sq m dedicated secure spaces (one per country) where CI liaisons review inspector notes before export, compartmented from general inspection areas. Red-team operational headquarters (separate, secure facility in neutral location or host country, estimated 150-200 sq m) where red-team operators plan and log attempted compromise scenarios. No external communication from CI spaces except via air-gapped channels to bilateral co-chair office. Budget from USD 750M security/CI envelope.

5. Vendor Binding and Equipment Identity Verification Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Vendor Binding and Equipment Identity Verification Lead manages the complete vendor-binding pipeline and clean-room examination centers from Month -2 through Month 12+. This role operates layered fallback evidence ladders, conducts vendor classification by Month 10 (2027-08-12), and escalates vendor refusals to principals. Sustained presence ensures vendor compliance tracking and unverifiable-equipment classification before Phase One verdict. Examiners staffing clean rooms are also full-time (estimated 30–50 FTE across both centers and all shifts).

Explanation: Manages the complete vendor-binding pipeline: identifies critical vendors, negotiates participation terms, establishes the pre-qualified vendor registry, and implements the three-tier fallback evidence ladder for vendors who refuse or whose attestation keys are compromised. Operates or oversees accredited clean-room examination centers where refusing vendors submit units for supervised testing. Conducts vendor-census classification by Month 10 (2027-08-12), assigns equipment to unverifiable status if vendor attestation cannot be independently validated, and escalates vendor refusals to principals within 5 days. This role prevents vendor-concentration risk (estimated 10-40% equipment unverifiable) from becoming a Phase One killer.

Consequences: Without explicit vendor-binding authority and clean-room fallback, vendor refusal is an unmanaged failure pathway. If a critical vendor refuses or keys are compromised, equipment at that vendor's cluster becomes unverifiable; if unverifiable exceeds 3% per site, the site fails Phase One outright. Estimated 10-40% of equipment at risk. Without this role, Go decision is blocked. Vendor is also a binding lever: without vendor commitment to reporting and confidentiality duties, access to evidence and identity corroboration is lost.

People Count: Min 2-3 per country (vendor lead + examiner coordinators), full-time from Month -2 through Month 12+, plus examiners staffing clean rooms (estimated 4-6 per center per shift, 2 centers, 3 shifts = 24-36 examiners; estimate 30-50 total vendor-team FTE). Clean-room construction and security USD 30-50M within secure-facilities envelope. Funded from USD 500M testing envelope and USD 750M secure-facilities envelope.

Typical Activities: Identifies critical vendors (>2% of declared equipment at any site) and negotiates participation terms by Month -1 (2026-09-12).
