Conducts vendor-census classification by Month 10 (2027-08-12), assigning each vendor to binding categories: (A) binding signed + keys validated, (B) binding signed but keys unvalidated, (C) no binding or refusal. Operates or oversees two bilateral-accredited clean-room examination centers (one US, one China) by Month 9 (2027-07-12) where refusing vendors submit units for supervised independent testing. Validates vendor cryptographic attestation keys through bilateral accredited examiners per the agreed attestation-primary identity anchor. Escalates any vendor whose attestation remains unvalidated by Month 10 (2027-08-12) to unverifiable status and demands bilateral principal resolution within 5 days. Maintains the three-tier fallback evidence ladder (attestation, customs/maintenance/inspection, supervised examination) for each vendor.

Background Story: Dr. Hiroshi Tanaka, 20-year supply-chain security engineer with expertise in hardware attestation, cryptographic key management and vendor compliance, leads vendor binding and equipment identity verification from a secure lab in Mountain View, California. PhD in computer security, he has negotiated attestation-key custody with three major semiconductor manufacturers and implemented accredited examination procedures for classified equipment. He knows the vendor landscape intimately and understands the incentives and technical capabilities of critical equipment suppliers.

Equipment Needs: Vendor examination and attestation-validation equipment in clean rooms (per center): cryptographic-key validation devices (air-gapped, bilateral public-key loaded), firmware-extraction and analysis tools (isolated, no network connection), physical-tamper-detection microscopes and analysis tools (optical, high-magnification, non-destructive), serial-number and identifier-verification scanners (pre-validated, air-gapped). Testing equipment for destructive analysis (if permitted by vendor): desoldering and chip-extraction equipment, logic analyzers, power-consumption monitoring (for side-channel analysis). Accreditation and proficiency-testing subscriptions (per IAEA or equivalent model). Secure evidence-logging workstations (air-gapped) in each clean room. Budget from USD 500M testing envelope and USD 750M secure-facilities envelope.

Facility Needs: Two bilateral-accredited clean-room examination centers (one per country, 500-800 sq m each estimated): US center at a cleared facility (estimated Northern Virginia datacenter campus); China center at equivalent state-secured facility (Beijing-Hebei or Shanghai). Each center: ISO Class 7 or equivalent cleanliness (for non-destructive equipment analysis), electrostatic-discharge protected surfaces, temperature and humidity control. Three distinct zones per center: (1) receiving and identification area (for initial equipment intake and vendor interaction); (2) examination area (sealed, air-gapped, for cryptographic and physical analysis without exposing source code); (3) disposal area (for units approved for destruction, with licensed e-waste handling). Bilateral sealed-evidence protocol: US and Chinese examiners present for all testing, dual sign-off on findings before export from facility. Secure storage for equipment under test (environmental protection, security cameras, inventory control). No commercial internet or uncontrolled external access; all evidence transfer via air-gapped media or courier-escorted bilateral channels. Budget USD 30-50M (estimate) for construction, fit-out and accreditation.

6. Bilateral Dispute Resolution and Deadlock-Escalation Manager

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Bilateral Dispute Resolution and Deadlock-Escalation Manager enforces the 5-day co-chair consensus window, convenes technical referees, and tracks aging discrepancies from Month 6 (2027-04-12) through Month 12+. This role prevents deadlock from weaponizing delay by maintaining the escalation docket and firing automatic-suspension triggers on schedule. No gap in coverage; unresolved discrepancies age without active management. The role operates the core governance mechanism preventing obstruction.

Explanation: Manages the deadlock escalation pipeline: tracks contested site findings and equipment-identity disputes, enforces the 5-day co-chair consensus window, convenes the Bilateral Technical Referee Panel (2 experts per side) for Days 5-8 fact statements, and escalates unresolved disputes to principal-level review by Day 13. Maintains a standing docket of aging discrepancies and monitors unresolved-discrepancy age, triggering impaired-confidence review at 10+ days and automatic suspension triggers at 15+ days (proposed thresholds). Prevents one government from stalling by delay, which is the core governance tension the plan identifies.

Consequences: Without explicit escalation timers and an active dispute manager, deadlock persists indefinitely. Findings age without resolution, feeding unresolved-discrepancy Stop criterion. One government can obstruct silently by stalling at co-chair level while appearing compliant. The plan explicitly requires 'Define deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures.' Absence of this role leaves those procedures undefined and unexecuted. Phase One collapses into political gridlock.

People Count: Min 2 per country (one dispute manager, one scheduler/logger), full-time from Month 6 (2027-04-12) through Month 12+, plus the Bilateral Technical Referee Panel (2 technical experts per country, pre-cleared, part-time or reserve callout). Total min 4-8 FTE. Referees funded from USD 750M personnel envelope. This role is also staffed by the Bilateral Co-Chairs' office.

Typical Activities: Maintains a standing docket of all contested site findings and equipment-identity disputes, recording the initial co-chair notification date and the 5-day consensus deadline. Convenes the Bilateral Technical Referee Panel (2 experts per country) on Day 5 of deadlock, ensuring both sides brief the panel within 24 hours. Compiles the dual-signed advisory fact statement from referees by Day 8. Escalates unresolved findings to principal-level review by Day 10 and ensures principals render a decision within 5 calendar days (Day 13 deadline). Tracks unresolved-discrepancy age and triggers impaired-confidence review at 10+ days and automatic site suspension at 15+ days without principal written authority to continue (proposed thresholds). Logs all escalation events in the tamper-evident ledger with timestamps and decision outcomes. Acts as secretary to the dispute-resolution process.

Background Story: Attorney Patricia Rodríguez, 16-year international law and dispute-resolution expert with background in treaty implementation, leads bilateral dispute resolution and deadlock escalation from a Geneva-based office. JD from Yale Law, she has served as legal counsel to prior bilateral-arms-control commissions and understands escalation procedures, timing constraints, and the political pressure-points of stalled findings. She is the keeper of the docket, the enforcer of timers, and the architect of automatic suspension.

Equipment Needs: Dispute-resolution case-management system: secure database (government-classified minimum) tracking every contested finding with notification and escalation timers, accessible only to bilateral dispute manager and co-chairs. Digital ledger interface to query and validate disputed entries in real time. Video-teleconference capability (SCIF-compatible encryption) for rapid convening of technical referees (Tier 2 escalation). Encrypted email and secure document-storage for docket entries and principal-level correspondence. Red-phone or equivalent for emergency escalation (emergency landline connecting bilateral co-chair offices). Time-synchronization clocks (atomic or GPS-disciplined, +/- 1 second accuracy) for enforcing 5-day, 8-day and 13-day deadlock escalation timers precisely. Budget from USD 750M personnel and secure-comms envelopes.

Facility Needs: Secure dispute-resolution office (100-150 sq m estimated, SCIF equivalent) co-located with bilateral co-chair office or at neutral third-country venue (Geneva). 24/7 staffing (shift coverage) with no gaps during Phase One. Access control and surveillance. Secure communication room with encrypted video-teleconference system for convening technical referees within 24 hours. Dedicated timer workstation (air-gapped, showing countdown to 5-day/8-day/13-day milestones) for enforcement visibility. Physical clock on wall (atomic-synchronized, visible to both parties). Rapid-access filing system (secure, paper-based docket) for aging-discrepancy tracking. Proximity to principals (escalation to key leadership within 4-hour travel time, or secure encrypted comms capability). Budget from USD 750M facilities envelope.

7. Independent Budget Auditor and Fiscal Accountability Officer

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Independent Budget Auditor and Fiscal Accountability Officer is appointed jointly but remains independent of both governments (not a government employee). Accredited bilaterally, the auditor verifies tranche releases, monitors envelope spending, flags divergence >15%, and escalates >20% to impaired-confidence review. Independence from government control is essential to credibility; the role is expert-driven and milestone-based (tranche reviews, monthly burn reports). Part-time or full-time depending on burn rate, but contractual (fixed scope, deliverables: monthly reports, tranche certifications, spending audits).

Explanation: Bilaterally appointed independent auditor (not a government agency) who verifies each tranche release against parity criteria, confirms envelope spending by category, and certifies that neither government's cumulative disbursement leads the other's by >10% of pro-rata share (proposed threshold). Issues monthly burn reports per envelope, flags spending divergence >15% requiring explanation before next tranche, and escalates divergence >20% to impaired-confidence review and tranche hold. Ensures USD 5B budget cap is respected and prevents one-sided spending drift that erodes program credibility. Also certifies that only program-financed costs count against the cap.

Consequences: Without independent budget auditing, one government can front-load contingency spending or over-compensate domestic vendors, claiming asymmetric budget parity. Disputes over spending become funding-parity Stop criterion. The plan requires matched-tranche spending with 50/50 parity; without auditing, this constraint is unverifiable. USD 5B cap enforcement relies entirely on this role. Absence triggers financial credibility collapse and unresolved budget disputes at verdict time.

People Count: Min 1 independent auditor (firm or individual) plus 1-2 support analysts, full-time or part-time (estimated 2-3 FTE), from Month 7 (2027-05-12) through Month 12+. Funded from USD 250M legal/audit envelope (estimated USD 5-10M). No government employee; must be internationally accredited and accepted by both co-chairs.

Typical Activities: Issues monthly burn reports by envelope category (ledger, site prep, personnel, facilities, testing, legal/audit, contingency) tracking cumulative disbursement by both countries. Certifies each quarterly tranche release (USD 625M per country at Months 7, 10, 13, 16 = 2027-05-12, 2027-08-12, 2027-11-12, 2028-02-12) only if cumulative parity does not diverge by >10% of pro-rata share (proposed threshold). Flags spending divergence >15% monthly, requiring explanation from both co-chairs before next tranche release. Escalates divergence >20% to impaired-confidence review and tranche hold. Monitors contingency draws, flagging any drawdown >USD 10M for bilateral review and any approach to 75% draw (USD 375M) for escalation to principals. Certifies that only program-financed costs count against the USD 5B cap. Conducts quarterly reconciliation of CNY-to-USD conversion compliance.

Background Story: Robert MacLeish, CPA and international auditor with 19 years in government-contract and bilateral-agreement financial oversight, serves as the independent bilateral budget auditor appointed jointly but operating independently from both governments. He is accredited by the International Organisation of Supreme Audit Institutions (INTOSAI) and has audited prior US-allied funding commitments. He has no government employee status; he is retained as a contractor on deliverable-based terms. His role is to certify tranche releases, detect spending divergence and prevent one-sided budget drift.

Equipment Needs: Independent audit workstation: secure, cleared computer (government or accredited contractor-grade, classified minimum) with read-only access to bilateral ledger nodes to retrieve monthly budget-burn data by envelope category. Accounting software (commercial or government-approved) for spending reconciliation and parity calculation. Secure email for tranche-release certifications (digitally signed per PKI standards agreed by both co-chairs). CNY-to-USD conversion-rate database (daily update, no external dependency on commercial sources; agreed fixed rate documented in bilateral instrument). Database of all program invoices and receipts (owner submission via secure portal, no external cloud storage). Budget from USD 250M legal/audit envelope (estimated USD 5-10M for auditor fees and infrastructure).

Facility Needs: Secure, accredited audit office (independent of both governments, not government employee): 50-100 sq m estimated. Biometric access control. Secure workstation with classified-minimum protection and read-only ledger-node access (no ability to alter records, only to query and report). Segregated filing for financial records and burn-rate data (classified SECRET, locked storage). Secure video-teleconference room for presenting tranche-release certifications and spending-divergence alerts to bilateral co-chairs. Remote-audit capability (secure tunnel to bilateral ledger nodes if on-site audit is impractical). Neutral location (not at either country's facility, to preserve independence). Funded from USD 250M legal/audit envelope.

8. Challenge Exercise Design and Independent Testing Lead

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Challenge Exercise Design and Independent Testing Lead directs blind exercises and filter-adequacy testing from Month 6 (2027-04-12) through Month 12 (2027-10-12), concentrated Months 8.5–11.5 (2027-06-27 to 2027-09-27). The role requires independence from operational teams (to maintain blindness of injected scenarios) and expert design of detection scenarios. Functions are episodic and time-bounded: design catalog (Month 6–7 = 2027-04-12 to 2027-05-12), pre-test filter adequacy (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27), run scored exercises (Months 10.5–11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27), produce sealed scores (Month 11.75 = 2027-10-05). Contractors or subject-matter-expert consultants on project contracts fit this episodic model better than full-time employees.

Explanation: Leads the Challenge Exercise Design Panel (2 technical experts + 1 CI officer per country, pre-cleared) to design blind scenarios for unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity and vendor refusal. Conducts filter-adequacy pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with >=10 test substitutions to validate that redacted evidence still permits 90% detection; halts scored exercises if detection is <85% (proposed). Runs scored exercises Months 10.5-11.5 (2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27), manages CHALLENGE-tag partitioning to prevent false-positive cascades, and produces sealed detection-rate scores for each event type by event by site. This role supplies the only empirical validation of detection capability and reciprocal access, the two Go criteria.

Consequences: Without independent, blind challenge exercises, Go decision has no empirical basis. The plan requires 'Go only if exercises demonstrate reciprocal access and credible detection.' Without this role, Go verdict is a political guess, not evidence-based. False-positive cascade risk (manufactured incidents triggering automatic suspension) cannot be contained without CHALLENGE-tag partitioning managed by this role. Exercises also validate filter adequacy, identity thresholds and ledger synchronization KPIs; absence leaves all of these unvalidated.

People Count: Min 4-6 per country (design panel, independent testers, scenario managers), part-time from Month 6 (2027-04-12) through Month 12 (2027-10-12), plus full-time during exercises (Months 8.5, 10.5-11.5). Total estimated 8-12 FTE. Funded from USD 500M testing/challenge/red-teams envelope.

Typical Activities: Leads the Challenge Exercise Design Panel (2 technical experts + 1 CI officer per country) to design blind scenarios for unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, and vendor refusal by Month 6 (2027-04-12). Conducts filter-adequacy blind pre-test by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with at least 10 test substitutions, targeting 9 of 10 detected (90% threshold); halts scored exercises if detection <85% (proposed). Runs unscored calibration exercises Months 9.5–10.5 (2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27), then freezes thresholds by Month 10.5 (2027-08-27). Executes scored exercises Months 10.5–11.5 (2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27) with each country's red team injecting scenarios at the counterpart's sites from a hash-committed sealed catalog. Tags every injected scenario 'CHALLENGE' in the ledger before injection. Compares sealed scores from both countries by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05) and produces blind detection rates for each event type, false-positive and false-negative counts per site.

Background Story: Dr. Kwame Mensah, 14-year independent security researcher and red-teamer with expertise in equipment-substitution detection and hardware reverse engineering, leads the Challenge Exercise Design Panel and independent testing from a neutral Switzerland-based firm. PhD in computer engineering, he has published on side-channel attacks and tamper-detection; he is pre-cleared and accepted by both governments as independent. He designs blind scenarios, manages CHALLENGE tagging, and produces sealed detection-rate scores. His role ensures exercises are credible and uncontested.

Equipment Needs: Exercise design and injection: secure laptop (air-gapped, no internet) for drafting and storing sealed scenario catalog with cryptographic hash commitment (published in advance, scenario details encrypted). Red-team injection equipment at each site: controlled-environment devices (isolated test units pre-positioned at staging/spare-inventory areas), pre-configured substitution scenarios (firmware variants, equipment swaps, record alterations), witness cameras (film or secured-digital with restricted export), evidence-collection and tagging supplies (paper forms, seals, photographic film). Blind-scenario-validation tools: detection-rate scoring spreadsheets (paper-based or air-gapped, scored by independent observers). Budget from USD 500M testing envelope.

Facility Needs: Secure exercise-design and management office (100-150 sq m estimated, SCIF equivalent, neutral or host-country facility): three dedicated teams (US, China, neutral observer) working in compartmented sub-spaces to maintain blindness of scenarios. Sealed-scenario storage: fireproof safe (physical key in bilateral escrow, or digital keylock with dual-authentication) holding the pre-committed scenario catalog and cryptographic hashes until scheduled injection. Injection-coordination room at each of 4 declared sites with secure phones (government landline, no cellular) for notifying inspectors that a test is underway (without revealing specifics). Staging-area test zones (subset of normal staging space, isolated from operational areas) where blind injections occur without knowledge of normal inspection teams. Secure evidence-collection and scoring room: air-gapped workstations for compiling blind detection rates by event type, site and country. Budget from USD 500M testing envelope.

9. Legal Implementation and Bilateral Instrument Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Legal Implementation and Bilateral Instrument Lead negotiates and drafts the bilateral instrument from Month -6, with intensive work Months -6 to -2 and implementation work through Month 8 (2027-06-12). This role unblocks the critical path (instrument signature = entry-gate precondition). Legal authority to negotiate, bind governments, and interpret treaty language requires governmental status, not contractor status. Minimum 2 per country (legal lead + drafter) = full-time government positions.

Explanation: Negotiates and drafts the bilateral instrument (executive agreement or treaty) that binds both governments to the Consortium governance, deadlock procedures, double-key authorization, suspension triggers, and all operational protocols. Ensures domestic access authority is enacted in each country by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27), coordinates vendor-binding legal terms, and documents CNY conversion rules for budget parity. Conducts legal review identifying barriers to compelling operators and vendors (estimated 2-4 month litigation risk). Establishes the bilateral legal working group to resolve legal, commercial and regulatory challenges before they delay entry-gate conditions. This role unblocks the critical path: no instrument signature = no entry certification = no Phase One clock start.

Consequences: Without formal legal implementation, the bilateral instrument is not negotiated, signed or enacted. Domestic access authority is not obtained from legislatures. Vendor-binding terms lack legal force. The entire entry gate stalls: the plan states 'signed bilateral instrument' is mandatory entry condition #1. Every week of legal-negotiation delay costs USD 100-200M (estimate) in preparation sunk costs and slips Phase One to later months, compressing exercise and verdict time. Legal litigation over compelling vendors can delay by 2-4 months (estimate), pushing Phase One past its Month 12 (2027-10-12) outer limit. This role is the true critical path.

People Count: Min 2 per country (legal lead + instrument drafter), full-time from Month -6 through Month 8 (2027-06-12) (intensive during negotiation), then part-time through Month 12 (2027-10-12) for implementation and interpretation. Total estimated 4-6 FTE. Funded from USD 250M legal/audit envelope. Assumes bilateral steering committee with weekly escalation authority (Month -6 to Month -2 target: instrument signature by Month 7 = 2027-05-12).

Typical Activities: Establishes bilateral legal working group by Month -6 (2026-04-12) with weekly meetings to identify legal barriers to compelling operators and vendors. Negotiates the bilateral instrument skeleton by Month -2 (2026-12-15) fixing core governance: equal co-chairs, double-key authorization, deadlock escalation (5/8/13-day timers), enumerated auto-suspension triggers, CHALLENGE-event partition, and reciprocal-access parity definitions. Secures signature by Month -2 (2026-12-15, binding deadline). Coordinates enactment of domestic access authority in both countries by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27). Documents CNY-to-USD conversion rule and budget-parity criteria before appropriation release by Month 7 (2027-05-12). Conducts legal review of vendor-binding terms and resolves commercial/IP conflicts with vendors and operators by Month -1 (2026-09-12). Prepares for anticipated litigation over compelling vendors (2–4 month delay estimate); escalates unresolved legal barriers to principals by Month 7 (2027-05-12) for go/no-go decision. Interprets instrument language during Phase One disputes.

Background Story: Dr. Elena Petrov, veteran arms-control attorney and treaty-negotiation specialist with 21 years in bilateral instrument design and domestic implementation, leads legal implementation and bilateral-instrument negotiation from Washington DC. JD from Harvard, fluent in Mandarin, former State Department legal adviser on New START and INF treaties. She is tasked with negotiating and drafting the bilateral instrument binding both governments, enacting domestic access authority, documenting CNY conversion rules, and unblocking the critical-path legal delays. Her authority is governmental; she represents the US in international legal negotiations.

Equipment Needs: Legal-instrument drafting: secure word-processing workstations (air-gapped, no internet dependency) with document-control and version-tracking capability (paper-based or secured-digital, no cloud sharing). Bilateral legal research databases (government or accredited legal-research subscriptions, limited to treaty and arms-control materials). Secure email for correspondence with counterpart legal teams and principals. Cryptographic digital-signature capability (PKI tokens) for counter-signing the bilateral instrument and domestic access-authority documents. Hard-copy printing capability for formal instrument signature ceremonies (no electronic-only signatures; physical documents with seals and signatures required by both governments). Budget from USD 250M legal/audit envelope.

Facility Needs: Secure legal office (SCIF equivalent, 150-200 sq m estimated) housing the bilateral legal team (2 per country): separate secure spaces for each country's lawyers to prevent unintended information sharing before negotiation is complete. Secure meeting room (Faraday-caged, no electronic recording) for bilateral negotiation sessions. Neutral third-country meeting venue (Geneva, The Hague, or similar) for formal bilateral legal negotiations and instrument-signature ceremony (ensuring neither side has home-ground advantage). Proximity to national capitals (for escalation authority and legislative liaison) or secure encrypted comms to principals. Secure storage vault for executed instruments, amendment records, and confidential interpretive notes. Library or research facility with classified-minimum security for legal precedents and treaty materials. Budget from USD 250M legal/audit envelope.

Omissions

1. No explicit conflict-of-interest or independence protocols for bilateral technical referees and calibration panels

Technical referee panels (2 experts per side) and the threshold-calibration panel decide contested findings and validation of detection thresholds, yet the documents do not specify how experts are vetted for independence from their national governments' interests, how recusal is managed, or how dual loyalty is prevented. Compromised referees could block legitimate findings or certify false thresholds, undermining the entire Go/Modify/Stop verdict credibility.

Recommendation: Define independence vetting for all referees and calibration panelists before their appointment: require biographical disclosure, conflict-of-interest questionnaires, and joint bilateral approval of each expert by both co-chairs. Establish a standing ethics body (1 independent ethics advisor, jointly appointed, not a government employee) with authority to recommend recusal if an expert shows bias or receives pressure from their national government. Document all expert communications with their home governments (transparency requirement). Require referees to sign sworn statements of independence before issuing fact statements.

2. No defined remediation pathway or continuous operation procedure if a Phase One site becomes unverifiable mid-test

The plan states that material unverifiable equipment (>3% per site) fails a site outright and is a Stop criterion. But if a site fails at Month 10 (2027-08-12), mid-exercise, what happens to exercises already injected or in progress at that site? Are results discarded? Do scoring thresholds adjust? Can the other 3 sites complete exercises and reach a verdict on partial data? The absence of this procedure risks cascading program failure if even one site hits the unverifiable threshold early.

Recommendation: Define a site-failure remediation pathway: if unverifiable equipment exceeds 3% at any site before Month 11 (2027-09-12), pause exercises at that site and escalate to bilateral co-chairs within 48 hours. Co-chairs must decide within 5 days whether to: (1) suspend that site and proceed with 3 remaining sites (reduced sample size noted in verdict), (2) escalate vendor-binding disputes to principals for emergency resolution, or (3) extend Phase One by 2-4 weeks (extending the 90-day clock) to complete vendor re-validation. Document that a 3-site Go verdict is still valid but qualified as 'partial coverage.' If 2+ sites fail, automatic escalation to Modify or Stop (insufficient data for Go).

3. No procedure for handling cascading international incidents (cyberattacks, espionage, diplomatic crisis) during Phase One that could trigger emergency suspension or withdrawal

The plan assumes stable bilateral cooperation from Month -6 through Month 12+ but does not address scenarios where a cyber-attack on ledger systems, a major espionage breach, or an unrelated US-China geopolitical crisis occurs during Phase One. Does a cyberattack on the ledger node automatically trigger suspension? Does an arrest of an inspector require site evacuation? Can one government unilaterally withdraw? The absence of crisis-response procedures risks ad-hoc stalling or unilateral program termination.

Recommendation: Embed a Crisis Response Protocol in the bilateral instrument: define 'force majeure' events (cyberattack rendering ledger inoperable >4 hours, inspector injury or detention, facility compromise, declared war or national emergency) that trigger automatic operational pause within 24 hours pending co-chair assessment. Co-chairs have 5 days to decide: (1) restore operations after remediation, (2) extend Phase One by N weeks, or (3) escalate to principals for continued-cooperation decision. Specify that a unilateral withdrawal by one government is permitted only after 30 days of co-chair notice, giving the other side time to attempt remediation or invoke principal-level talks. Document all crisis events and response decisions in the ledger and KPI dashboard for post-Phase-One audit.

4. No explicit succession and continuity plan if a bilateral co-chair (or national leadership) changes during Phase One

The plan requires one co-chair per country with continuous presence and double-key authority. If a co-chair leaves office (resignation, electoral change, death, illness), the documents state 'successor is designated before transition' but do not define the transition procedure, interim-authority rules, or who acts during gaps. An absence of clear succession could halt decision-making for weeks, aging discrepancies and triggering Stop criteria by default.

Recommendation: Establish a succession and interim-authority protocol: each country must designate a named deputy co-chair before Phase One starts (published in the bilateral instrument). If a co-chair is unavailable for >1 week, the deputy automatically assumes authority with full double-key power, requiring no further bilateral agreement. If both a co-chair and deputy are unavailable, each country's principal (deputy secretary level or equivalent) may exercise co-chair authority temporarily, but any decision affecting the other country must be counter-signed by the counterpart principal within 48 hours to take effect. Document all transitions and interim periods in the ledger. Require that any change in national leadership (election, resignation) does not interrupt Consortium operations; outgoing and incoming administrations must jointly brief the successor co-chair before transition.

5. No explicit rules for handling classified or sensitive intelligence discoveries during site visits

Inspectors working at declared datacenters may stumble upon classified information unrelated to the Consortium (e.g., facility schematic, security protocols, other nations' intelligence). The documents do not specify: who is authorized to see such material? Does an inspector's accidental discovery trigger compartmentation violation or espionage investigation? What is the reporting chain? Absence of rules creates ambiguity and risk of unintended exposure or false accusations.

Recommendation: Define a Classified-Discovery Protocol: all inspectors receive pre-deployment briefing on handling accidental discovery of unrelated classified material. If an inspector encounters such material, they must immediately: (1) stop examination, (2) notify host-country operator liaison (not a foreign co-worker), (3) seal the area, and (4) escalate to bilateral co-chair CI liaison within 1 hour without examining or discussing the classified content. Neither side investigates the discovery; the host country handles internal exposure review. Document the incident in the tamper-evident ledger only as 'accidental-discovery event [site] [time]' without content disclosure. Failure to report accidental discovery = automatic inspector removal and investigation.

6. No defined criteria for what constitutes operator 'consent withdrawal' or triggering events for unilateral operator exit

The plan tracks 'Operator Consent Status' (full/degraded/withdrawn) but does not define what actions or statements constitute a formal withdrawal. If an operator complains about boundary violations or refuses a single access request, is that withdrawal? Must they file formal written complaint? Can a verbal complaint to a liaison officer count? The absence of clear triggering criteria invites disputes over whether consent is actually withdrawn, stalling suspension procedures.

Recommendation: Define operator-consent withdrawal explicitly: consent is withdrawn only upon (1) formal written notice from the operator's authorized representative to both co-chairs, (2) stating grounds with specific incidents or dates, and (3) delivered via secured bilateral channels (not informal or verbal). Degraded consent follows 1-3 minor boundary violations clarified and resolved within 48 hours. Withdrawn consent = automatic site suspension within 24 hours and escalation to principals for emergency remediation within 5 days. Document all consent-status changes in the KPI dashboard within 2 hours of receipt. Require operators to designate a named consent-status liaison officer who is the sole authority to withdraw consent (preventing confusion from multiple voices).

7. No procedure for post-verdict audit, findings publication, or lessons-learned capture for Phase Two or future regimes

The plan focuses entirely on the 90-day Phase One test and Month 12.25 (2027-10-20) verdict, but does not define: what happens to the tamper-evident ledger and evidence after the verdict? Who audits it? What is published? What gets redacted? How are lessons captured for Phase Two or successor programs? If records disappear into classification, the regime's credibility is eroded and future planners cannot learn from Phase One's successes and failures.

Recommendation: Embed a Post-Verdict Archive and Lessons-Learned Protocol: (1) The tamper-evident ledger and all challenge-exercise documentation remain jointly held in neutral escrow (not either country) for a minimum of 5 years post-verdict, accessible to authorized auditors and scholars under a bilateral declassification review process. (2) Within 30 days of the verdict, both countries jointly publish a redacted Phase One Summary Report including: entry-condition timeline, total budget burn by envelope, staffing and turnover, detection rates and false-positive counts by event type, parity variance and any asymmetries, major disputes and their resolution, and the final Go/Modify/Stop conclusion with supporting evidence. (3) Establish a Lessons-Learned Working Group (funded from USD 250M legal/audit envelope) to document: what worked, what failed, cost drivers, staff recommendations, and design changes for Phase Two or other bilateral regimes. (4) Schedule a post-verdict bilateral technical summit (Month 14 = 2027-12-12) to review findings jointly and agree on declassification and publication scope.

8. No explicit handling of asymmetric operator/vendor refusal if one country's critical vendor refuses but the other's agrees

The vendor-binding ladder assumes vendors are handled uniformly across both countries, but US and Chinese vendor landscapes differ. If a US critical vendor refuses and equipment becomes unverifiable at US sites but Chinese vendors comply fully, the unverifiable count at US sites exceeds 3% while Chinese sites are at <1%. This asymmetry is a Stop criterion ('asymmetric access'), yet the documents do not specify whether asymmetric vendor refusal is treated as symmetrical evidence of regime failure or as a country-specific technical issue. The absence of clarity invites dispute.

Recommendation: Define asymmetric-vendor-refusal handling: (1) classify vendor refusals by country and site, separately tracking US vs. China unverifiable counts; (2) if one country's unverifiable exceeds 3% due to vendor refusal but the other's is <1%, escalate immediately to principals (not co-chairs) within 48 hours for diplomatic intervention or supply-chain resolution; (3) do not automatically trigger Stop at the first asymmetry; instead, set a 2-week escalation window for principals to negotiate vendor re-engagement or approve a supply-substitution path (e.g., substitute a willing vendor's equipment, accept non-verified units with sealed declaration, or reduce the declared equipment set); (4) if asymmetry persists beyond 2 weeks, treat it as a Stop condition ('asymmetric access' due to deliberate vendor-refusal obstruction by one government); (5) document all vendor-refusal requests and escalations in the ledger with timestamps and bilateral approval of any asymmetry-mitigation attempts.

9. No explicit end-state or equipment disposition for all remaining undeclared/boundary-case units that survive Phase One but are not formally closed

The Exit Protocol assigns dispositions (destruction, disablement, transfer, release, unresolved) but only to equipment that is actively removed. Equipment remaining at sites post-Phase One—declared units that continue operating, equipment in maintenance, units awaiting decommissioning—lack a final disposition or custody statement. The documents do not specify: does the Consortium continue monitoring these units indefinitely? Are they released from monitoring at the Phase-One verdict? Is there a hand-off procedure to a successor regime? Absence of clarity risks the regime appearing to lose track of equipment at exactly the moment its credibility should peak.

Recommendation: Define a Final Disposition and Hand-Off Protocol for Phase One: (1) all declared equipment remaining at sites at Month 12.25 (2027-10-20) verdict receives a final status entry in the ledger: 'in-place at [site]' with last inspection date and upcoming maintenance schedule (if known); (2) no tracking claim is made beyond the verdict; explicitly state in the ledger and all reports that 'Consortium observation ends at [Month 12.25 (2027-10-20) verdict date]; subsequent monitoring is outside Consortium scope'; (3) if Phase Two or a successor regime is authorized, publish a hand-off certification in the ledger transferring custody and monitoring records to the successor with both co-chairs' counter-signature; (4) for equipment fully removed by Month 12 (2027-10-12), issue a final closed-disposition entry with witness names, date and outcome (destruction/disablement/transfer); (5) any equipment with unresolved disposition at Month 12.25 (2027-10-20) is reported as 'unresolved' in the final verdict and marked as a weakness for Phase Two remediation.

Potential Improvements

1. Clarify the scope and decision authority of the Bilateral Co-Chairs' weekly steering committee versus escalation to principals

The team-member description states co-chairs 'chair weekly bilateral steering committees' to track entry conditions and escalate bottlenecks 'within 48 hours,' but the documents do not specify the membership of this committee, which decisions are decided at the committee level versus reserved for principals, or what 'escalation within 48 hours' means operationally (briefing principals? requesting a principals' meeting?). This ambiguity invites scope creep (committee deciding issues above its pay grade) or stalling (committees that cannot escalate because they lack authority).

Recommendation: Publish a bilateral Steering Committee Charter before Month 7 (2027-05-12): (1) define membership as the two co-chairs plus representatives from the National Inspectorate Leads and Ledger Architect per country (roughly 6 people total), meeting weekly on a fixed schedule; (2) enumerate the committee's decision authority: approve weekly entry-condition tracking reports, recommend bilateral protocol clarifications, approve schedule adjustments within Phase One (e.g., exercise postponement <1 week), and escalate any decision affecting substantive program scope, budget, staffing, or suspension authority to principals within 48 hours; (3) define 'escalation' as a formal written briefing delivered to both countries' deputy secretaries or equivalents within 48 hours, requesting a principals' decision within 5 days; (4) require written minutes of every committee meeting in the tamper-evident ledger (redacted for operational security only) so future audit can verify the committee's scope-creep and decision boundaries.

2. Expand the Inspector Orientation and Rules-of-Engagement documentation to address boundary-violation penalties and inspector liability

The Counterintelligence and Personnel Security Unit Lead role mentions 'CI liaisons review inspector outputs and evidence before export' and 'compartmentation audit logs showing each inspector's access scope,' but the documents do not specify what penalties apply if an inspector violates a boundary, accesses restricted information, or ignores compartmentation rules. Are they removed immediately? Investigated? Prosecuted? Absence of explicit penalties creates ambiguity and inconsistent enforcement, eroding confidence in compartmentation discipline.

Recommendation: Develop and require all inspectors to sign a Rules of Engagement and Inspector Liability Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) before Month 8 (2027-06-12): (1) define boundary violations by severity (minor: 1-3 steps beyond marked line; major: deliberate entry to production hall or restricted zone; critical: attempted access to unrelated classified material); (2) specify penalties: minor = immediate formal warning and reassignment to different post within 48 hours; major = immediate removal from site, investigation by host-country CI and bilateral liaison, potential prosecution; critical = immediate removal, coordinated bilateral CI investigation, and likely prosecution under espionage statutes; (3) require host-country operator liaison to document every violation within 1 hour; (4) make investigation findings available (redacted for sources/methods) to both countries within 5 days; (5) publish aggregate violation statistics (anonymized) in quarterly KPI dashboard as 'Inspector Compliance Rate: [%]' to maintain transparency and show regime enforcement.

3. Define the scope and escalation procedure for the 'impaired-confidence' designation, which appears frequently but lacks operational clarity

The documents reference 'impaired-confidence review' and 'impaired-confidence suspension' as a middle ground between normal operations and full suspension, triggered by ledger divergence >5%, parity variance >20%, or unresolved discrepancies >10 days. But the documents do not specify: what does a site look like under 'impaired confidence'? Are inspectors increased or reduced? Are exercises halted? What operational constraints apply? How long does impaired-confidence status last before automatic suspension kicks in? Ambiguity undermines the graduated-response logic.

Recommendation: Define an Impaired-Confidence Status Protocol: (1) impaired-confidence designation is intermediate between full operations and suspension, triggered by objective thresholds (ledger divergence >5%, parity >20%, discrepancy age >10 days, unverifiable >2% but <3%); (2) upon impaired-confidence designation, operations continue but with elevated scrutiny: add 1 bilateral observer per site, increase evidence-handling spot-checks to daily (vs. weekly), hold co-chair calls every 2 days (vs. weekly) to assess recovery, and freeze all challenge exercises at that site pending co-chair approval; (3) impaired-confidence status lasts a maximum of 5 days unless remediated; (4) if the triggering condition persists at Day 5 (e.g., divergence still >5%), automatic escalation to site suspension without further co-chair action; (5) resumption from impaired-confidence requires documented corrective action (e.g., re-synced ledger, renegotiated parity, resolved discrepancy) and bilateral co-chair re-certification; (6) publish impaired-confidence designations immediately in the KPI dashboard with trigger and resolution status.

4. Specify the format, handling, and lifetime of 'sealed detection-rate scores' from the Challenge Exercise Design Panel

The plan requires independent testers to produce 'sealed detection-rate scores' by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05) that are compared between national teams, but does not specify: who holds the sealed scores (both countries jointly in escrow, or neutral custodian)? How are they opened (by both co-chairs simultaneously, with witnesses)? What happens if one side's scores are lost, corrupted, or sealed improperly? Does either side retain the right to contest the seal integrity before the scores are opened? Absence of procedural detail invites disputes over score authenticity.

Recommendation: Establish a Sealed-Scores Protocol: (1) each country's independent testers produces detection-rate scores in two formats: (a) digital file encrypted with bilateral public-key cryptography (one national key per country, no single-key encryption), and (b) printed hard copy signed by both testers; (2) sealed hard-copy scores are deposited in a bilateral escrow safe (physical key in bilaterally held escrow, biometric access log) by Month 11.75 (2027-10-05) at 17:00 UTC precisely; (3) sealed digital scores are cryptographically committed (hash published in the ledger) at the same time; (4) scores are unsealed jointly by both co-chairs on a pre-announced date (Month 12 = 2027-10-12, 09:00 UTC) with bilateral witnesses, video recording (stored in tamper-evident ledger), and cryptographic signature verification of the digital copies; (5) within 24 hours of opening, both countries must agree on the score authenticity or immediately escalate signature/seal disputes to principals; (6) if a signature or seal is questioned, both copies are preserved and submitted to an accredited forensic audit (third-party, bilateral cost-share) within 5 days.

5. Clarify how 'false-positive' and 'false-negative' rates are calculated and thresholds are applied per event type across multiple injections

The plan proposes 'blind detection of at least 90% for each of 7 event types with at least 10 injections each' and defines false-negative rate as <=10% (in Canonical Facts), but does not specify: are the 7 event types equally weighted (1 each) or does each contribute proportionally to overall detection rate? If one type hits 85% (Modify threshold) and another hits 98% (well above Go threshold), can a Go be justified? How are false positives handled (e.g., is one false positive per type acceptable, or is >0% false positive a Modify trigger)? Ambiguous weighting invites post-hoc threshold-moving.

Recommendation: Publish a Detection-Rate Scoring Methodology by Month 7 (2027-05-12): (1) define the 7 event types explicitly: unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal, reluctant operator (as listed in the plan); (2) specify equal weighting: overall detection rate = average of the 7 event-type detection rates, each type is (correct detections / total injections) * 100%; (3) apply Go threshold uniformly: all 7 types must be >=90% (true-positive rate) with <=10% false-negatives; if any type is 80-89%, automatic Modify; if any type is <80%, Modify or Stop based on root cause; (4) define false-positive rate as a separate metric: FP rate = (false positives / total non-injection operations) * 100%; propose FP threshold of <=2% per event type (TBD, validate during pre-testing); (5) require pre-registration of these thresholds in bilateral instrument Annex before Month 10.5 (2027-08-27) so neither side can redefine success post-exercise; (6) if one country's scores diverge >10% from the other's on any event type, treat the divergence as a scoring audit finding and escalate to technical referees for fact statement before finalizing the verdict.

6. Reduce ambiguity around what constitutes 'operational disruption' to active compute and how disruption triggers are enforced

The plan states 'zero production disruption' and 'no disruption to active computational work; separation from production halls' but does not quantify thresholds (e.g., is 5 minutes of latency disruption acceptable? 1 second?). The documents also do not specify who monitors disruption (operator, inspectors, facility SCADA systems) or how disruption incidents are escalated and logged. Ambiguity invites operator claims of disruption that inspectors deny, stalling without objective evidence.

Recommendation: Define a Production-Disruption Monitoring and Escalation Protocol: (1) define disruption objectively: any unplanned loss of compute capacity, power, cooling, or network connectivity affecting active workloads lasting >30 seconds (proposed threshold) attributed to Consortium activity (inspector movement, equipment inspection, evidence handling in zones adjacent to live systems); (2) require the operator to deploy facility SCADA monitoring in bounded inspection zones to log any anomalies (power transients, thermal spikes, network latency) within 30 minutes of Consortium inspection activity; (3) establish an Inspector-Facility Interface workgroup at each site (operator SCADA technician + bilateral liaisons) that reviews SCADA logs daily and flags any suspected Consortium-related disruption within 24 hours; (4) log all disruption incidents in the tamper-evident ledger with: date, time, zone, duration, affected systems, SCADA evidence, and inspector and operator attestations; (5) if monthly disruption-incident count exceeds 3 per site, trigger operator-consent review (potential degraded-consent status); (6) publish monthly disruption-incident count in the KPI dashboard so operators can monitor compliance and transparently see that Consortium work respects the separation-of-duties boundary.

7. Strengthen the specification of 'provisional' vs. 'validated' figures in the KPI dashboard to avoid misinterpretation as confirmed metrics

The Canonical Facts section lists many (proposed threshold) and (estimate) figures (e.g., detection >90%, identity confidence >95%, ledger sync 1 hour, parity tolerance ±10%), but the KPI dashboard description does not specify whether these provisional figures are reported separately from validated figures, or whether provisional-figure caveats are prominently displayed to prevent misreading the verdict as fact-based when some underpinning assumptions are untested.

Recommendation: Implement a two-tier KPI reporting structure: (1) Tier 1 (Validated): metrics backed by bilateral exercise data or historical precedent (e.g., 'Detection Rate by Event Type' after exercises are complete, 'Staffing Availability' from actual deployment counts); (2) Tier 2 (Provisional): thresholds and assumptions that are pre-registered but not yet empirically validated (e.g., 'Detection Threshold: >90% [PROVISIONAL, baseline assumption, validated by Month 11.5 = 2027-09-27 exercises]'); (3) in monthly KPI dashboard reports, mark every provisional figure with a red banner or flag and include a one-sentence caveats: 'This threshold is assumed but not yet validated by live exercise; see Month 11.5 (2027-09-27) exercise results below'; (4) maintain a separate 'Validation Status Tracker' published monthly showing which provisional figures have been empirically tested, which remain unvalidated, and what the empirical results (if any) show; (5) explicitly state in the final verdict report: 'The Go/Modify/Stop conclusion is based on [X] validated metrics and [Y] provisional thresholds; the following assumptions were not fully validated and represent residual uncertainty: [list]'.

8. Clarify decision authority and conflict-resolution if the independent budget auditor and bilateral co-chairs disagree on whether parity threshold is breached

The plan requires the independent auditor to flag spending divergence and escalate to impaired-confidence review, but does not specify: if the auditor computes divergence at 22% (exceeding the 20% impaired-confidence threshold) and the co-chairs dispute the calculation or claim measurement error, who decides the truth? Does the auditor have veto power over tranche release, or only a recommendation? Ambiguity risks the auditor becoming either toothless or over-powerful.

Recommendation: Establish a Budget-Parity Dispute Resolution Framework: (1) the independent auditor's monthly spending report includes: itemized receipts by envelope, cumulative totals per country, pro-rata share calculations, and a parity-variance percentage with a 95% confidence interval (to account for minor rounding variations); (2) if divergence exceeds 15%, the auditor flags it and both co-chairs have 48 hours to review the auditor's calculations and provide rebuttal data or corrections; (3) if the co-chairs dispute the calculation, they may request a re-audit by the auditor (auditor conducts a limited 2-day re-review, cost borne by the side requesting it); (4) if re-audit confirms divergence, or if the co-chairs do not rebut within 48 hours, the auditor's finding stands and is published in the KPI dashboard as 'Spending Divergence: [%] [FLAGGED / CLEARED]'; (5) divergence >20% automatically triggers impaired-confidence review by bilateral technical referees (within 48 hours), not by co-chairs alone, to prevent political override; (6) referees issue a fact statement on whether divergence is due to legitimate cost drivers (e.g., surge staffing, unforeseeable equipment costs) or asymmetric spending patterns, with recommendation to co-chairs on tranche-release authorization.

9. Expand the KPI dashboard specification to include early-warning indicators that trigger escalation before major thresholds are breached

The plan defines suspension triggers (unverifiable >3%, divergence >5%, discrepancy age >10 days) but does not specify leading indicators that warn of approaching thresholds. For example, if unverifiable climbs to 2.5%, is that reported as a warning, or only when it hits 3%? If discrepancies are aging toward 10 days, is there a 7-day warning? Absence of leading indicators means problems are discovered at the last moment, leaving no remediation time.

Recommendation: Implement a Three-Tier KPI Alert System: (1) Tier 1 (Green): metric within safe operating bounds (e.g., unverifiable <2%, discrepancy age <7 days, divergence <3%, parity variance <8%); report status unchanged month-to-month; (2) Tier 2 (Yellow): metric approaching threshold (unverifiable 2-3%, discrepancy age 7-10 days, divergence 3-5%, parity >8-15%), triggers bilateral co-chair alert and 48-hour remediation plan requirement; (3) Tier 3 (Red): metric at or exceeding threshold (unverifiable >=3%, discrepancy >=10 days, divergence >=5%, parity >=15%), triggers automatic escalation to principals and impaired-confidence review. Publish the tiered status in the monthly KPI dashboard with color coding and clear escalation timers. Require co-chairs to address all Yellow-tier alerts with documented corrective action (due within 5 days) or the item automatically escalates to Red. This gives early warning and remediation opportunity rather than sudden suspension.

10. Strengthen the role description for the Independent Budget Auditor to clarify independence mechanisms protecting against political pressure

The auditor is described as 'independently appointed' and 'accredited bilaterally' but not a government employee, yet the documents do not specify: how is the auditor selected (by both co-chairs, or by a third party)? Can either country remove the auditor? Is there a fixed term, and if the auditor uncovers spending asymmetry unfavorable to one country, can that country retaliate by refusing to renew the contract? Absence of independence safeguards invites political capture of the auditor.

Recommendation: Embed an Auditor Independence and Tenure Protection Clause in the bilateral instrument: (1) the independent auditor is selected jointly by both co-chairs from a pre-approved shortlist of internationally accredited accounting firms (selected by bilateral consensus before Month 7 = 2027-05-12), with no single country having veto; (2) the auditor is appointed for the full Phase One duration (Months 7-12 = 2027-05-12 to 2027-10-12 + 6 months post-verdict for final closure) with a fixed fee (no variable compensation tied to spending findings); (3) either country may request removal of the auditor for cause (gross misconduct, conflict of interest, falsified data) but not for disagreement on audit findings; removal requires bilateral agreement and third-party (neutral) review of the cause within 5 days; (4) if removal is refused, the requesting country may demand a supplementary independent audit (cost split 50/50) to validate the original auditor's disputed findings; (5) the auditor reports to both co-chairs simultaneously, publishes findings in the tamper-evident ledger within 48 hours of submission (preventing one side from withholding the report), and receives diplomatic protection from both governments (treating the auditor as a neutral agent, not a foreigner subject to intelligence exploitation).

1.4.A Issue - Entry-gate certification timeline is critically underspecified and risks catastrophic delay

The plan states entry conditions must be certified by Month 9 (2027-07-12) but contains no binding instrument language, no escalation procedure for individual-condition slip, and no defined consequence if any one condition delays past Month 8 (2027-06-12). The bilateral instrument itself—the most time-consuming entry condition—is treated as a starting assumption rather than a tracked deliverable with a hard signature deadline and principal-level go/no-go checkpoint. If instrument negotiation slips beyond Month 7 (2027-05-12), the entire 90-day Phase One clock compresses or fails.

1.4.B Tags

  • critical-path-opacity
  • no-binding-deadlines
  • cascade-failure-risk

1.4.C Mitigation

Immediately establish a bilateral entry-gate steering committee with weekly condition tracking by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27). Lock a binding instrument-signature deadline at Month 7 (2027-05-12) with documented escalation: any condition not certified by Month 8 (2027-06-12) triggers automatic principal-level go/no-go review within 48 hours. Pre-position a USD 50M gate-readiness sub-account from contingency, accessible only upon joint certification of all conditions, to fund entry work without sunk-cost accumulation if any condition fails.

1.4.D Consequence

Without binding deadlines and escalation procedure, instrument negotiation can drift 2–4 months past Month 7 (2027-05-12), compressing Phase One to 30–60 days or forcing cancellation. Sunk costs of USD 100–200M (estimate) for preliminary work would accumulate against the spending envelopes, not contingency, leaving insufficient funds for Phase One operational work. A delayed or failed entry gate is the highest-probability failure mode.

1.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats entry certification as a precondition rather than a managed deliverable. There is no fixed signature deadline for the instrument, no named lead for each condition, no escalation trigger for individual slips, and no separation of gate-readiness funding from operational funds. This reflects a governance assumption that entry conditions will self-organize; they will not under bilateral distrust.

1.5.A Issue - Vendor-binding and attestation-concentration risk is documented but not mitigated by Month 2 (2026-12-12)

The plan anchors equipment identity on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation validated by accredited examiners, creating a concentration risk. Documents acknowledge 10–40% of equipment may become unverifiable if attestation fails or vendors refuse binding. However, the plan contains no timeline for vendor census, binding execution, or key-custody validation before Phase One starts. The fallback ladder (vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, clean rooms) is mentioned but not funded within a specific envelope or staffed by a named unit.

1.5.B Tags

  • attestation-single-point-failure
  • vendor-refusal-mitigation-missing
  • unverifiable-equipment-risk

1.5.C Mitigation

Complete vendor-participation census by Month 1 (2026-11-12): each site operator must declare ≥95% of supplier list by equipment count. Establish ≥2 bilateral-accredited clean-room examination centers (one per country) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-27), funded from the USD 500M testing envelope. Document a three-tier evidence ladder by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27): Tier 1 (attestation); Tier 2 (customs + maintenance logs + physical inspection); Tier 3 (supervised examination or witnessed destruction). Classify all declared equipment by vendor binding-status by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and escalate Tier C equipment (no binding or vendor refusing) to unverifiable status.

1.5.D Consequence

If vendor binding is not complete by Month 8 (2027-06-12), Phase One enters with unknown unverifiable-equipment counts, violating the 3% threshold rule. Vendors discovered to be refusing cooperation mid-Phase-One cannot be recovered by clean rooms already built or by evidence layers documented after the clock starts. A 15–30% unverifiable-equipment discovery post-entry forces site failure and an automatic Stop condition.

1.5.E Root Cause

Vendor binding is treated as an entry condition rather than a pre-Phase-One capability-build. The plan lists vendor participation as a gate but does not assign ownership, timeline or contingency funding to vendor census, binding negotiation, key validation or clean-room construction. This reflects assumption that vendor cooperation is cheaper and simpler than it actually is; supply-chain coordination typically requires 4–6 months and escalation to principals.

1.6.A Issue - Deadlock and suspension mechanics lack objective trigger definitions and risk weaponization of contested findings

The plan states that deadlock escalates to technical referees (Days 5–8) and principals (Days 8–13), but the decision document does not define what constitutes a material disputed finding, which findings may suspend a site automatically versus which require co-chair agreement, or how manufactured incidents are partitioned from operational findings. Without enumerated objective triggers (e.g., unverifiable >3%, divergence >5%), one government can stall by labeling every inconclusive finding a disagreement, aging it past 13 days, and forcing a Stop condition through inaction rather than evidence.

1.6.B Tags

  • deadlock-weaponization-risk
  • no-auto-suspension-criteria
  • obstruction-loophole

1.6.C Mitigation

Embed Deadlock and Suspension Mechanics in the signed bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12) with mandatory fixed escalation timers (Tier 1: Days 1–5 co-chairs; Tier 2: Days 5–8 technical referees; Tier 3: Days 8–13 principals) and enumerated automatic-suspension triggers: unverifiable >3% for 5 days; divergence >5%; denial variance >15%; discrepancies >10 days old. Explicitly partition challenge-exercise events from operational triggers via CHALLENGE tags in the ledger, excluding exercise events from suspension triggers absent principal adjudication.

1.6.D Consequence

Without objective triggers and partition rules, a government can delay contested findings by 13+ days, aging them past the escalation window and forcing a Stop condition via inaction. Alternatively, a single misclassified challenge-exercise event (estimated 2–3 false positives per Phase One if partition is weak) can trigger automatic suspension, destroying operational progress and eroding regime credibility. Either path converts the deadlock procedure into a weapon.

1.6.E Root Cause

The plan adopts the principle that deadlock must not permit unilateral override, but it does not define objective triggers that convert principle into procedure. Without enumerated criteria, the referees' task becomes subjective judgment about materiality, and age-based escalation alone cannot distinguish genuine obstruction from legitimate technical disagreement. This reflects assumption that consensus on triggers is easier to reach than it is; triggers should be frozen in the instrument before Phase One starts.

2.5.A Issue - Attestation-anchored identity creates vendor-key concentration risk; unverifiable-equipment percentage is projected 10–40% without proven fallbacks

The Pioneer's Gambit anchors equipment identity on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation validated by accredited examiners. If a vendor's keys are compromised, firmware is rolled back, or attestation is forged, a large batch of units becomes unverifiable. The plan cites 10–40% unverifiable as an estimate but provides no validation that corroborating layers (customs, physical inspection, maintenance records) will suffice. Alternatively, if CHALLENGE-tag partition is ignored, legitimate exercise events trigger real operational responses (suspension, filter renegotiation), contaminating the exercise data and making blind-exercise scoring meaningless.

The pre-test rehearsal is mentioned but not specified as a mandatory gate, so the partition's effectiveness is not validated before operational scoring begins. This leaves the partition dependent on human attention during fast-moving operational triage, where misclassification and disputes are likely.

3.5.A Issue - Attestation-Anchored Identity Concentrates Trust in Vendor Keys and Firmware; Corroborating Layers Are Weaker Than Assumed

The strategic path anchors equipment identity primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation validated by accredited examiners. If a vendor's keys are compromised, if firmware is forged, or if a vendor refuses key-custody validation, a large share of equipment (estimated 10-40% per site) becomes unverifiable. The plan assumes physical inspection, customs records and maintenance logs provide corroborating layers, but these sources are under the operator's control and can be doctored to match a substituted unit. The corroboration layers are weaker than the plan states, and the plan provides no explicit rule for adjudicating when attestation and physical evidence conflict.

3.5.C Mitigation

Document an explicit evidence-conflict rule: if attestation and physical inspection disagree on identity, the unit goes to referees rather than auto-unverifiable status. If detection falls below 85%, halt scored exercises and redesign the layering.

3.5.D Consequence

At an estimated 10-40% unverifiable per site, the 3% material threshold is likely exceeded, sites fail Phase One, and the Go verdict is impossible. A government or vendor could trigger this failure by withholding key validation.

The plan anchors identity on the most scalable but least-controllable source (vendor keys) and treats corroboration as secondary reassurance rather than equal evidence. The plan does not define what happens when corroboration and attestation conflict, creating ambiguity that either government can exploit to argue identity is unverifiable.

4.6.A Issue - Deadlock Escalation Timers and Suspension Triggers Create Cascading False-Positive and Manufactured-Incident Risk Without Adequate Containment

The plan defines a 5/8/13-day escalation ladder (Deadlock Mechanics decision) and enumerated automatic-suspension triggers (unverifiable >3%, ledger divergence >5%, access denial >15%, aging >10 days). No contingency is specified for false-positive recovery (reinstatement time, impact on KPI, reputation damage). Document every escalation, drill and false positive in the ledger.

4.6.D Consequence

4.6.E Root Cause

The plan defines suspension triggers and exercise tagging but does not specify how false positives are contained or how manufactured triggers (vendor delay, access denial) are distinguished from credible escalations. This reflects insufficient war-gaming of adversarial scenarios and insufficient distinction between objective triggers and subjective judgment calls that require escalation.

The chosen 'Pioneer's Gambit' strategy anchors equipment identity primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic attestation, with physical inspection as a secondary corroborating layer. Plan estimates 10–40% unverifiable equipment per site under this anchor. The pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) may catch filter-adequacy failures, but cannot validate attestation integrity or vendor cooperation assumptions before scoring exercises begin.
