  • Design and publish exit-disposition rules by Month 7 (2027-05-12) specifying evidence requirements for each of the 5 Exit Protocol dispositions (witnessed destruction, permanent disablement, transfer, documented release, unresolved), including witness counts, sampling procedures, pre-declaration requirements and the exact wording that marks the boundary of Consortium knowledge.

8.3 Follow Up Consultation

At the next consultation (Month 6, 2027-04-12), review vendor-binding status and attestation-key validation results; confirm clean-room centers are operationally ready; validate legal compulsion authority for private vendors; and review the Threshold Calibration Panel's preliminary findings. Discuss any vendors still unable to bind and escalation options (refusal ladder, unverifiable classification). Confirm ICC staffing roster and duty-officer training schedule. Review any changes to site locations or operator participation that affect the Phase One setup. Lock the Challenge-Exercise Misclassification Protocol and confirm the Month 8.75 (2027-07-05) misclassification drill schedule.

8.4.A Issue - Entry-Gate Timing Is Dangerously Ambiguous and Threatens Phase One Clock Validity

The pre-project assessment correctly flagged entry-gate stall as a high-probability failure pathway (6–12 months typical, estimate), yet the project plan provides no binding escalation rule tied to certification delay. The principal go/no-go at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27) is noted but lacks teeth: no automatic resource hold, no tranche freeze, no published deadline beyond which Phase One is formally cancelled. If Month 9 (2027-07-12) slips to Month 11 (2027-09-12), the 90-day window compresses from 2027-07-12–2027-10-12 to 2027-09-12–2027-12-12, overlapping the winter holiday cycle and staff leave, which will reduce presence and presence-detection credibility.

8.4.B Tags

  • entry_gate_ambiguity
  • clock_validity_risk
  • no_escalation_teeth
  • compressed_exercise_window
  • political_delay_exposure

8.4.C Mitigation

Lock a single, non-negotiable certification deadline of Month 9 (2027-07-12) at 09:00 UTC in the bilateral instrument signed by Month 7 (2027-05-12). Define the consequence explicitly: any condition uncertified by Month 9 (2027-07-12) at 17:00 UTC triggers automatic 48-hour principal escalation with a binary decision: proceed with available conditions and document omissions in the ledger, or formally cancel Phase One and return unspent tranche 1 funds. Publish the decision by Month 9 (2027-07-12) at 17:00 UTC. Freeze the 90-day Phase One window to Months 9–12 (2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12) with no extension except by principal double-key re-authorization within 7 days of Month 12 (2027-10-12). Mark any slipped condition in the KPI dashboard as an audit finding.

8.4.D Consequence

Without a locked gate, the program can drift into Month 11 (2027-09-12) or later, compressing the operational window below statistical significance for blind-challenge detection (proposed: 70 injections across 7 event types requires stable staffing and ~7 weeks minimum). A late start also bunches Phase One into winter holiday periods, reducing inspector availability and parity credibility. Worst case: no Phase One occurs, USD 100–200M (estimate) entry-cost burn is absorbed, and the program ends before testing begins.

8.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats entry conditions as procedural prerequisites rather than as hard-gate decisions with binding closure. The Month 12 (2027-10-12) 'outer limit' was intended as a planning buffer but is being read as ambiguity. No single decision-maker or escalation rule was named to break ties on borderline conditions (e.g., one vendor partially bound, one site inspector approval pending). The pre-project assessment flagged this but the plan did not incorporate the recommended locked deadline and principal escalation rule.

8.5.A Issue - Unverifiable-Equipment Threshold at 3% Is Unvalidated and Vulnerable to Exploitation Via Vendor Refusal

The pre-project assessment recommended vendor binding by Month 2.5 (2026-12-27) with a three-tier evidence ladder and explicit escalation to unverifiable status. However, the project plan defers vendor binding to Month 8 (2027-06-12), only 1 month before Phase One clock start. This timing leaves no recovery path if vendors refuse or attestation keys fail validation during the pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27): if 3% of equipment is unverifiable at that point, the site is already in automatic suspension, and there is no time to activate clean-room centers or re-bind vendors. The plan also does not address whether the 3% is measured by unit count (e.g., 3 of 100 devices) or by criticality; neither does it define which government is responsible for equipment that fails identity during intake—a source of disputes.

8.5.B Tags

  • unvalidated_threshold
  • vendor_refusal_concentration
  • attestation_key_risk
  • timing_cascade_failure
  • unverifiable_classification_ambiguity
  • no_recovery_path

8.5.C Mitigation

Complete vendor binding and attestation-key validation by Month 7 (2027-05-12), 2 months before Phase One, not Month 8 (2027-06-12). Run a full vendor census by Month 6 (2027-04-12): each vendor must confirm participation, supply cryptographic key fingerprints, and schedule independent validation testing. For any vendor refusing or unable to validate keys, activate pre-positioned clean-room examination centers by Month 6.5 (2027-04-27) and conduct supervised testing of a random sample (>=10 units per vendor) to establish a baseline detection capability under fallback evidence. Document results in the ledger with attestation-key validation status per vendor. Calibrate the 3% unverifiable threshold against this validated baseline: if vendors representing >5% of declared equipment cannot validate attestation, re-negotiate the threshold jointly or escalate to principals by Month 7 (2027-05-12). Define unverifiable classification rule: any equipment failing intake identity procedures is classified unverifiable; unverifiable items discovered post-intake remain unverifiable and count toward the cumulative threshold. Exclude unverifiable units from the opening inventory baseline so their absence is traceable in the ledger.

8.5.D Consequence

If vendor binding slips or attestation keys fail validation in Month 8 or 8.5 (2027-06-27), 10–40% of equipment could be unverifiable at Phase One clock start, triggering automatic site suspension under the 3% rule. The site fails outright, and the program loses credibility after USD 2–3 billion (estimate) in preparation costs. Alternatively, sites might start Phase One with unverifiable-equipment counts unknown, so disputes over which equipment is unverifiable arise mid-operation and cause deadlock cascades. Without a validated threshold and clear classification rule, the 3% becomes a political target rather than a technical fact.

8.5.E Root Cause

The plan inherited the 3% unverifiable threshold from the pre-project assessment without validating it against actual vendor participation rates or attestation-key custody. Vendor binding was deferred to Month 8 (2027-06-12) to save near-term costs, but this leaves only 1 month for recovery if vendors refuse. The plan also did not specify how unverifiable equipment discovered after intake is counted toward the threshold, which creates ambiguity for late-game disputes.

8.6.A Issue - Challenge-Exercise Partition and False-Positive Escalation Rule Are Defined But Not Operationalized; Misclassification Risk Remains Medium-High

The pre-project assessment estimated 2–3 false-positive incident risks per Phase One if partition is weak. The plan acknowledges this and calls for CHALLENGE tagging and partition, but does not specify the operational detection, escalation and reinstatement workflow. For example: if the intake protocol flags a CHALLENGE substitution as 'unverifiable equipment,' does the system automatically notify co-chairs or only log it? Does an automated suspension trigger occur, or is escalation manual? If the exercise-design panel discovers mid-test that a CHALLENGE event was misclassified by inspectors as operational, how is the correction applied retroactively to the KPI dashboard and ledger? The plan also does not address the training, audit and sign-off procedures to ensure inspectors and systems recognize CHALLENGE tags reliably.

8.6.B Tags

  • partition_not_operationalized
  • misclassification_detection_undefined
  • 2_hour_escalation_not_proceduralized
  • no_automated_tagging_control
  • audit_trail_for_reinstatement_missing
  • inspector_training_gap

8.6.C Mitigation

Define a Challenge-Exercise Misclassification Protocol by Month 8 (2027-06-12) with the following components: (1) Automated detection: the ledger ingestion system must verify every non-CHALLENGE event against the challenge-exercise catalog and halt acceptance if an injected scenario is recorded without the CHALLENGE tag; log all tag-match attempts in a separate 'partition-audit' log. (2) Real-time alert: if an automated flag occurs, a joint duty officer (one from each country) must be notified within 15 minutes with the flagged event, CHALLENGE-tag status, and reason code; the duty officers jointly decide within 30 minutes whether to escalate to principals or mark as reconciled. (3) Principal escalation: if escalation occurs, both co-chairs and their designated adjudication referees are notified within 1 hour (not 2 hours, to allow for time-zone delay) with the full event record, CHALLENGE-tag evidence, and a preliminary assessment. (4) Reinstatement procedure: once principals decide to reinstate a suspended site, the ledger records a 'MISCLASSIFICATION_RESOLUTION' entry with the decision text, signatures and effective-date timestamp; the KPI dashboard is updated to exclude the misclassified event from all thresholds and backfills metrics as if the event did not occur. (5) Inspector training: conduct a 1-hour mandatory training for all inspectors at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) covering CHALLENGE-tag recognition, the escalation workflow, and the non-suspension rule, with a signed acknowledgment in each inspector's file. Conduct a final dry-run misclassification drill at Month 8.75 (2027-07-05) simulating a misclassified event and measuring the time from flag to co-chair notification.

8.6.D Consequence

Without operationalization, a CHALLENGE event that is genuinely flagged as anomalous by inspectors or automated systems will trigger a suspension that then requires a 2-hour emergency escalation across time zones, during which the site is offline and operations are halted. If the escalation procedure is informal or absent, co-chairs may not respond within 2 hours, and the site suspension persists, destroying operational credibility. Alternatively, inspectors may learn to ignore CHALLENGE tags or to suppress legitimate anomaly alerts to avoid false-positive cascades, eroding detection capability. A misclassification incident that is not quickly resolved also becomes an aging discrepancy, which triggers another automatic suspension under the 10-day aging rule, compounding the failure.

8.6.E Root Cause

The plan treats CHALLENGE partition as a labeling rule rather than as an operational workflow. The pre-project assessment correctly identified false-positive cascade risk and called for 'explicit CHALLENGE-event partitioning' and procedures, but the project plan incorporated only the policy ('tagged events cannot trigger suspension') without the operational procedures (who detects, how detection is automated, how escalation is triggered, how reinstatement is recorded). No procedure document, training plan or dry-run drill is scheduled.

Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Entry-gate sunk-cost burn threatens program viability if any of seven conditions slip beyond Month 9 (2027-07-12). Estimated USD 100–200M in preparatory costs (facility hardening, inspector vetting, vendor engagement) must be absorbed within spending envelopes, not contingency. If instrument negotiation or access-authority enactment delays past Month 8 (2027-06-12), Phase One operational window compresses from 90 days to 30–60 days or program is cancelled. Principal go/no-go checkpoint at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27) is noted but lacks binding escalation timers or decision authority that forces a timely defer/proceed/stop decision, leaving the gate to drift past the outer limit of Month 12 (2027-10-12).

  2. Attestation-key concentration creates 10–40% unverifiable-equipment exposure (estimate) with no pre-Phase-One fallback validation. Identity is anchored primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic keys validated by accredited examiners, yet vendor-binding and clean-room-center operationalization are deferred to Month 8 (2027-06-12)–Month 9 (2027-07-12), leaving only 1 month for recovery if vendors refuse or keys fail validation. If unverifiable count exceeds the 3% threshold before Phase One clock stops, sites fail automatically under enumerated suspension triggers. Three-tier fallback evidence ladder (attestation, customs+maintenance, supervised exam) is documented but clean-room centers (USD 30–50M estimate) and bilateral examination protocols remain unoperationalized.

  3. False-positive cascade and challenge-exercise misclassification risk consume 3–7 operational days per incident (estimate) with weak containment procedures. The plan estimates 2–3 false-positive events per Phase One if CHALLENGE-tag partition is weak. A single misclassified exercise event can trigger automatic suspension (e.g., unverifiable >3% or discrepancy age >15 days), requiring a 2-hour principal escalation to reinstate. Misclassification drill is scheduled for Month 8.75 (2027-07-05), only 6 weeks before scored exercises begin, leaving insufficient time to harden procedures if weaknesses are discovered. No automated CHALLENGE-tag detection control is specified; enforcement depends on human triage during operational tempo.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Positive: Credible, hard-to-contest Go/Modify/Stop verdict enables strategic clarity for both governments at Month 12.25 (2027-10-20). Blind detection exercises (>=70 injections across 7 event types), sealed bilateral scoring, and thresholds locked before exercises begin reduce post-hoc dispute over verdict legitimacy. If Go is delivered with documented >=90% detection and <=10% parity variance, both governments gain empirical basis to justify Phase Two investment or alliance adjustments to legislatures. This interacts with entry-gate timing: a delayed gate (slipping past Month 9 = 2027-07-12) compresses the exercise window from 70 days to 30-40 days, reducing injection density and statistical power, which weakens the verdict's defensibility and increases Modify/Stop likelihood despite adequate operational performance. Recommendation: lock Phase One clock at Month 9 (2027-07-12) with principal go/no-go escalation at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27); treat later starts as requiring re-certification of all entry conditions.

  2. Negative: Vendor-refusal cascade and unverifiable-equipment threshold breach (>3%) risk automatic site suspension before Phase One completes, triggering early Stop verdict. Deferred vendor binding to Month 8 (2027-06-12) and untested clean-room centers create a 1-month recovery window if attestation keys fail or vendors refuse. Estimated 10-40% equipment may become unverifiable; if unverifiable exceeds 3% for 5 consecutive days, automatic suspension fires under enumerated triggers. This cascades with false-positive misclassifications (estimated 2-3 per Phase One): a single CHALLENGE event misclassified as operational could trigger unverifiable-equipment escalation or divergence alert, piling multiple auto-suspension triggers simultaneously. Phase One could halt after 30-40 days with insufficient exercise data for any verdict. Recommendation: complete vendor binding and attestation validation by Month 7 (2027-05-12); operationalize clean-room centers by Month 6.5 (2027-04-27); conduct full pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with >=10 injected substitutions (target 9 of 10) and halt scored exercises if detection falls below 85%.

  3. Negative: False-positive cascade and misclassification escalation consume 3-7 operational days per incident (estimate), compressing exercise window and weakening detection-rate empirical basis. A single CHALLENGE event mistakenly flagged as operational triggers automatic escalation to principals within 2 hours; reinstatement requires decision overhead. Estimated 2-3 false positives per Phase One consume 6-21 days of operational capacity lost to escalation and audit. This interacts with staffing buffers: if surge reserves (10% standing + 20-30% floaters) are consumed by escalation duty-officer rotations across time zones, inspector availability for exercises drops, reducing blind-injection density and detection-rate statistical confidence. At threshold: if more than 3 false positives occur, impaired-confidence review is triggered, triggering site suspension or verdict delay. Recommendation: pre-test CHALLENGE-partition and misclassification escalation workflow by Month 8.75 (2027-07-05) with live 2-hour principal-escalation drill; embed automated CHALLENGE-tag detection in the ledger system; implement false-positive audit trail and cap misclassifications at <=2 per site per phase before automatic impaired-confidence trigger.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Establish a bilateral steering committee with weekly entry-condition tracking and locked deadlines by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27). Priority: Critical. Expected impact: reduces sunk-cost burn risk (USD 100–200M estimate) by forcing early visibility of slippage and triggering principal escalation within 48 hours if any condition misses its sub-deadline. Prevent drift past Month 9 (2027-07-12) clock start. Implementation: designate bilateral condition-tracking lead per country; publish a consolidated status dashboard (instrument signature Month 7 = 2027-05-12, access authority Month 7.5 = 2027-05-27, vendor binding Month 8 = 2027-06-12, single gate Month 9 = 2027-07-12); document that any condition >2 weeks behind schedule escalates to principals for a defer/reduce-scope/stop decision.

  2. Conduct filter-adequacy blind pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with >=10 injected substitutions per event type; halt scored exercises if detection falls below 85%. Priority: Critical. Expected impact: prevents discovery of identity-confidence collapse (95% proposed threshold) mid-Phase-One, which would trigger automatic site suspension and force early Stop verdict. Cost: ~USD 2–5M (estimate) within testing envelope; time: 1–2 weeks per test cycle. Implementation: procure test units with authentic substitutions (wrong serial, firmware rollback, physical tampering, attestation forgery); apply proposed redaction rules; measure blind-detection rate; document non-redactable fields locked before any operational equipment is processed.

  3. Complete vendor binding and attestation-key validation by Month 7 (2027-05-12); operationalize >=2 clean-room examination centers by Month 6.5 (2027-04-27). Priority: Critical. Expected impact: reduces vendor-refusal cascade and unverifiable-equipment risk from 10–40% to <5% per site, eliminating automatic site suspension from exceeding the 3% threshold (proposed). Cost: USD 30–50M (estimate) for clean rooms, already budgeted in secure-facilities envelope. Implementation: complete vendor census Month 6 (2027-04-12); validate cryptographic keys through bilateral examiners Month 6.5 (2027-04-27); run supervised testing of >=10 units per refusing vendor; classify equipment by binding status (A/B/C) and auto-escalate Tier C to unverifiable; provide 2-month recovery buffer before Phase One clock.

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Ledger divergence exceeds reconciliation capacity if network partition or key-custody failure occurs mid-Phase-One (Likelihood: Medium). Proposed 4-hour divergence-detection window and 24-hour reconciliation closure assume no sustained network outage or cryptographic key compromise. A 48+ hour undetected ledger divergence (e.g., IPsec tunnel failure, custodian facility compromise) at Month 10-11 (2027-08-12 to 2027-09-12) would render both ledger copies unverifiable until forensic recovery completes; estimated 2-7 day operational halt per incident. This compounds with false-positive cascade: if a divergence is disputed and a CHALLENGE event is simultaneously misclassified, escalation pathways collide—principals must adjudicate both divergence authenticity and exercise legitimacy simultaneously, delaying both decisions. Contingency: establish dedicated network monitoring with <1-hour detection SLA for IPsec anomalies; pre-stage offline ledger-copy recovery media in bilateral custodian escrow; test forensic recovery capability to completion within 24 hours by Month 8 (2027-06-12).

  2. Domestic legal authority enactment may stall on vendor-compulsion scope disputes, delaying entry gate 2-4 months (Likelihood: High). US federal courts may challenge whether private vendors can be compelled to accept Chinese inspection; Chinese state-enterprise ambiguity may exempt critical vendors from binding. Legal litigation or legislative amendment could push access-authority enactment past Month 8 (2027-06-12), consuming USD 50-100M (estimate) and shifting Phase One start to Month 11-12 (2027-09-12 to 2027-10-12). This cascades with vendor binding: if access authority is unresolved, vendors cannot be formally notified of participation requirements, delaying participation census completion (planned Month 6 = 2027-04-12). Combined slippage (legal + vendor binding) consumes the entire Month 8-9 (2027-06-12 to 2027-07-12) buffer. Contingency: commission legal review by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27) identifying court-challenge risk and legislative amendment scope; establish parallel funding for expedited legislative tracks (budget USD 20-30M estimate from legal envelope); escalate unresolved litigation to principals by Month 6 (2027-04-12) for decision on site-scope reduction or access-authority narrowing.

  3. Staffing recruitment and CI vetting cannot be expedited below 2-3 months for 350-500 cleared personnel without relaxing single-person-critical-function rule (Likelihood: Medium). Estimated vetting timeline (background, financial, polygraph, reciprocal clearance) requires concurrent batching and bilateral observation, with at least 200 cleared by Month 2 (2026-12-12) as interim milestone; late-discovered clearance denials cascade into shortage of inspectors for the Month 8 (2027-06-12) staffing dry-run. If >10% of candidates are rejected post-vetting (estimated 20-30 rejections per 200-person batch), surge-reserve buffers (10% standing + 20-30% floaters) are consumed, leaving no capacity for leave or emergency rotation during Phase One. This interacts with inspector tenure limits: if 6-month rotation and 2-month breaks cannot be enforced due to shortage, compartmentation discipline degrades and counterintelligence-exposure risk increases. Contingency: conduct expedited CI vetting on the initial 200 candidates (highest-sensitivity roles) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27) under bilateral observation; establish overflow candidate pool (150-300 additional candidates pre-vetted) by Month 1 (2026-11-12); authorize supplementary staffing appropriation (USD 30-50M estimate) by Month 6 (2027-04-12) if rejection rates exceed 10%.

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Vendor attestation keys remain uncompromised and accredited bilateral examiners can validate keys within 4-hour SLA by Month 10 (2027-08-12). Impact if false: If key compromise or examiner validation delays exceed 4 hours at any critical vendor (>5% equipment), equipment escalates to unverifiable status. Estimated 10-40% of equipment at risk per site; exceeding 3% threshold triggers automatic site suspension and early Stop verdict, eliminating Phase One testing window (90 days compressed to 30-40 days operational). This compounds attestation-key-concentration risk (Medium likelihood): if vendor-binding completion slips past Month 7 (2027-05-12), only 1 month remains for fallback clean-room centers (USD 30-50M estimate) to become operational before clock start. Recommendation: Validate bilateral examiner key-validation latency and forensic-recovery capability by Month 8 (2027-06-12) using actual vendor key samples; execute full attestation dry-runs at all 4 sites Month 8 (2027-06-12) and measure participation rates; if any critical vendor's keys cannot be validated within 4 hours, pre-escalate to principals for alternate binding pathway decision by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27).

  2. Assumption: Ledger synchronization can achieve 1-hour checkpoint exchange and 4-hour divergence detection with <5% false-positive rate under 10x normal event load. Impact if false: If actual synchronization latency exceeds 1 hour (realistic under network partition or IPsec tunnel congestion), divergence-detection window drifts past 4-hour target; undetected tampering risk climbs by estimated 20-30% per incident. Materiality threshold (>5% disputed events) may not trigger automatic impaired-confidence review within the decision window, aging unresolved divergences until >15-day Stop criterion fires. This interacts with false-positive cascade (Medium likelihood): if divergence detection produces >5% false positives during ledger stress-test, automated impaired-confidence triggers misfire, consuming escalation capacity that should be reserved for real divergences. Cost impact: undetected divergences require 2-7 day forensic recovery (estimated) at neutral-custodian escrow (USD 20-30M budget), burning operational time mid-Phase-One. Recommendation: Conduct 1-week ledger stress-test at Month 8 (2027-06-12) under 10x event load with real-time latency monitoring; measure actual synchronization, divergence detection and reconciliation times; if latency exceeds 1-hour KPI or false-positive rate >5%, halt Phase One until hardened transport (dedicated fiber, redundant IPsec) is operational and tested.

  3. Assumption: 350-500 cleared inspectors can be recruited, vetted (background, financial, polygraph, reciprocal clearance) and deployed with zero single-person-critical-function violations by Month 8 (2027-06-12). Impact if false: Typical CI vetting cycles (6-12 months estimate) compressed to 2-3 months creates batch bottleneck; if >15% of candidates are rejected post-polygraph or reciprocal clearance is disputed, surge reserves (10% standing + 20-30% floaters) are consumed, leaving <5% staffing contingency. During Phase One Months 10-11 (2027-08-12 to 2027-09-12), 15% leave + unplanned absences could drop staffing below 80% operational threshold, triggering automatic operational curtailment and reduced exercise injection density (estimated 30-40% reduction in blind-challenge executions). This cascades with tenure-limit enforcement: if staffing shortage forces >6-month site assignments, compartmentation discipline degrades, counterintelligence-exposure risk increases by estimated 20-30%, and operator confidence declines. Cost impact: USD 30-50M (estimate) supplementary staffing appropriation if shortfall exceeds 10%. Recommendation: Begin expedited CI vetting on initial 200 candidates (highest-sensitivity inspectors) by Month 1 (2026-11-12) under bilateral observation; maintain overflow candidate pool (150-300 additional pre-vetted) by Month 2 (2026-12-12) for surge deployment; conduct staffing dry-run at Month 8 (2027-06-12) modeling leave/tenure/rotation and document any function falling below 2-FTE minimum; escalate staffing shortfall >10% to principals by Month 6 (2027-04-12) for supplementary appropriation decision.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. KPI 1: Blind-Detection Rate by Event Type (Target: ≥90% per type, Halt if <85% pre-test). Measures whether layered evidence and operator-gateway filtering retain sufficient detail to detect substituted equipment, inaccurate records, and vendor refusal across 7 event types with ≥10 injections each (70 total). Success requires ≥9 of 10 detections per type by Month 11.5 (2027-09-27) scoring window. Interacts with filter-adequacy assumption: if redaction strips non-redactable fields (serial, firmware, attestation digest), detection drops below 85% at pre-test Month 8.5 (2027-06-27), triggering halt and renegotiation before Phase One clock. Recommendation: log every redaction decision with reason code in the ledger; conduct monthly filter-drift audits during Phase One; if detection degrades >5% between months, escalate to bilateral engineers for rule adjustment within 48 hours.

  2. KPI 2: Cumulative-Disbursement Parity (Target: ±10% pro-rata tolerance; Flag >15% monthly divergence). Tracks whether each country's spending (ledger, site prep, personnel, facilities, testing, legal, contingency) remains balanced within ±10% of its USD 2.5B allocation, detecting asymmetric cost-shifting or front-loaded spending. Escalates >15% monthly divergence to principals for explanation before tranche 2 release Month 10 (2027-08-12). Interacts with contingency-burn risk (Medium likelihood): if one country front-loads vendor compensation or facility hardening, cumulative divergence climbs; early detection triggers impaired-confidence review and tranche hold. Recommendation: publish independent budget auditor's monthly burn report (ledger envelope, site prep, personnel, security) by the 5th business day of each month; classify all spending by envelope and country; escalate >20% divergence automatically to impaired-confidence review.

  3. KPI 3: Reciprocal-Access Parity Variance (Target: ≤10% between matched sites; >15% for 2 weeks = Impaired Confidence). Measures whether inspectors from each country receive equivalent access to equipment, maintenance records, evidence handling and exit witnessing at matched sites, normalized by declared equipment count. Compares approval rates for inspector-hour requests, sampling access and filter-rule audits. Go decision requires variance ≤10% at verdict Month 12.25 (2027-10-20). Interacts with site-equivalence assumption and false-positive cascade (Medium likelihood): if one site denies access for legitimate reasons (customs delay, operator maintenance), variance climbs; if a CHALLENGE event is misclassified as an access denial, automated impaired-confidence trigger fires prematurely. Recommendation: log every access denial with reason code and justification within 24 hours; calculate weekly approval-rate delta per matched pair; publish parity variance in KPI dashboard with ≥2-week trend; if variance exceeds 15% for 2 consecutive weeks, escalate to bilateral operations directors within 48 hours.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objective: Deliver a credible, hard-to-contest Go/Modify/Stop verdict on bilateral equipment-change verification by Month 12.25 (2027-10-20). The report aims to guide bilateral execution of a 90-day Phase One operational test (Months 9–12, 2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12) at 4 matched US-China declared sites, grounded in blind-detection exercises (≥70 injections across 7 event types), sealed bilateral scoring, and enumerated suspension triggers. Deliverables include detailed governance procedures (5-day deadlock escalation, automatic suspension rules, CHALLENGE-tag partition), entry-condition timelines with principal go/no-go checkpoint (Month 7.5 = 2027-05-27), and a complete work-breakdown structure mapping all tasks to funding envelopes and staff roles. Intended audience: bilateral co-chairs, principals, finance authorities, and participating operators/vendors who must certify entry conditions and fund Phase One.

  2. Key Decisions Informed: (1) Entry-gate timing and binding escalation authority; (2) Vendor-binding strategy and clean-room fallback operationalization; (3) Deadlock and false-positive containment procedures embedded in the bilateral instrument. The report quantifies sunk-cost exposure (USD 100–200M estimate if gate slips past Month 9 = 2027-07-12), unverifiable-equipment risk (10–40% estimate without pre-Phase-One vendor validation), and false-positive cascade impact (3–7 operational days per incident estimate). It establishes objective decision rules (e.g., unverifiable >3% for 5 days = automatic suspension; detection <85% at pre-test = halt scored exercises) that substitute procedural clarity for political negotiation, enabling principals to decide scope reduction, deferral, or cancellation without bilateral deadlock.

  3. Version 2 Differs from Version 1 by: (1) Locking all provisional thresholds (identity confidence >95%, unverifiable ≤3%, parity variance ≤10%, ledger sync ≤1 hour, detection ≥90%) with explicit validation methods and halt gates (filter-adequacy pre-test Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27 with <85% minimum); (2) Embedding deadlock escalation language, enumerated auto-suspension triggers, and CHALLENGE-tag partition rules directly in the bilateral instrument (signed Month 7 = 2027-05-12) rather than treating them as procedural guidance; (3) Adding a comprehensive work-breakdown structure with named responsible parties, funding sources, and task sequencing tied to entry-condition deadlines and readiness rehearsals. Version 1 identified gaps; Version 2 operationalizes the closure.

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Vendor-Binding Timeline and Attestation-Key Validation SLA (4-hour latency assumption) are not validated against actual vendor participation or examiner capacity. Critical because: if vendors representing >5% of equipment cannot validate cryptographic keys within the 4-hour SLA by Month 10 (2027-08-12), equipment escalates to unverifiable status; exceeding the 3% threshold (proposed) triggers automatic site suspension. Consequence of relying on unvalidated data: a single vendor delay or key-custody failure discovered mid-Phase-One forces clean-room fallback (USD 30–50M estimate) already operationalized, but if examiner capacity is insufficient or bilateral protocols are incomplete, escalation cascades into site suspension. Recommendation: By Month 7 (2027-05-12), execute attestation dry-runs at all 4 sites using actual vendor key samples; measure examiner validation latency against the 4-hour SLA; document any vendor unable to participate and classify as Tier C (unverifiable); validate that clean-room centers can absorb the Tier C load without exceeding Month 9 (2027-07-12) operational start.

  2. Ledger Synchronization Latency and Divergence-Detection False-Positive Rate are modeled but not stress-tested before Phase One. Critical because: the 1-hour checkpoint-exchange KPI and 4-hour divergence-detection window (proposed) assume no network partition, IPsec tunnel congestion, or cryptographic-key custody delays; false-positive divergence detection (proposed: <5% rate, not verified) could trigger auto-suspension on legitimate checkpoints. Consequence of incorrect assumptions: if actual synchronization latency exceeds 1 hour under 10x normal event load (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-12 to 2027-09-12), undetected divergence window grows from 4 hours to 12+ hours, increasing tampering and forensic-recovery cost (USD 20–30M estimate from ledger envelope). Recommendation: Conduct a 1-week ledger stress-test at Month 8 (2027-06-12) under 10x event-load injection; validate synchronization latency, divergence detection and reconciliation closure times against KPI targets; if any KPI slips >10%, halt Phase One and harden transport (dedicated fiber, redundant IPsec) before scored exercises begin.

  3. Filter-Adequacy Detection Rate Under Redacted Evidence Is Assumed at >85% (proposed halt threshold) but Untested Against Non-Redactable Field Dependencies. Critical because: the minimum evidence schema (serial, firmware, attestation digest, timestamp, physical identifiers; cluster membership and power state redactable) assumes >=2 independent corroboration layers remain sufficient for 95% (proposed) identity confidence after redaction; if redaction strips contextual fields (e.g., cluster-membership pattern changes that correlate with substitution), detection rate degrades below 85%. Consequence of unvalidated assumption: blind pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) with >=10 injected substitutions discovers <85% detection, forcing filter renegotiation between Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) and Phase One clock (Month 9 = 2027-07-12), compressing redaction-rule redesign and operator-gateway re-implementation to 2 weeks (insufficient for bilateral review cycles). Recommendation: Run filter-simulation by Month 8 (2027-06-12) on >=70 test substitutions (10 per event type) applying actual redaction rules; measure detection-rate impact per redactable field; lock non-redactable fields and corroboration-layer agreement in the bilateral instrument by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27); if simulation reveals <85% detection, escalate to principals for filter redesign or schedule extension decision.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Bilateral Principal Commitment to Binding Entry-Gate Deadlines and Escalation Authority (Month 7.5 = 2027-05-27 go/no-go decision). Critical because: the plan's viability depends on a hard principal decision to defer, proceed with reduced scope, or stop if any of 7 conditions will not certify by Month 9 (2027-07-12). Without explicit written escalation authority and binding timers, gate work drifts past Month 9 (2027-07-12), sunk-cost exposure grows to USD 100–200M (estimate) against spending envelopes, and Phase One operational window compresses from 90 days to 30–60 days or closes entirely. Recommendation: Convene co-chairs and national principals by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27) to jointly sign a Binding Entry-Gate Charter documenting: Month 7 (2027-05-12) instrument signature, Month 7.5 (2027-05-27) principal checkpoint decision with explicit defer/proceed/stop options, automatic 48-hour escalation rule if any condition slips, and pre-authorized contingency paths (e.g., subset of sites, phased access authority).

  2. Operator Confidentiality Guarantees and Compartmentation Effectiveness Validation Before Operator Contracts Are Signed (target Month 6 = 2027-04-12). Critical because: operators will not consent to resident foreign inspectors without credible assurance that zone boundaries, filter rules, and evidence handling protect unrelated proprietary information and workload confidentiality. Unvalidated compartmentation or filter-adequacy assumptions discovered post-Phase-One-start erode operator confidence, risking site withdrawal (automatic operator-consent-withdrawal suspension under enumerated triggers). Impact: loss of 20–40% operator support across all sites could cascade into a Stop verdict for multiple sites simultaneously due to material unverifiable equipment or asymmetric access. Recommendation: By Month 5.5 (2027-03-27), conduct a formal operator-consultation workshop with all participating site managers covering: final evidence schema, redaction-gateway rules and audit procedures, zone-boundary maps, filter-decision logging, and third-party (independent auditor) validation of compartmentation compliance; obtain signed operator confidentiality consent and consent-status baseline before any inspector deployment.

  3. Certified Vendor-Participation Census and Attestation-Key Validation Results by Month 7 (2027-05-12), With Principal Escalation Authority for Any Vendor Representing >5% Equipment That Cannot Validate Keys. Critical because: vendor binding and clean-room operationalization (planned Months 6.5–9 = 2027-04-27 to 2027-07-12) determine whether unverifiable-equipment risk can be contained below the 3% (proposed threshold) threshold before Phase One clock starts. Without documented attestation-validation results and clean-room readiness confirmation from principals by Month 7 (2027-05-12), Phase One may launch with unknown unverifiable-equipment counts, triggering automatic site suspension at Month 9.5 (2027-07-27) if counts exceed 3%. Impact: estimated 10–40% equipment unverifiable per site if vendor binding incomplete; exceeding 3% forces automatic site suspension and early Stop verdict. Recommendation: Publish vendor-participation census results and attestation-validation status (Tier A/B/C classification per vendor, unverifiable count per site) by Month 7 (2027-05-12) with principal review and approval; escalate any vendor >5% equipment unable to validate keys to principals within 24 hours of Month 7 (2027-05-12) for decision on alternate binding pathway, clean-room capacity scaling, or site-scope reduction.

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Vendor participation and attestation-key validation latency (4-hour SLA) remain achievable without COVID-like supply-chain disruption or geopolitical vendor sanctions. If revised: sanctions on critical vendors (>5% equipment) between now and Month 7 (2027-05-12) could force Tier C (unverifiable) classification of 15–30% equipment per site, exceeding the 3% (proposed) threshold and triggering automatic site suspension before Phase One clock starts. This cascades into entry-gate failure because vendors cannot be bound and unverifiable forecast cannot be corrected before Month 9 (2027-07-12) certification. Recommendation: conduct bilateral vendor-risk assessment by Month 1 (2026-11-12) flagging geopolitical or export-control exposure for each critical vendor; establish contingency vendor list (alternate suppliers per equipment category) and pre-negotiate binding terms as backup pathway if primary vendor becomes unavailable.

  2. Assumption: Bilateral legal authority to compel private vendors and operators can be enacted domestically without litigation delays exceeding 4 weeks by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27). If revised: litigation over vendor-compulsion scope (e.g., US constitutional due-process challenge, Chinese state-enterprise exemption) could delay access-authority enactment to Month 9–10 (2027-07-12 to 2027-08-12), consuming 2–4 months (estimate) and shifting Phase One start past Month 12 (2027-10-12) outer limit. Sunk-cost exposure rises from USD 100–200M (estimate) to USD 150–300M (estimate) against spending envelopes. Recommendation: escalate unresolved litigation risk to principals by Month 5 (2027-03-12); authorize supplementary legal appropriation (USD 30–50M estimate) by Month 6 (2027-04-12) if litigation is active; prepare contingency scope-reduction pathways (e.g., exclude disputed vendor categories, narrower access authority) for bilateral decision by Month 6.5 (2027-04-27).

  3. Assumption: Challenge-exercise false-positive rate can be held below 3 incidents per Phase One with CHALLENGE-tag partition and 2-hour escalation procedures (not pre-validated). If revised: actual false-positive rate during unscored calibration exercises (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27) exceeds 3 per site, cascading false-positive cascades consume 3–7 operational days per incident (estimate) and reduce blind-injection density by 30–40%, weakening detection-rate statistical power and forcing Modify verdict despite adequate underlying capability. Cost: estimated 6–21 days operational loss (estimate) per Phase One. Recommendation: during unscored calibration (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27), track false-positive incident count and confidence-degradation impact daily; if false-positive count reaches 3 before scored exercises begin (Month 10.5 = 2027-08-27), automatically halt scored exercises and conduct bilateral misclassification-procedure audit with principal decision on whether to proceed with modified thresholds or defer Phase One verdict.

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Clarify Contingency-Draw Authority and Spending Timeline for Gate-Readiness Sub-Account (USD 50M from USD 500M contingency). Impact: if gate-readiness sub-account draws are not pre-authorized with clear trigger criteria, sunk-cost burn during entry-condition work (Months 0–9 = 2026-10-12 to 2027-07-12) accumulates against the USD 1.0B site-preparation envelope, leaving insufficient free contingency (USD 450M after gate sub-account) for Phase One operational surges. Recommendation: document explicit draw triggers: condition-slip acceleration costs (legal expedite, vendor re-negotiation, site-survey repeat) must be approved within 48 hours by bilateral co-chairs; cap total gate-readiness draws at USD 50M; if draws approach USD 40M by Month 6 (2027-04-12), escalate to principals for decision on deferral or supplementary appropriation.

  2. Confirm Clean-Room Examination Center Cost Attribution and Funding Source (USD 30–50M estimate within secure-facilities envelope). Impact: the canonical facts map clean-room construction and security to the USD 750M secure-facilities envelope, leaving only USD 700–720M for hardened ledger-node facilities, counterintelligence compartmentation spaces, and CI personnel vetting infrastructure. If clean-room estimates grow beyond USD 50M or bilateral agreement assigns cost to the USD 500M testing envelope (examiner staffing and test runs), budget reallocation could underfund ledger hardening (proposed: USD 100–150M estimate for nodes + escrow). Recommendation: by Month 2 (2026-12-12), produce bilateral cost breakdown for clean-room construction (facility, security, compliance certification) and examiner staffing (training, equipment, operational cycles); lock funding source in the bilateral instrument; if total exceeds USD 50M, escalate to principals for envelope reallocation or supplementary appropriation decision.

  3. Resolve CNY-to-USD Conversion Rule and Compensation Asymmetry Risk Within the USD 500M Per-Country Site-Preparation Share. Impact: each country compensates its own operators and vendors from its USD 500M per-country site-preparation share using a single fixed CNY conversion rule (proposed; not yet documented). If China's operator or vendor compensation costs are denominated in CNY at exchange rates >7 CNY/USD (estimate), or if US compensation rates are inflated relative to market (e.g., overtime, security premiums), cumulative-disbursement parity variance could exceed the 10% tolerance (proposed threshold), triggering budget audit and tranche hold. Consequence: delayed Phase One start and loss of political momentum. Recommendation: by Month 6 (2027-04-12), jointly document the fixed CNY conversion rate for all Chinese compensation; validate operator/vendor compensation quantum against bilateral equivalence benchmarks (e.g., market survey, prior contract rates); lock compensation ceilings per country in the bilateral instrument before tranche 1 release (Month 7 = 2027-05-12); publish total budgeted compensation per country in the KPI dashboard monthly to enable real-time divergence detection.

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Bilateral Co-Chair Authority and Decision-Making Scope (Double-Key Authorization Rule). Essential because: the plan mandates co-chair sign-off on all major decisions (budgets, protocol changes, site findings, suspension orders, verdict) without a casting vote or escalation procedure if co-chairs disagree at the 5-day deadlock window. Unclarity on co-chair authority boundaries risks one chair claiming veto over decisions the other considers operational (e.g., suspension triggers, filter-rule adjustments). Impact: deadlock persists beyond 5 days, unresolved discrepancies age past the 10-day impaired-confidence threshold toward the 15-day suspension threshold, and automatic suspension fires without bilateral consensus, forcing principal escalation that co-chairs could have resolved at their level. Recommendation: document explicit co-chair authority charter by Month 7 (2027-05-12) specifying which decisions require double-key (budgets >USD 10M, suspension triggers, filter changes) vs. which are operational delegations (inspector assignments, daily access denials); establish 48-hour principal escalation only for operator or vendor refusal (2 hours for CHALLENGE misclassification); deadlocks follow referee panel Days 5-8 and principal review Days 8-13.

  2. Independent Budget Auditor Independence and Tranche-Release Authority. Essential because: the auditor certifies fiscal parity (±10% pro-rata tolerance) before each tranche release (Months 7, 10, 13, 16 = 2027-05-12 to 2028-02-12), yet the plan does not specify whether the auditor has veto power over tranche release or only a recommendation authority. If either government can contest an auditor finding and block tranche release pending re-audit, the program stalls; if the auditor's findings are overridden by co-chairs, fiscal parity controls collapse. Impact: estimated 2–4 week delay per parity dispute (estimate), contingency burn accelerates, and one government may be front-loading costs without consequence. Recommendation: embed auditor independence and binding authority in the bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12): auditor certifies parity monthly; >15% divergence flags spending explanation requirement; >20% divergence holds tranche release pending principal bilateral decision within 5 days; auditor has no discretion to override objective parity calculation.

  3. Incident Command Center Duty Officer and Escalation Authority (Misclassification and Deadlock Response). Essential because: the plan specifies a 2-hour principal escalation SLA for misclassified CHALLENGE events and a 5-day deadlock escalation, yet does not name who staffs the ICC duty-officer roster, how time-zone coverage is ensured, or what authority duty officers have to declare a misclassification or trigger escalation without bilateral co-chair consensus. Unclarity risks: escalation delays exceed 2 hours, CHALLENGE misclassifications are not flagged until after suspension fires; deadlock timers are not enforced because no officer is tasked with tracking the 5-day window. Impact: estimated 3–7 day operational loss per false-positive cascade (estimate); unresolved deadlocks age indefinitely without documented triggering. Recommendation: designate a 24/7 ICC duty-officer roster (min 1 officer per country per shift) by Month 7 (2027-05-12) with explicit authority to: detect CHALLENGE misclassification within 30 minutes and notify both co-chairs automatically; track deadlock age daily, refer to the referee panel at Day 5 and to principals at Day 8 without co-chair consensus; document all escalations in the ledger within 1 hour of decision.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Filter-Adequacy Blind Pre-Test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27) Must Precede Operator-Gateway Finalization (Month 7.5 = 2027-05-27); Sequencing Reversal Risks Undetected Inadequacy. The non-redactable schema is locked in the instrument at signature (Month 7 = 2027-05-12); the blind pre-test at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27) only validates gateway implementation, and any later filter change is a double-key protocol change through an annex, so filtered evidence must retain ≥85% (proposed threshold) substitution-detection capability. If pre-test discovers <85% detection due to aggressive redaction, filter redesign and operator-gateway re-implementation must compress into the 2-week window between pre-test (Month 8.5 = 2027-06-27) and Phase One clock (Month 9 = 2027-07-12). Bilateral review cycles cannot complete in 2 weeks; Phase One may launch with unvalidated filters. Recommendation: lock the non-redactable schema at signature (Month 7 = 2027-05-12), complete filter-adequacy simulation by Month 8 (2027-06-12), conduct blind pre-test to validate gateway implementation at Month 8.5 (2027-06-27), and handle any later filter change as a double-key annex through Month 9 (2027-07-12).

  2. Vendor Binding and Clean-Room Operationalization (Month 6.5-9 = 2027-04-27 to 2027-07-12) Must Precede Unverifiable-Equipment Threshold Validation (Month 9 = 2027-07-12); Late Completion Leaves No Recovery Path. Vendor-participation census (Month 6 = 2027-04-12), attestation-key validation (Month 6.5 = 2027-04-27), and clean-room operational readiness (Month 9 = 2027-07-12) are sequenced to complete before Phase One clock starts, but if any slip past Month 8 (2027-06-12), only 1 month remains to activate fallback examination or escalate unverifiable-equipment forecast to principals. Estimated 10-40% (estimate) equipment unverifiable per site if vendor binding incomplete; exceeding the 3% (proposed threshold) threshold at Phase One start (Month 9 = 2027-07-12) triggers automatic site suspension under enumerated triggers before a single exercise injection. Recommendation: compress vendor census to Month 5.5 (2027-03-27), attestation validation to Month 6.5 (2027-04-27), and clean-room trials to Month 8 (2027-06-12), creating a 4-week buffer before Phase One clock; if any vendor >5% equipment cannot validate keys by Month 7 (2027-05-12), escalate to principals immediately for alternate binding or threshold adjustment.

  3. Counterintelligence Vetting Completion (Month 2 = 2026-12-12) and Staffing Dry-Run (Month 8 = 2027-06-12) Must Validate Tenure and Leave Buffers Before Surge-Capacity Allocation; Reversed Order Risks Staffing Shortfall Mid-Phase-One. CI vetting (background, polygraph, reciprocal clearance; at least 200 cleared by Month 2 = 2026-12-12 as interim milestone, at least 80% of target staff cleared by Month 8 = 2027-06-12 with no function under 2 FTE as the gate) must complete before staffing dry-run (Month 8 = 2027-06-12), which models 24/7 shift rotation, leave buffers (15% proposed threshold), surge reserves (10% standing + 20-30% floaters proposed threshold) and tenure enforcement. If vetting slips past Month 3 (2027-01-12), the 5-month staffing dry-run window compresses to 2-3 months, leaving insufficient time to identify shortfalls or recruit backups before Phase One. Staffing falls below the 80% (proposed threshold) minimum deployment threshold during Months 10-11 (2027-08-12 to 2027-09-12), reducing inspector availability by 20-40% (estimate) and compressing blind-exercise injection density. Recommendation: begin expedited vetting on initial 200 candidates (highest-sensitivity roles) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27), clear at least 200 by Month 2 (2026-12-12) and at least 80% of target staff by Month 8 (2027-06-12), conduct full staffing dry-run, sized from actual vetting throughput (pilot of 10-20 candidates per country), (all shifts, all sites, leave/tenure/rotation modeling) by Month 8 (2027-06-12), and validate surge-capacity deployment procedures before Phase One.

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Phase Two Scope and Funding Authorization Remain Undefined; Ambiguity Risks USD 2.5–5.0B Supplementary Appropriation Without Strategic Justification. The plan allocates USD 5.0B to Phase One only; post-verdict funding for Phase Two (additional sites, continuous operation, deeper vendor integration) is an open decision with no scope criteria or cost model. If Phase Two requires USD 2.5–5.0B (estimate) additional appropriation by Month 13 (2027-11-12) and Congress/Beijing have not pre-authorized supplementary funding, Phase Two cannot proceed, stranding the Phase One investment and eroding bilateral confidence. Recommendation: by Month 12 (2027-10-12), establish a Phase Two decision framework specifying: Go triggers Phase Two authorization for 8–12 sites (estimate USD 2.5B additional); Modify triggers corrective trials within 12 months (estimate USD 500M–1.0B); Stop closes the program.

  2. Tranche 3-4 Release Contingent on Non-Stop Verdict (Month 13 = 2027-11-12 Onward); No Procedure Defined for Resolving Disputed Verdicts or Deferring Phase Two Commitment. Tranches 3-4 (USD 2.5B combined, USD 1.25B per country) release only after a Go or Modify verdict and new bilateral budget authorization. If the verdict is Modify (correctable weaknesses identified), neither government may accept the other's judgment on corrective-action adequacy, stalling Phase Two commitment indefinitely. Tranche 3-4 funds accumulate unspent, generating opportunity-cost questions about alternative uses (estimate: 2–4 month delay per dispute). Recommendation: lock bilateral agreement by Month 11 (2027-09-12) defining objective Modify-acceptance criteria (e.g., detection 80% to <90% with a correctable cause, parity variance <12%, ledger latency <2 hours) and specifying remediation scope; if criteria are met, tranche 3 releases automatically by Month 14 (2027-12-12).

  3. CNY Conversion Rate and Operator Compensation Asymmetry May Consume Free Contingency (USD 450M) if Chinese Cost Drivers Exceed Bilateral Benchmarks. Each country compensates its own operators and vendors from its USD 500M per-country site-preparation share; China uses CNY denominated in USD at a fixed conversion rule (not yet documented). If Chinese compensation costs exceed market rates (estimate: 5–10x variance possible) or US rates include security/overtime premiums, cumulative-disbursement parity divergence could reach 20% (proposed threshold) by Month 10 (2027-08-12), triggering tranche hold and consuming USD 50–100M (estimate) from free contingency for audit and re-negotiation. Recommendation: by Month 6 (2027-04-12), jointly establish fixed CNY conversion rate and operator/vendor compensation ceilings per site; publish budgeted compensation per country in the KPI dashboard monthly; escalate >15% divergence to independent auditor within 48 hours for bilateral principal decision.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Transparent, Real-Time KPI Visibility Maintains Leadership Momentum and Operator Confidence Throughout the 90-Day Window. Monthly KPI dashboard publication (detection rate by event type, parity variance, ledger latency, unverifiable count, false-positive incidents, funding timeliness) enables both co-chairs to track progress against frozen thresholds and demonstrate credibility to operators and principals. If KPI reporting lapses or is delayed >5 business days, perceived operational opacity erodes operator consent and political backing. Recommendation: designate a dedicated KPI-reporting officer per country; publish a scrubbed dashboard by the 5th business day of each month showing all metrics with threshold status (green/yellow/red); escalate yellow-tier metrics within 48 hours with documented corrective actions.

  2. Documented Principal Escalation Decisions and Binding Timers Prevent Indefinite Deadlock That Consumes Motivation by Compressing the Exercise Window. Deadlock escalation (5/8/13-day timers: referee panel Days 5-8, principal review Days 8-13) embedded in the bilateral instrument by Month 7 (2027-05-12) ensures that contested findings do not age unresolved beyond 15 days, triggering automatic site suspension and eroding operational confidence. Without locked timers and decision authority, leadership teams encounter indefinite procedural stalls (estimated 2–4 weeks per dispute) that compress the remaining 70-day exercise window below statistical power. Recommendation: publish a bilateral escalation procedures manual by Month 9 (2027-07-12); track deadlock age daily in the KPI dashboard; trigger impaired-confidence review for any finding >10 days unresolved and treat >15 days as a Stop candidate with automatic suspension absent a written principal decision.

  3. Clear Phase Two Authorization Criteria and Supplementary-Funding Pathway Enable Teams to Invest Phase One Effort Toward Documented Strategic Continuation. Absence of Phase Two scope criteria (e.g., Go triggers authorization for 8–12 sites at USD 2.5B; Modify triggers 12-month corrective trials at USD 500M–1.0B) leaves inspectorate staff uncertain whether their Phase One work will have strategic value post-verdict, reducing daily motivation. If Phase Two is abandoned due to budget ambiguity, USD 5B Phase One investment appears spent without lasting capability. Recommendation: by Month 11 (2027-09-12), establish a bilateral Phase Two decision framework locking objective Go/Modify/Stop acceptance criteria and corresponding funding authorization triggers; publish framework in advance so teams understand how Phase One performance maps to Phase Two commitment.

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Automate Weekly Entry-Condition Tracking Dashboard and Principal Escalation Alerts (Reduce Manual Reporting by 80%; Save ~10 Staff-Hours/Week). Implement a shared bilateral spreadsheet or lightweight database auto-calculating condition status (instrument signature, access authority, vendor binding, site selection deadline compliance) against locked timelines; trigger automated email alerts to co-chairs and principals when any condition drifts >2 weeks behind schedule. Interacts with entry-gate sunk-cost risk (USD 100–200M estimate if gate slips): real-time visibility enables 48-hour principal escalation without bilateral deliberation delay. Implementation: designate a bilateral condition-tracking officer per country by Month 0.5 (2026-10-27); deploy shared tracking spreadsheet with conditional-formatting alerts (green/yellow/red status) by Month 1 (2026-11-12); configure automated weekly summary email to both co-chairs by Month 1.5 (2026-11-27).

  2. Automate Ledger Divergence Detection and Materiality Alerts (Reduce Manual Reconciliation by 60%; Accelerate Detection from 4-Hour to <30-Minute SLA). Implement automated divergence-detection algorithm in the bilateral ledger system that compares signed checkpoints hourly, flags mismatches >5 discrepancies per site per week automatically, and notifies duty officers within 30 minutes (vs. proposed 4-hour manual detection window). Interacts with ledger-divergence risk (Medium likelihood, 2–7 day operational halt per incident estimate): automation eliminates human bottleneck in mismatch discovery, enabling faster escalation and reconciliation. Implementation: develop divergence-detection algorithm specification by Month 7 (2027-05-12); integrate into ledger system codebase by Month 8 (2027-06-12); stress-test under 10x event load by Month 8.5 (2027-06-27); deploy live monitoring dashboard with alerts by Month 9 (2027-07-12).

  3. Automate KPI Calculation and Threshold-Status Reporting (Reduce Monthly Manual Compilation by 90%; Enable Same-Day Publication). Implement automated KPI pipeline that pulls detection rates, parity variance, ledger latency, unverifiable counts, false-positive incidents, and funding timeliness from ledger and operational logs; auto-calculates against frozen thresholds; flags yellow/red alerts; publishes scrubbed dashboard by the 3rd business day of each month (vs. proposed 5th business day target). Interacts with motivation and momentum maintenance: real-time transparency maintains operator confidence and political backing. Saves ~40 staff-hours/month on manual metric compilation and bilateral reconciliation. Implementation: design KPI-calculation specification by Month 8 (2027-06-12); implement automated pipeline by Month 9 (2027-07-12); conduct validation run during unscored calibration exercises (Months 9.5–10.5 = 2027-07-27 to 2027-08-27); deploy live dashboard by Month 10 (2027-08-12).

Q1: What is the 'Consortium' and what is its primary purpose?

A1: The Consortium is a bilateral US-China verification mechanism testing whether declared-equipment changes at matched datacenters can be credibly detected through layered evidence, mirrored inspectorates, and double-key governance. Phase One is a 90-day operational test (Months 9–12, 2027-07-12 to 2027-10-12) with a Go/Modify/Stop verdict. Scope is limited to changes only (arrivals, removals, maintenance); excludes total-capacity estimates, workload inspection, and proof of absent hidden facilities.

Q2: What does 'double-key authorization' mean in the context of this plan, and why is it important?

A2: Double-key authorization means both countries' representatives (co-chairs) must jointly approve all major decisions—budgets, protocol changes, site findings, suspension orders, verdicts—without a casting vote or majority override. Neither government can act unilaterally. This prevents one party from obstruction by ensuring deadlocks escalate to principals with fixed timers (5/8/13 days) and objective suspension triggers, not political negotiation.

Q3: What is an 'enumerated automatic-suspension trigger' and what happens when one is activated?

A3: An enumerated automatic-suspension trigger is an objective condition that suspends a site automatically without requiring bilateral co-chair agreement. Examples include: unverifiable equipment exceeds 3% for 5 days; ledger divergence exceeds 5%; access denial variance exceeds 15%; contested findings remain unresolved >15 days. When triggered, the site halts operations pending a principal-level double-key decision on resumption conditions (documented corrective action required).

Q4: What is the 'CHALLENGE-tag partition' and why is false-positive cascade containment described as a critical risk?

A4: CHALLENGE-tag partition means every injected exercise scenario is cryptographically tagged before injection; tagged events cannot trigger suspension or impaired-confidence review without principal-level adjudication. This prevents misclassified test substitutions from cascading into automatic suspension. The pre-assessment estimates 2–3 false-positive incidents per Phase One; each consumes 3–7 operational days and erodes regime credibility. A false positive cascade (e.g., three CHALLENGE events misclassified as operational triggering three auto-suspensions) can consume 21 days and compress the exercise window below statistical power for detecting real threats.

Q5: Why is the entry-gate timeline (seven mandatory conditions certified by Month 9, 2027-07-12) described as a 'critical-path risk' and what is the USD 50M escrow sub-account?

A5: The entry gate is a critical path because seven conditions (signed instrument, appropriations, access authority, site selection, inspector approval, operator/vendor participation, provisional schedule) typically require 6–12 months to align bilaterally, yet must all be certified simultaneously by Month 9 (2027-07-12) or Phase One never starts. Slippage burns an estimated USD 100–200M in preparatory costs (facility hardening, inspector vetting) against the spending envelopes, not contingency, leaving insufficient free funding for Phase One surges. The USD 50M escrow sub-account (USD 25M per country, inside the USD 500M contingency) is accessible only upon joint certification of all seven conditions, preventing sunk-cost accumulation if the gate fails.

Q6: What is the 'attestation-key concentration risk' and why does it represent a fundamental tension between scalability and security?

A6: Attestation-key concentration means equipment identity is anchored primarily on vendor-issued cryptographic keys validated by accredited examiners. This scales efficiently across many units but creates a single-point-of-failure: if a vendor's keys are compromised, forged, or withheld, an estimated 10–40% of equipment becomes unverifiable, exceeding the 3% (proposed threshold) material threshold and triggering automatic site suspension. The plan mitigates this through three-tier corroboration (attestation, customs records, physical inspection) and clean-room fallback examination, but each fallback layer is slower, costlier (USD 30–50M estimate), and depends on vendor cooperation or post-hoc forensics rather than preventive key custody.

Q7: Why does the plan explicitly exclude proof of 'absent hidden facilities' and total-capacity estimation, and what does this mean for the Go verdict's strategic implications?

A7: The plan's scope is limited to declared-equipment changes only (arrivals, removals, maintenance) at participating sites; it does not attempt to prove that no other equipment exists elsewhere or that the declared equipment represents a government's full inventory. This boundary is stated explicitly because verifying absence requires either intrusive inspections across all facilities or forensic supply-chain audits, which are infeasible bilaterally without legal frameworks that do not yet exist. A Go verdict means 'detected changes credibly at declared sites,' not 'no hidden capacity exists' or 'we know total capacity.' This limitation is intentional and defensible for Phase One but leaves a residual strategic vulnerability: either government could maintain undeclared equipment beyond the four participating sites, and the Consortium provides no assurance that declared sites represent a meaningful fraction of total deployment.

Q8: What ethical considerations arise from resident mirrored inspectors working continuously at counterpart sites, and how does the plan balance transparency against counterintelligence exposure?

A8: Resident mirrored inspectors stationed 24/7 at each other's sites maximize detection capability (directly observing unreported arrivals) but create high-value espionage targets. Ethical tensions include: (1) inspectors' safety and consent—they work in a counterpart environment under compartmentation rules that may isolate them professionally; (2) operator confidentiality—inspectors have access to sensitive facility information and must credibly shield it from exfiltration; (3) counterintelligence discipline—the plan requires vetting, tenure limits (6-month maximum), and insider-threat red-team testing, which can compromise inspector dignity and psychological safety if executed coercively. The plan addresses these through bilateral CI vetting, embedded host-country liaison oversight (monitoring boundary compliance, not inspecting inspector loyalty), and operator-consent tracking (public consent status in KPI dashboard). However, residual risk remains: an operator may perceive inspectors as intelligence collectors despite controls, eroding trust, or an inspector's family contacts abroad may trigger heightened scrutiny, creating psychological pressure.

Q9: What does it mean that the plan treats 'unresolved discrepancies >15 days' as both a Stop criterion and an automatic-suspension trigger, and what is the controversy around this dual logic?

A9: An unresolved discrepancy aged >15 days triggers two mechanisms: (1) automatic site suspension under enumerated triggers (not requiring bilateral co-chair consensus), and (2) a Stop-criterion candidate (contributing to the final Go/Modify/Stop verdict). This dual logic creates a controversial procedural tension: a single aged finding can cascade into operational shutdown (suspension) while simultaneously poisoning the verdict (Stop) without explicit principal review of the finding's substance. The controversy: does automatic suspension on age protect against obstruction (preventing one party from stalling indefinitely), or does it weaponize delay-based gamesmanship (a government can manufacture a minor discrepancy, let it age 15 days, and force suspension)? The plan mitigates this by requiring that discharge of the auto-suspension rule include a 'documented corrective action from the responsible government,' but the threshold for what constitutes 'corrective action' is not defined.

Q10: Why is the 'principal go/no-go checkpoint at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27)' described as having 'no teeth' despite being a decision point, and what is the risk if this checkpoint produces a deferral decision?

A10: The principal checkpoint at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27) is designed to force an explicit bilateral decision on whether to proceed with entry certification, defer Phase One, or stop the program if any of the seven entry conditions will not certify by Month 9 (2027-07-12). However, the checkpoint lacks 'teeth' because: (1) it is a bilateral decision point, not a unilateral escalation rule (either government can claim the other obstructed a condition, stalling the checkpoint decision itself); (2) no automatic consequence is defined if the checkpoint produces a deferral (e.g., does deferral trigger supplementary appropriation, or do both governments absorb sunk costs?); (3) the outer limit for entry certification is Month 12 (2027-10-12), creating a 4.5-month buffer after the checkpoint where conditions could slip without triggering another decision point. The risk: if the checkpoint produces a 'defer 2 months' decision at Month 7.5 (2027-05-27), Phase One start shifts to Month 11 (2027-09-12), compressing the 90-day operational window to 30–60 days (October–December 2027, overlapping winter holidays and staff leave). A shortened window reduces blind-exercise injection density from the planned 70+ injections to 30–40 injections, weakening detection-rate statistical power and forcing a Modify or Stop verdict despite adequate underlying capability.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

Either legal lead documents any required approval (legislative, appropriations or access authority) that cannot finish by Month 7.5 (2027-05-27) without a negotiating exception.
A2 Vendor-issued attestation keys will be validated within a 4-hour SLA by accredited examiners from both countries, and critical vendors will accept binding, keeping unverifiable equipment at or below 3% per site. Any vendor representing more than 5% of declared units declines binding or key custody validation, or median validation latency exceeds 4 hours.
A3 Inspectors, operators and both governments will observe the CHALLENGE-tag partition and the deadlock timers (5/8/13 days) in good faith, so manufactured or misclassified events and delay tactics cannot cascade into suspension or Stop. Build a two-country spend model by envelope with a draft CNY conversion rule and compensation ceilings, then run low, medium and high surge cases with the legal/audit working group. Either delegation declares in the workshop that it would reject a Modify or Stop outcome, publish its own score, or seek reopening of thresholds after results are known.
