Contradictions between the core documents, after repair.

Consistency: first pass found 1 high / 7 medium / 0 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 32 edits → 1 high / 6 medium; round 2: 47 edits → 1 high / 8 medium. Published: round 1 (fewest high-severity issues). Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (1 high / 6 medium / 1 low).

1. Late gate 'compresses' the 90-day window vs clock that starts only after certification, with a fixed verdict date (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Project plan, SMART Time-bound; canonical phase_one_window_and_baseline / gate outer limit: Project plan (Time-bound): clock starts Month 9 (range Months 6-12), runs Months 9-12, verdict at Month 12.25; entry certification outer limit Month 12. The 90 days starts only after all conditions are certified.
  • Review 1 #1, Review 2 #1, Review 4 #2, Review 10 #2, Self-audit #5 mitigation: A delayed gate 'compresses Phase One operational window from 90 days to 30-60 days'; 'shifting Phase One start to Month 11-12'; 'defer Phase One to Month 11'; 'exercise window from 70 days to 30-40 days'.
  • Why it conflicts: A clock that starts at certification cannot be shortened by a late gate. A Month 11-12 start would end near Months 14-15, so a verdict at Month 12.25 is impossible. The documents mix a fixed calendar verdict with a floating clock and a 'compressed' 90 days. The '70-day exercise window' also matches neither the calibration plus scored windows (about 2 months) nor the 90-day window.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the user constraint that the 90-day clock runs in full after certification. Define the verdict as clock end plus about 0.25 month, so Month 12.25 applies only to a Month 9 start. State the consequence of a later start (verdict, tranche 3 and tranche 4 dates shift), and drop 'compression to 30-60 days' wording. If a shorter window is wanted, treat it as a changed design and a double-key decision.

2. Supplementary appropriations vs USD 5B hard cap and Month 7 appropriation date (🔴 High)

  • Canonical total_budget_usd, fallback_fit_to_cap_and_dates, entry_condition_deadlines: USD 5.0B hard cap, 50/50; a supplementary appropriation exceeds the cap; appropriations are enacted at Month 7.
  • Review 4 #3, Review 5 #3, Review 10 #2, Review 11 #1, Self-audit #6: 'authorize supplementary staffing appropriation (USD 30-50M estimate) by Month 6'; 'authorize supplementary legal appropriation (USD 30-50M) by Month 6'; 'supplementary appropriation' for contingency/gate readiness.
  • Why it conflicts: A supplementary appropriation adds money above the hard cap, and it is scheduled for Month 6, before the base appropriation exists at Month 7. Several mitigations therefore rest on a funding source the plan excludes.
  • Suggested resolution: Replace 'supplementary appropriation' with in-cap options: double-key contingency draw (>USD 10M), envelope reallocation, or descoping/subset-of-pairs. Any request to raise the cap is a separate principal decision outside this plan.

3. What tranches 3-4 (USD 2.5B combined) fund vs 'Phase One only' vs Phase Two needing new money (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Review 14 #1-2; Exec summary Timeline and Budget; canonical tranche_schedule: USD 5B is allocated to 'Phase One only'; tranches 3-4 (USD 2.5B combined, USD 1.25B per country) release at Months 13 and 16 only after a non-Stop verdict and new double-key budget authorization.
  • Review 14 #1-2, Self-audit #15, Pitch Stakeholder Benefits: Phase Two 'requires USD 2.5-5.0B additional appropriation' (8-12 sites, 'USD 2.5B additional'); Modify corrective trials USD 500M-1.0B; 'tranche 3 releases automatically by Month 14' once criteria are met; Pitch claims 'full USD 5 billion accountability'.
  • Why it conflicts: Half the budget is held until after a 90-day test that ends at Month 12, yet the documents say Phase One alone uses the USD 5B and that Phase Two needs new money. It is not stated what tranches 3-4 pay for or whether Phase Two money counts inside or beyond the cap. 'Automatically by Month 14' also conflicts with canonical tranche 3 at Month 13 and with the new double-key authorization.
  • Suggested resolution: Decision required before the instrument is signed. Options: (a) tranches 3-4 are the Phase Two/continuation budget inside the cap, with scope and criteria defined by Month 11; (b) tranches 3-4 fund Phase One tail costs (verdict, adjudication, disposition closure, wind-down) and Phase Two is entirely outside the cap; (c) tranches 3-4 are unreleased reserve returned on Stop or Modify. Whichever is chosen, remove 'automatic' release and keep the double-key authorization.

4. Funding for entry-gate work before appropriations; sub-account availability (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical entry_condition_deadlines / tranche_schedule; Self-audit #18: Appropriations are enacted and tranche 1 released at Month 7. The USD 50M gate-readiness sub-account (inside contingency) is 'accessible only at certification' (Month 9).
  • Premortem FM1, Review 4 #3, Review 11 #1, Exec summary Risks, Review 3 #3: Gate-readiness draws are tracked 'before Month 6' (tripwire USD 40M); 200 staff cleared by Month 2; clean rooms operational by Month 6.5; entry-gate sunk cost USD 100-200M (estimate) absorbed in envelopes from Month 0.
  • Why it conflicts: Spending is scheduled from Month 0-6, but the envelopes, contingency and sub-account are funded by appropriations that exist only from Month 7. The sub-account is described both as usable before Month 6 and as available only at certification. No document identifies the source of pre-Month 7 sunk cost.
  • Suggested resolution: Decision required. Options: (a) each government bridges pre-appropriation work from its own budget as a pre-agreed national advance later credited to its contribution; (b) tranche 1 or the sub-account is released earlier than Month 7 by an interim authority; (c) pre-Month 7 early targets (vetting, clean rooms) move after Month 7 or shrink to what the sub-account covers. Whichever is chosen, state when the sub-account becomes available and what the USD 100-200M sunk cost is charged to.

5. Vendor binding, attestation dry-run and clean-room dates (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical entry_condition_deadlines, clean_room_cost_estimate; Review 3 #1; FM2: Vendor binding, site selection, inspector approval and schedule at Month 8; supplier-list declarations at Month 7.5; clean rooms operational by Month 9. Review 3 #1's own tracker lists 'vendor binding Month 8'.
  • Review 3 #3, Review 2 #2, Review 8 #1, Review 9 #3, Review 13 #2, Review 5 #1: 'Complete vendor binding and attestation-key validation by Month 7'; clean rooms 'by Month 6.5'; attestation dry-runs 'by Month 7' (Review 8) vs 'Month 8' (Review 5); 'Month 5.5' census compression.
  • Why it conflicts: The same milestone has two month numbers, sometimes in one review. Binding at Month 7 precedes the Month 7.5 supplier declarations needed to know which vendors exist, and falls in the instrument-signature month. Clean rooms at Month 6.5 precede tranche 1 (Month 7) and differ from 'operational by Month 9'. Only the Exec summary labels Month 7 and Month 6.5 as internal early targets.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep Month 8 as the binding deadline and Month 9 as clean-room operational readiness. Label Month 7 (dry-run, census) and Month 6.5 as internal early targets everywhere. Move the supplier-list-dependent census or binding step to follow the Month 7.5 declarations, and pick one attestation dry-run month.

6. Limit on misclassified challenge events (false positives) (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical detection_thresholds, challenge_partition: False-positive limit is TBD; tagged CHALLENGE events cannot trigger suspension, impaired-confidence review or KPI violation.
  • Review 2 #3, Review 10 #3, Premortem FM3, Pitch: 'more than 3 false positives' triggers impaired-confidence review; 'cap at <=2 per site per phase'; 'below 3 incidents per Phase One' vs 'exceeds 3 per site'; 'CHALLENGE misclassifications >=2 at any site' tripwire; 'false-positive tolerance enforced'.
  • Why it conflicts: Four incompatible limits (total vs per site; >3, <=2, >=2, =3) are given for the same event. 'False positive' also means both a misclassified exercise event and a spurious detection in the false-positive/negative KPI.
  • Suggested resolution: Decision required: set one limit, state per-site or per-phase and whether the bar is '>' or '>=', and calibrate it in the unscored exercises (Months 9.5-10.5). Name misclassified exercise events separately from KPI false positives.

7. Staff vetting: 200 cleared by Month 2 vs 2-3 month minimum and 6-12 month norm (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 4 #3, Review 5 #3, Review 13 #3, Self-audit #5: Vetting 'cannot be expedited below 2-3 months'; typical cycles 6-12 months (estimate); >=80% of target staff cleared by Month 8.
  • Review 4 #3, Review 5 #3, Review 13 #3, Premortem FM4: 'Begin expedited vetting on initial 200 ... by Month 1.5, clear at least 200 by Month 2' (Review 13); 'complete expedited CI vetting ... by Month 1.5' (Review 4); 'begin by Month 1' (Review 5); premortem early warning '<200 cleared by Month 2'.
  • Why it conflicts: A start at Month 1.5 with completion by Month 2 (or completion by Month 1.5) allows 0-2 weeks, against a stated 2-3 month minimum. Start dates also differ (Month 1 vs Month 1.5). The Month 2 date also falls before any appropriation.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the stated minimum vetting duration, then derive the interim milestone from it. Set one start date and an interim date at least the minimum duration later, and recalibrate the early-warning tripwire to the Month 8 gate of 80%. The pilot of 10-20 candidates per country should set the realistic cycle time.

8. Filter-schema lock and pre-test sequencing against the signed instrument (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 13 #1 body; canonical readiness_rehearsals, evidence_schema: Non-redactable schema is locked in the instrument at signature (Month 7); pre-test at Month 8.5 uses >=10 injected substitutions, target 9 of 10, halt if <85%.
  • Review 13 #1, Review 8 #3, Review 3 #2, Pitch Risks: Review 13 #1 title: pre-test 'Month 8.5 must precede operator-gateway finalization Month 7.5'; Review 8 #3: lock non-redactable fields 'by Month 7.5' (after Month 7 signing); Review 3 #2: '>=10 injected substitutions per event type'; Pitch: '>85% detection gate'.
  • Why it conflicts: A Month 8.5 step is required to precede a Month 7.5 step. The schema lock falls both at and after signature. Two sample sizes (10 vs 70) are given for the same pre-test. The pitch's '>85%' differs from 'halt if <85%' at exactly 85%. A failed pre-test would force renegotiation of an already signed instrument without an agreed path.
  • Suggested resolution: Lock the non-redactable schema at signature (Month 7). Treat filter-rule changes after the pre-test as double-key annexes. Use one pre-test definition (>=10 injected substitutions, target 9 of 10, halt <85%) and keep the 70-injection simulation as a separate Month 8 activity. Fix the reversed heading and the Pitch wording.

9. Thresholds locked at signature vs calibrated and frozen at Month 10.5 (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical exercise_schedule; Premortem FM9: Calibration exercises run Months 9.5-10.5; thresholds are frozen at Month 10.5 before scored exercises; figures are proposed until then.
  • Review 7 #3, Self-audit #3 and #11: 'Locking all provisional thresholds ... directly in the bilateral instrument (signed Month 7)'; 'any threshold change post-signing requires principal double-key re-authorization within 5 days'; 'any threshold change after Month 10.5 requires principal double-key reauthorization'.
  • Why it conflicts: Thresholds cannot be both final at Month 7 and calibrated against Month 9.5-10.5 data. A permitted double-key change after the Month 10.5 freeze also conflicts with FM9, where a threshold change after freeze is a tripwire and rejection of frozen thresholds closes the program.
  • Suggested resolution: State that the instrument locks the proposed thresholds and the calibration/freeze procedure. Values become final at Month 10.5, and a change after the freeze is a Stop-path event, not a routine re-authorization.

10. Verdict specification differs from canonical and premortem values (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical identity_confidence_threshold, unverifiable_threshold; Premortem FM9: Identity confidence >95% required per unit; unverifiable <=3% per site. FM9 tripwire: national score divergence >10 points on any event type.
  • Self-audit #11 mitigation: Identity KPI: 'acceptance = >=95% of units with >=2 layers agreeing'; dispute rule: 'if country scores diverge >5 points, convene technical referees'; parity 'for final 4 weeks'.
  • Why it conflicts: A per-unit confidence of >95% is a different metric from '>=95% of units agree', which would admit up to 5% disagreeing units against an unverifiable cap of 3%. Score divergence triggers at 5 points in one document and 10 in another, so the sealed-score dispute path is unclear.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep per-unit confidence >95% (provisional) and the 3% unverifiable cap. Keep the 5-point level as the referee trigger and the 10-point level as the FM9 tripwire only if both are labelled as stages, otherwise pick one. Mark all as proposed thresholds.

11. Pitch and long-term vision exceed declared-equipment verification scope (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical scope_exclusions, business_framing_not_applicable: Scope is declared-equipment change verification at participating sites only. No total-compute estimate, no hidden-facility proof, no foreign-hosted infrastructure, no comprehensive AI-governance regime. Partnership and promotional framing is not applicable.
  • Pitch: Collaboration Opportunities and Long-term Vision: Operators 'can federate with non-participating sites to define the broader AI-infrastructure landscape'; Phase Two '8-12 global' sites; 'integrated with broader AI-governance frameworks'; extend to semiconductor manufacturing, power systems, critical infrastructure; 'Vendor Partnerships', 'competitive' roles, 'relationship capital'.
  • Why it conflicts: Federating with non-participating sites and mapping the 'broader landscape' edges toward capacity and hidden-facility questions that are excluded. The long-term vision adds a comprehensive governance and multi-domain regime. Partnership and procurement language contradicts the not-applicable business framing.
  • Suggested resolution: Delete the federation item and the multi-domain, allied-expansion and governance-integration claims, or mark them explicitly out of scope. Replace 'partnership/competitive' wording with governance and fiscal-accountability language. Phase Two scope stays 'open'.

12. Timing of unverifiable-equipment suspension and challenge events in baseline days (⚪ Low)

  • Canonical auto_suspension_triggers, phase_one_window_and_baseline: Suspension requires unverifiable >3% of covered units for 5 consecutive days; Days 1-5 are reserved for the opening-inventory seal, with no challenge exercises or equipment movements.
  • Review 13 #2, Review 9 #3, Self-audit #20: Exceeding 3% 'at Phase One start triggers automatic site suspension ... before a single exercise injection'; suspension 'at Month 9.5'; 'by Month 9.25'; a 'misclassified CHALLENGE event during opening-inventory baseline (Days 1-5, Months 9-9.25)'.
  • Why it conflicts: Suspension is described as immediate, at Month 9.25, or at Month 9.5, though it requires 5 consecutive days. A CHALLENGE event cannot occur in Days 1-5 because exercises are barred then, and Days 1-5 do not span Months 9 to 9.25.
  • Suggested resolution: Use '>3% for 5 consecutive days' everywhere and give relative dates (Day 6 at the earliest). Remove the CHALLENGE-in-baseline cascade or recast it as a violation of the baseline rule.

Summary

The plan is largely consistent with the canonical facts on budget envelopes, tranche amounts, compensation share (USD 500M per country), deadlock and aging timers and the exercise schedule, and most earlier repairs hold. Remaining gaps concern money and time: the verdict date versus a floating 90-day clock, funding of pre-appropriation work, supplementary appropriations that breach the hard cap, and what tranches 3-4 actually fund. Several review recommendations still carry pre-reconciliation dates (vendor binding Month 7, vetting Month 2) and inconsistent false-positive limits. Three of the findings need a project decision rather than text edits: the pre-Month 7 funding source, the use of tranches 3-4, and the misclassification limit.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

Contingency was corrected: the USD 50M gate-readiness sub-account sits inside the USD 500M contingency, so a free-contingency fact (USD 450M, USD 225M per country) was added and the exposure comparison (USD 160-340M, or 260-540M with gate sunk cost) now uses 450M, with a note that a fully drawn sub-account pushes the high exposure case past the 375M trigger. Internal conflicts were resolved: the 10-day divergence suspension contradicted the Day 15 suspension rule and became impaired-confidence review only; the unverifiable threshold now reads >3% in both facts; and the exercise schedule no longer allows a threshold freeze (Month 11 = 2027-09-12) inside the scored window (Months 10.5-11.5 = 2027-08-27 to 2027-09-27). Basis texts that mixed old calendar dates with clock-start offsets (exercise schedule, vendor-refusal deadline) were rewritten as offsets from the Month 9 (2027-07-12) clock start, the headcount arithmetic wording was fixed (6 people per shift, 25.2 x 1.15 x 1.10 = ~32, x 8 = 256), and the matched-site basis was merged into site_set to stay within the fact limit. All other sums, products and dates (envelopes 5.0B, tranches 4 x 625M, 70 injections, Month 12.25 = 2027-10-20 verdict) were recomputed and retained.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
"The Consortium", a jointly governed United States–China mechanism with one narrowly defined mission: verify material arrivals, installations, removals, transfers, maintenance changes, and decommissioning of frontier-relevant computing equipment at a small, matched set of declared datacenters.

Assume both countries’ leaders believe uncontrolled frontier AI threatens national security and their continued political control. They provide direct political backing and sufficient domestic authority to compel participation. Do not assume trust, legal symmetry, or willingness to expose sensitive technology.

Phase One is a 90-day operational test, but its clock begins only after both governments have signed the bilateral instrument, appropriated their contributions, enacted domestic access authority, selected participating sites, approved inspectors, secured necessary operator and vendor participation, and adopted the provisional covered-equipment schedule. Treat these as mandatory entry conditions, not work performed during the 90 days.

Budget is USD 5 billion, contributed exactly 50/50: USD 2.5 billion from each country. Use this provisional allocation: USD 1.25 billion for secure ledger, attestation, evidence and communications systems; USD 1 billion for participating-site preparation and operator compensation; USD 750 million for inspectors, technical personnel, training and translation; USD 750 million for secure facilities, cybersecurity and counterintelligence; USD 500 million for independent testing, challenge exercises and red teams; USD 250 million for bilateral legal implementation and independent auditing; and USD 500 million for contingency and surge capacity. Every expense must map to an envelope. Compensation to domestic operators and vendors is administered by their own government and charged against its contribution.

"The Consortium" is a sovereign public-sector national-security program, not a for-profit project, business, nonprofit corporation, investment, partnership opportunity, or revenue-generating institution. If the report format requires business purpose, pitches, investors, customers, revenue, sponsorship, fundraising, return on investment, market demand, profitability, or promotional calls to action, mark them “Not applicable” and substitute mission justification, public value, strategic necessity, appropriations governance, and fiscal accountability.

Address only declared-equipment change verification at participating sites. Do not estimate either country’s total computing capacity, verify workloads, inspect model weights, prove the absence of hidden facilities, cover foreign-hosted infrastructure, or create a comprehensive AI-governance regime. Do not permanently anchor covered equipment to a current manufacturer, product, architecture, or performance unit. Accountable specialists must maintain a confidential, versioned technical schedule.

Governance must use equal national co-chairs and double-key authorization for budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension. No chair may have a casting vote, and no majority procedure may allow one country to overrule the other. Define deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures. Do not use a generic Project Sponsor, investor board, sponsorship coordinator or public stakeholder-satisfaction process.

Model staffing from participating-site count, shift coverage, mirrored national teams, separation of duties, leave coverage and surge requirements. This is not a small project team. Do not use single-person critical functions, part-time or temporary-agency inspectors, or fictional employee biographies. Include full-time mirrored inspection, technical, legal, cybersecurity, counterintelligence, translation, audit, logistics and adjudication units.

Create a replicated, tamper-evident ledger with independently verifiable national copies, immediate local event recording and bounded counterpart synchronization. Establish an Intake Protocol that verifies equipment identity in controlled staging areas before installation. Use layered evidence, potentially including independently validated cryptographic attestation, physical inspection, shipment and customs records, equipment identifiers, maintenance records, infrastructure changes and witnessed movement. No single source is decisive.

Protect workloads, customer data, model weights, network topology, security architecture, source code and unrelated infrastructure through bounded inspection zones and filtered evidence. Require operators to bind manufacturers, maintenance providers and logistics companies to reporting, confidentiality, escort and evidence-preservation requirements. When a critical vendor refuses, use vendor-supervised testing, filtered evidence, accredited independent examiners, secure clean-room procedures or validated attestations. If these cannot produce sufficient evidence, classify the equipment as unverifiable; if material, the site fails Phase One.

Define an Exit Protocol assigning every departure a disposition: witnessed destruction, verified permanent disablement, transfer to another participating site, documented release beyond the monitored system, or unresolved disposition. Never imply continued knowledge beyond the agreed boundary.

Run live exercises involving unreported arrival, substituted equipment, inaccurate records, delayed access, disputed identity, vendor refusal and a reluctant operator. Conduct tests in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without interrupting active computational work.

Organize the work breakdown around these top-level workstreams: bilateral authority and reciprocity gate; site eligibility and matched selection; inspectorate deployment and information barriers; intake and identity verification; ledger recording and synchronization; installation, maintenance and third-party access; exit and disposition verification; live challenge exercises; discrepancy adjudication and suspension; and the final decision. Do not substitute generic project-initiation, stakeholder-engagement, requirements-gathering or project-closure phases.

The KPI dashboard must cover blind-challenge detection by event type, false negatives and positives, equipment-identity confidence, event-recording and synchronization latency, ledger divergence and reconciliation time, reciprocal-access parity, unresolved discrepancy age, unverifiable equipment, vendor-refusal outcomes, IP or cybersecurity incidents, production disruption, funding timeliness and audit exceptions. Justify thresholds. Mark unsupported figures provisional or TBD and specify how they will be validated.

Conclude **Go** only if exercises demonstrate reciprocal access and credible detection; **Modify** if correctable weaknesses remain; and **Stop** if access is asymmetric, material equipment remains unverifiable, a government shields an operator, evidence systems diverge without resolution, or either country withholds funding. State that success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites.

Banned words: blockchain.

Prompt Screening

Verdict: 🟢 USABLE

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete, detailed project: a bilateral US–China equipment-change verification program with a USD 5 billion budget split into allocated envelopes, a 90-day test with defined entry conditions, governance rules, staffing model, workstreams, KPIs and Go/Modify/Stop criteria. Its formatting constraints are scope and style requirements for the plan, not attempts to manipulate the system.

Redline Gate

Verdict: 🟡 ALLOW WITH SAFETY FRAMING

Rationale: The prompt requests a governance, budgeting and verification-protocol plan for a bilateral compute-monitoring mechanism; this is policy-level planning, so help should stay conceptual and avoid operational detail on defeating or exploiting security controls, intrusion tactics, or sensitive technical specifics.

Violation Details

Detail Value
Capability Uplift No

Premise Attack

Why this fails.

Premise Attack 1 — Integrity

Forensic audit of foundational soundness across axes.

[STRATEGIC] A US–China body that verifies only equipment changes at a few declared, matched datacenters certifies the one thing a determined party would never risk (what it chose to show) while excluding hidden facilities, total capacity and workloads, so even its best result, a "Go", does not reduce the threat that justifies it.

Bottom Line: REJECT: Spending USD 5 billion on a double-vetoed, declared-sites-only equipment ledger buys a certificate that cannot speak to the threat it was created for, and it creates a standing intelligence interface between the two rivals.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The scope bars verification of total computing capacity, workloads and hidden facilities, so a clean ledger at the 'small, matched set of declared datacenters' is fully compatible with unlimited frontier compute elsewhere, and a 'Go' says nothing about the national-security risk the leaders fear.
  • Sites are chosen by the governments themselves and 'matched', and the live exercises run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas 'without interrupting active computational work', so the 90-day test measures detection in the least sensitive corners of the least sensitive sites and cannot extrapolate to anything that matters.
  • Every site finding, sanction and suspension needs double-key authorization with no casting vote, so the country whose site is implicated can block the finding against itself; the body is built to adjudicate violations yet gives the accused a veto over its own verdict.
  • USD 750 million (user constraint) is earmarked for secure facilities, cybersecurity and counterintelligence, plus mirrored inspectors from each side inside the other's frontier datacenters: the budget openly treats the inspectorate as an intelligence threat, so the mechanism doubles as an espionage channel that each state has reason to exploit and to exaggerate.
  • The 90-day test begins only after treaty signature, appropriation, domestic access law, site selection, inspector approval, vendor buy-in and the covered-equipment schedule are all complete, so the hard question of whether two rivals will ever accept these terms is answered before the USD 5 billion (user constraint) is spent, and the test then only proves a mechanism that already needed political consensus to exist.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Site selection becomes a contest to offer the least revealing facilities and the most favorable 'matched' pairs; each country's agencies treat inspector vetting as a counterintelligence opportunity and slow-roll approvals, so the entry conditions never fully close.
  • 1–3 years: The ledger becomes the only authoritative record, so unrecorded capacity migrates to undeclared sites and the declared set turns into a showcase, while both governments cite 'verified' status in public to deflect scrutiny of everything outside the boundary.
  • 5–10 years: The institution is entrenched with its own budget lines and legal standing, and either becomes a diplomatic shield for unmonitored AI buildup or collapses in a mutual accusation of inspector espionage that leaves less bilateral contact than before it was created.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Russia's suspension of New START participation (2023): Moscow announced it would stop implementing the treaty's inspection and verification provisions, showing that bilateral inspection regimes between rivals end when political interest does.
  • Case/Incident — Iran's removal of 27 IAEA surveillance cameras (June 2022): the IAEA stated it could no longer have confidence in continuity of knowledge about centrifuge and related production, showing how fast monitoring lapses once the host withdraws consent.
  • Case/Incident — Collapse of the Biological Weapons Convention verification protocol talks (2001): the US rejected the draft protocol, citing risks to proprietary commercial and security information, the same industry-secrecy conflict this plan tries to manage with filtered evidence.

Premise Attack 2 — Accountability

Rights, oversight, jurisdiction-shopping, enforceability.

[STRATEGIC] — Sealed Door, Open Barn: a USD 5 billion (user constraint) two-key mechanism that, by its own charter, verifies only declared equipment changes at a small matched set of declared sites, and so certifies the one thing a cheating state would never put on the table while staying silent on hidden facilities, total capacity, workloads and model weights, the things that decide whether frontier AI is controlled.

Bottom Line: REJECT: Sealed Door, Open Barn describes a mechanism that locks the entrance it chose to guard and says nothing about the barn behind it, while handing each rival a view of the other's supply chain and a veto over the verdict. A narrowly verified ledger at declared sites will be mistaken for control of frontier AI, and that false assurance is worse than no mechanism at all.

Reasons for Rejection

  • It conscripts private operators, maintenance firms and logistics companies that never signed the bilateral instrument, forcing foreign-state inspectors into their staging areas, shipping records and maintenance logs under domestic compulsion, with no consent from them or from the customers whose data sits next door.
  • Every budget, finding, sanction and suspension needs both national keys with no casting vote, so each government can stall any finding against its own operator and nothing outside the two capitals can compel a verdict; the mechanism sits in a gap that neither state's courts nor any neutral body can reach.
  • Once rival intelligence services have mapped each other's equipment identifiers, vendor firmware paths and datacenter supply chains through escorted access, that knowledge cannot be recalled, and the template of foreign inspectors inside commercial facilities will be demanded by every other capital.
  • The money buys a narrow, self-selected sample: compliant sites, declared equipment, a 90-day test that starts only after treaty signature, appropriation, domestic access law, site selection, vendor buy-in and a covered-equipment schedule are all complete, and a clean ledger at those sites says nothing about compute placed anywhere else.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0–12 (2026-10-12 to 2027-10-12) — The Gate Becomes the Project: the mandatory entry conditions (signed instrument, matched appropriations, domestic access authority, vendor participation) absorb all political energy, so the test itself is repeatedly postponed while the mechanism's existence is already being cited as progress.
  • Months 12–48 (2027-10-12 to 2030-10-12) — Copycats Arrive: other states and blocs demand equal inspection rights or build rival regimes, and the declared-site model teaches every actor that the safe place to put sensitive compute is any site that is not declared.
  • Months 48–84 (2030-10-12 to 2033-10-12) — Assurance Theatre: clean ledger results at participating sites are read by officials and the public as evidence that frontier compute is under control, easing political pressure while capacity grows outside the monitored boundary.
  • Months 84–120 (2033-10-12 to 2036-10-12) — The Reckoning: the discovery of significant equipment or capability outside the boundary, or a leak from an inspected zone, discredits the ledger, leaves each government holding a detailed map of the other's supply chain, and collapses the mechanism the way inspection regimes have collapsed before.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — New START: on-site inspections were suspended in March 2020, Russia barred inspections at its facilities in August 2022, and Putin announced suspension of the treaty on 21 February 2023 (Arms Control Association reporting, https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2023-03/news/russia-suspends-new-start); the bilateral inspection model failed when politics soured, with no neutral party to restore it.
  • Case/Report — Iran and the IAEA: Iran stopped voluntary implementation of the Additional Protocol on 23 February 2021 under a parliamentary law and threatened to delete camera recordings after a three-month holding arrangement (reported by IranWatch/IRNA and others, https://www.iranwatch.org/library/governments/iran/islamic-republic-news-agency-irna/iran-disable-iaea-cameras-if-sanctions-not-lifted-3-months); monitoring equipment and evidence are only as durable as the host's consent.
  • Law/Standard — IAEA INFCIRC/153 (model comprehensive safeguards agreement): rests on a standing neutral international inspectorate with its own reporting line, a structure the Consortium's two-key, no-casting-vote design deliberately lacks.
  • Narrative — Front-Page Test: a leak from an escorted inspection reveals that a foreign government's inspectors recorded a commercial datacenter's maintenance contractors and shipment routes, and the headline writes itself: 'Rival-state inspectors given a map of our AI supply chain.'

Premise Attack 3 — Spectrum

Enforced breadth: distinct reasons across ethical/feasibility/governance/societal axes.

[STRATEGIC] A USD 5 billion US–China inspectorate verifying only declared equipment at matched sites certifies nothing about undeclared compute, manufacturing confidence while the real threat sits outside its boundary.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A bilateral inspectorate that can see only what two rivals choose to declare, and can be silenced by whichever rival it accuses, buys the appearance of control and not control itself.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The mandate expressly excludes total-capacity estimates, workload verification and proof of no hidden facilities, so a spotless ledger at the declared sites is fully compatible with unlimited compute elsewhere, leaving the leaders' stated fear of uncontrolled frontier AI untouched.
  • Double-key authorization with no casting vote and no majority override over site findings, sanctions and suspension lets the accused country veto the finding against itself, so the body meant to name violations can be gagged by the violator.
  • The 90-day clock starts only after the treaty is signed, funds appropriated, domestic access law enacted, sites chosen, inspectors approved, vendors secured and the schedule adopted, so Phase One tests cooperation only after every contested concession has already been won.
  • Allocating USD 750 million to secure facilities, cybersecurity and counterintelligence concedes that the inspectorate is itself an espionage conduit, since mirrored teams sit inside the most sensitive datacenters of two adversaries holding evidence about their equipment.
  • Equipment identity rests on vendor attestation, maintenance records and shipping paperwork from manufacturers and logistics firms outside the Consortium's control, and a refusing critical vendor leaves only the label 'unverifiable', so evidence quality is governed by the parties least bound to supply it.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Entry-condition negotiations over the provisional covered-equipment schedule, site matching and inspector approvals consume the opening months, with each country trading access concessions for narrower definitions, so the schedule that emerges is whatever both sides could afford to be seen.
  • 1–3 years: A Go verdict on 'monitored changes at participating declared sites' is quoted in diplomacy and markets as proof of oversight, while compute migrates to undeclared sites and foreign-hosted infrastructure that the mandate cannot see, hollowing out the assurance it advertises.
  • 5–10 years: Hardware generations turn over, the double-key schedule fights stall every revision, one funder withholds its USD 2.5 billion share or shields an operator, and the apparatus becomes a vestigial, permanently suspended structure that has still embedded inspectors and ledgers inside two national security perimeters.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — New START on-site inspections (2020–2023): inspections were halted from 2020 and Russia suspended participation in the treaty on 21 February 2023, showing that bilateral verification between adversaries stops when political will lapses.
  • Case/Incident — Treaty on Open Skies withdrawals (2020–2021): the United States' withdrawal took effect on 22 November 2020 amid disputes over restricted access, and Russia's withdrawal followed in 2021, showing that reciprocal access regimes collapse over asymmetric access complaints.

Premise Attack 4 — Cascade

Tracks second/third-order effects and copycat propagation.

The plan builds an elaborate, USD 5 billion verification apparatus around the one thing that cannot threaten either leader's goals: declared, cooperative sites. Everything that determines whether frontier AI is "uncontrolled" (undeclared capacity, diverted chips, workloads) is excluded by design, while the genuinely hard problems (espionage, vendor control, adjudicating an accused party) are pushed into pre-conditions that, if solved, would make a 90-day test unnecessary. The result is a certification machine that converts a narrow, easily staged success into a false impression of control.

Bottom Line: Abandon the premise: verifying change events at a handful of declared, hand-picked sites cannot deliver control over frontier AI, and the entry-condition structure ensures the real obstacles (undeclared capacity, espionage, adjudication of the accused) are never tested. The flaw is in what the Consortium is defined to see, not in how well it is run.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The Declared-Island Illusion: verification is limited to equipment changes at a small matched set of sites the host governments themselves choose and declare. The risk both leaders fear lives in the undeclared remainder, which the plan expressly refuses to examine (no capacity estimates, no hidden-facility assurance, no foreign-hosted infrastructure). A perfect score proves only that cooperative sites behave cooperatively. Worse, the existence of a clean ledger gives each side a plausible-looking shield behind which to shift real build-out off-ledger.
  • The Pre-Solved Test Paradox: the 90-day clock starts only after the treaty, appropriation, domestic access law, site selection, inspector approval, vendor participation and covered-equipment schedule are all complete. Every decision that could actually fail is placed outside the test. What is left to 'test' is the operation of a system whose entire political and legal difficulty was assumed away. If these entry conditions can be met, trust and access already exist; if they cannot, Phase One never begins. The plan has no honest path from today to Month 0 (2026-10-12) of its own clock.
  • The Inspector-as-Sensor Trap: mirrored full-time inspectors embedded in the other side's most sensitive compute facilities are, structurally, the best-placed intelligence collectors either state could ask for. 'Information barriers' and 'filtered evidence' require the host to decide what is filtered, which is exactly what the inspector cannot trust, while the inspector's competence is the same competence that yields espionage. Counterintelligence units on both sides will treat every inspector as a presumed collector, so the inspection access that the Go criterion demands is eroded by the counterintelligence posture the plan itself funds.
  • The Double-Key Doorstop: equal co-chairs, no casting vote, no majority procedure and double-key authorization for budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension means the accused party holds a key to its own finding. Deadlock, impaired-confidence and automatic-suspension procedures can be defined on paper, but automatic suspension becomes a unilateral off-switch (any side can trigger a dispute and freeze the regime) while adjudication of a real violation requires the violator's consent. The body is simultaneously unable to convict and trivially able to be killed.
  • The Staged-Honesty Gap: live exercises run in staging, spare-inventory, maintenance or expansion areas without touching active computation, and are conducted by the same governments that control the sites, schedule and the 'blind' challenge pool. Both hosts know a 90-day test is under way and that a Go verdict is the political prize. Detection rates measured against short, bounded, non-production scenarios say nothing about a determined actor operating in production halls over years, and the plan's thresholds are 'provisional or TBD' by its own admission. Equipment identity also depends on vendor-supplied attestation and cooperation from firms subject to export-control and sanctions pressure, which neither government fully commands.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0-18 (2026-10-12 to 2028-04-12) (estimate): the entry-condition list consumes all the time and political capital. The bilateral instrument, domestic access authority, matched-site selection and covered-equipment schedule each become separate bargaining arenas, and each side trades site 'matching' against the other's most sensitive facility. The 90-day clock does not start; the program is described as 'on track' while only the pre-gate is progressing.
  • Months 18-36 (2028-04-12 to 2029-10-12) (estimate): to satisfy 'matched' selection, both sides nominate sanitized, purpose-chosen sites that are not representative of frontier build-out. Intake staging areas become theatre, the real procurement flows are routed around them, and inspector approval lists are filled with the least-risky, least-capable candidates, hollowing out the detection capability the KPIs claim to measure.
  • Months 36-48 (2029-10-12 to 2030-10-12) (estimate): Phase One runs and almost certainly produces Go or Modify, because both governments are invested in a positive result, challenge scenarios are bounded and operators were prepared. Public and allied narratives start to treat the Consortium as evidence that frontier compute is being governed, even though the scope statement says it covers only monitored changes at declared sites.
  • Months 48-84 (2030-10-12 to 2033-10-12) (estimate): off-ledger expansion accelerates because the ledger sites are now the 'legitimate' compute and everything else is outside the regime. Each side accuses the other of using inspection data for targeting or exploiting vendor supply-chain secrets; a single publicized IP or counterintelligence incident, or a disputed finding that the double-key rules cannot resolve, triggers automatic suspension, and the half-built trust is spent.
  • Months 84-120 (2033-10-12 to 2036-10-12) (estimate): the Consortium becomes a stranded USD 5 billion institution with entrenched mirrored bureaucracies, a ledger whose national copies disagree about disputed history, and no political path to either expansion (the hard problems remain excluded) or dissolution (leaders cannot admit failure). The most dangerous residual is false confidence: policymakers who believe verification exists will be slower to react to the compute build-out that matters.

Evidence

  • UNSCOM (UN Special Commission, Iraq, 1991-1998): a verification body with a Security Council mandate and intrusive access was brought down by allegations that its inspections had been used for intelligence collection. Iraq expelled the inspectors in December 1998 on the charge that UNSCOM had become a spy agency, and former chief inspector Scott Ritter has stated that US intelligence penetrated the teams. This directly parallels the Inspector-as-Sensor Trap, and in the Consortium the inspected party is a peer with a far stronger counterintelligence service. Sources: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/shows/unscom/etc/synopsis.html ; https://en.wikipedia.com/wiki/UNSCOM
  • New START (US-Russia): even a mature treaty with a well-defined, countable object (deployed strategic launchers), decades of inspection practice and a purpose-built compliance commission saw on-site inspections stop in 2020 (initially attributed to COVID-19), Russia suspend participation in February 2023, and the treaty was due to expire in 2026. Post-expiry status is not verified. Verification regimes that depend on continuing mutual consent dissolve when politics change, and compute is far harder to count and far more fungible than missiles. Sources: https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2023-03/news/russia-suspends-new-start
  • The plan itself concedes that it will not estimate total computing capacity, prove the absence of hidden facilities, verify workloads or inspect model weights. There is no directly comparable bilateral on-site compute-verification regime between rivals; the plan is dangerously unprecedented in its specific folly of treating change-logging at declared sites as a proxy for control.

Premise Attack 5 — Escalation

Narrative of worsening failure from cracks → amplification → reckoning.

[STRATEGIC] — The Lamppost Ledger: By design, the Consortium verifies only the equipment changes that adversaries have already agreed to show, at sites they chose, on a schedule they control, so it will manufacture a flawless record of the one place the danger is not and let two rival governments read that record as safety.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A jointly governed inspectorate that can only confirm what two adversaries chose to declare, cannot compel either of them to accept a finding, and will be sold as assurance it cannot provide has no right to exist. The gate is closed.

Reasons for Rejection

  • It embeds the other side's permanent, full-time, mirrored inspectors, translators and technical staff inside each country's most sensitive compute facilities, and compels operators, vendors and site workers to submit to adversary scrutiny under domestic authority they cannot contest; the people carrying that burden never consented to being the verification surface of a geopolitical rivalry.
  • Double-key authorization on budgets, protocol changes, site findings, sanctions and suspension, with no casting vote and no majority rule, means every adverse finding needs the consent of the party being found against; the plan itself names a government shielding its operator as a Stop condition, which concedes that the accountability structure has no mechanism to prevent the very failure it defines.
  • The mission explicitly excludes total capacity, workloads, hidden facilities and foreign-hosted infrastructure, so the monitored perimeter is the cheapest part of the system to cheat around: a compliant ledger at declared sites coexists with unlimited undeclared build-out, and a USD 5 billion jointly held evidence apparatus, ledger copies, clean rooms and vendor channels becomes a single high-value espionage and sabotage target for both sides.
  • The value proposition rots at the point of use: the plan's own caveat that success covers only monitored changes at participating declared sites will not survive contact with politicians, press and markets, and a 'Go' verdict will be consumed as assurance about frontier AI risk generally, converting a narrow bookkeeping tool into false comfort that discourages the harder controls it cannot replace.

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months — The Cracks Appear: The mandatory entry conditions (signed instrument, appropriations, domestic access law, matched sites, approved inspectors, vendor participation, covered-equipment schedule) stall on the first asymmetry dispute, so the 90-day clock never starts; each side briefs that the other is stonewalling, and the first inspector approvals are contested as intelligence vetting.
  • T+1–3 years — Copycats Arrive: If any exercise is declared a pass, other states and blocs demand equivalent matched-site mechanisms or claim exemption, while the declared-site model teaches both parties to route frontier build-out through undeclared, foreign-hosted or reclassified capacity that is outside the mandate by definition.
  • T+5–10 years — Norms Degrade: 'Verified' becomes a diplomatic currency; unresolved discrepancies and 'unverifiable equipment' findings are traded as bargaining chips under double-key deadlock, and the inspectorate's access is quietly treated as a licence to collect intelligence on the host's security architecture, vendors and supply chain.
  • T+10+ years — The Reckoning: A major undetected frontier capability emerges outside the monitored perimeter while the Consortium's ledgers show a spotless record, destroying the credibility of verification as a concept, leaving a hardened, institutionalized suspicion between the two states and no trusted instrument at the moment one is most needed.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — New START inspections: The only comparable US–Russia on-site verification regime saw inspections suspended in March 2020 (pandemic) and then barred by Russia at its facilities in August 2022, followed by Russia's 'suspension' of participation in 2023; the treaty's scheduled expiry was in February 2026 (post-expiry status not verified). A mutual inspection regime between rivals survived only as long as the political climate did (https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2023-03/news/russia-suspends-new-start).
  • Case/Report — DOJ 'Operation Gatekeeper' (Hao Global): The Justice Department announced in December 2025 the disruption of a network that moved roughly USD 160 million of Nvidia H100/H200 GPUs to China between October 2024 and May 2025, using straw purchasers, domestic warehouses, falsified export paperwork and fake-brand relabeling; about USD 50 million of chips were seized. This shows that equipment identity and paperwork can be forged at scale, and that diversion happens in the channels a declared-site ledger does not see (https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdtx/pr/us-authorities-shut-down-major-china-linked-ai-tech-smuggling-network).
  • Case/Report — UNSCOM in Iraq (1990s): The UN weapons inspectorate was publicly accused by Iraq of espionage, and in 1999 press reports said US intelligence had used the inspection mission to collect information beyond its mandate; the episode shows that adversarial access to sensitive sites is inherently dual-use and ends in expulsion and delegitimization (details not re-verified).
  • Principle/Analogue — Verification theory (arms control): A verification regime is only as meaningful as the share of the threat inside its observation boundary; a precisely bounded regime that is blind to undeclared activity gives high confidence in a small subset and creates a 'streetlight effect' that substitutes measurability for relevance.
